Oṃ, salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas together with his beloved; obeisance, obeisance.
Oṃ, salutation to the sandals of Śrīvidyā.
Oṃ, homage to Śiva.

Oṃ! That which is the Real, the supreme light, the mass of consciousness flashing within as "I," which otherwise causes the entire universe—consisting of the triad of Māyā and the rest—to blossom forth.
May that very Light, from which arises the consciousness— both transcendent and immanent, higher and lower— that is born as the moon of the Śaktis,
and which is the source of the principles beginning with Śiva and ending with Earth, stand for our prosperity.
Oṃ! [I bow] to the venerable Śrītraiyambakanātha, who is honored by the primordial gurus; likewise to the other, Somānanda; and then to the supreme, excellent guru, the illustrious Lakṣmaṇagupta.
I take refuge in the illustrious Cukhulaka, and likewise in the supreme Guru Śrī Śambhunātha, the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka named Bhinavagupta, and the venerable Bhaṭṭārikā. || 2 ||
Oṃ! May Heramba and Baṭuka praise my vital breaths (prāṇa and apāna) for the sake of prosperity—those two pure breaths that move externally and internally, sustaining the body. || 3 ||

Oṃ. That certain Consciousness, which is like nectar and pure by nature, is the form of the Śūla [the Trident] consisting of the Mātrās and so forth, within which the entire universe is contained as if reflected in a mirror. 4.
Oṃ! O Great Mother, my own chosen deity, who manifests as the unity of Śiva and Śakti;
whose nature is to move both externally and internally, and who is the embodiment of consciousness, action, and knowledge.
Śrīvidyā, whose limbs are full and who contains the syllables *sā* and so forth, grants the desires of her practitioners;
having entered me, may she utterly destroy the darkness of my ignorance. (6)
Having observed this work of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), composed both in prose and verse, all readers will understand it; we ourselves are not capable of such a task. (7)
Therefore, today I compose this *Vimarśinī*, which follows the path of prose, straight in its structure, shoulders of meaning, and filled with the fragrance of delight for the learned. (8)
Just as [the commentary] on the *Pratyabhijñā* composed by the venerable former teachers, numbering two hundred [verses], was [written] in accordance with the lineage of the Gurus; || 9 ||
Let them laugh or let them revile me, for I am truly born from the descent of power (śaktipāta); who would wish to obstruct the waters flowing down from the world? 10.
May the gurus forgive me; may others also be my companions in merit.
I compose this concise commentary according to the extent of my own understanding. (11)
Indeed, in this world, discerning persons, having placed within their hearts their own welfare, the welfare of others, compassion, and so forth, intend to engage in or desist from activity;
for [they act] based on the possibility of one thing being established through another, or its impossibility otherwise. Thus it is.
This established sequence of instruction from the masters of the scriptures is known as the traditional lineage-succession.

And yet, out of compassion for the sake of others, he is setting forth this treatise for the purpose of attaining the experience of identity with the Supreme Lord within himself, and for the occasion of attaining the full realization of all perfections in another.
The author introduces the subject matter of the treatise.
Oṃ! Having somehow attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara, he desires to bring benefit even to ordinary people.
I shall establish that recognition, which is the cause for the attainment of all prosperity. || 1 ||

Having somehow attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara immediately following a birth that transcends previous births, one attains the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of that Lord— the knowledge directed toward Him— which is the cause for the attainment of all perfections.
I establish [the practice] through the application of words and cultivate it in its true nature,
because I desire to benefit all people; for by repeated practice of that, and not merely by its existence, there is the accomplishment of whatever is desired.
Such is the application of the words of the sūtra and so forth.

2a) Thus, having stated the meaning in general, they speak of it specifically: "Now, in the phrase 'servitude to Maheśvara,' who indeed is this Maheśvara? Is it the body, or the insentient [matter], or the organs of knowledge, or the organs of action, or the vital breath, or the mind?"

Or egoism (ahaṅkāra), or intellect (buddhi), or the aggregate of these—thus they say. And regarding Maheśvara: he is indeed "Maheśvara" because he is both great (mahat) and a lord (īśvara); thus, he is Maheśvara.

He is endowed with a multitude of qualities such as sovereignty and the like; for this very reason, he is supreme, the most excellent, and thus "consisting of all. He is said to be all-pervading, the self-nature of all, and the self-nature that transcends all.
And likewise, in the very case of recognition.
In the Lord who is ultimately real, whose mind is the manifold variety of the universe, who is like a perfectly level wall, and who is untouched by any contradictory states.

But regarding the primordial subject, whose form is eternally manifest, what means of knowledge could there be? For he is the one who partakes in all cognitions, and thus no [external] appearance can exist apart from him.
The liberated one considers this common object of cognition as non-different from his own self, just as Maheśvara does; the bound one, however, considers it as having absolute difference.
Indeed, for all living beings, one's own Self alone is the Great Lord;
He is the universal form, nourished by the undivided reflective awareness that "I am this. (4)
Thus, desiring to abide in the form of the world appearing as jars, cloths, and so forth, that very will—by virtue of this cause—is both agency and action. (5)
And so it is said in the Tantrāloka:
His form is light that never sets, even amidst both lights and darkness;
he alone is within, and within him are both lights and darkness.
He alone is the supreme lord, the intrinsic nature of all existents.
The entire collection of existent things belongs to the Lord alone, and His power consists of that very nature;
moreover, power does not seek separation from the possessor of power. (3)
2b) There is an eternal identity between these two, just as between fire and its burning power.
That very one is the god Bhairava, characterized as the cause of the universe. 4.
For that which is reflected in its entirety within the mirror of her own self by means of her power—
of that very [Self], the Supreme Goddess is eager for the reflective awareness of her own nature;
she whose fullness in all things is neither deficient nor excessive.
This god is constantly eager for the pleasure of play with this goddess.
The omnipresent Lord simultaneously ordains diverse acts of creation and dissolution;
that he performs what is exceedingly difficult to accomplish is indeed unsurpassed.

This very sovereignty, which consists of the nature of consciousness, is autonomy itself. Indeed, the characteristic of the insentient is its limited nature; for consciousness, being distinct from the insentient, is not measured by limits.

Thus, for this autonomous [Lord], because of the non-differentiation from his own innate power, the processes of emission and withdrawal, though residing within his own self, abide as his very nature. (9)
As for this which is called "light" and is manifested everywhere, since it cannot be denied, what is the use of postulating means of knowledge regarding it? (10)
Even those means of valid cognition which extend the life-force of objects—their supreme life-force is that very same Supreme Lord. (11)
In the Kāmika, it is stated for that very reason that [the Lord] is free from causal discourse;
for that God of gods, there exists no dependence upon another.
Since it depends upon that [Self], this [mind] is therefore established as dependent;
yet, due to its omnipresence, it is all-pervading, eternal, and devoid of beginning or end because of its nature as a fundamental reality. || 13 ||
Because he possesses all forms, he is the illuminator of the manifold variety of the conscious and the unconscious;
therefore, his possession of many forms is proclaimed in the *Dīkṣottara*.
The world, the body, light, space, sound, and the mantra—Śiva is said to be sixfold when differentiated by the bindu, nāda, and so forth. (15)
Whoever is established in the nature of that which they contemplate attains its very state;
through the realization of the Word of Space and the rest, liberation follows—of this there is no doubt. (16)
Thus, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta has stated this many times in various places.
This is evident in the *Tantrāloka* and other works, as well as in the Upaniṣads.

"Verily, from bliss alone these beings arise; in bliss they grow; toward bliss they are led; into bliss they enter. For bliss alone becomes the slayer and the benefactor—this is Brahman. 'Bliss,' [he says]. Knowing the bliss of Brahman, one does not..."

"And from what shall he have fear? [The answer is: "He who knows the bliss of Brahman, from whom words together with the mind return without reaching it, has no fear from anything whatsoever. [And: "From whom indeed all these beings are born, by whom, once born, they live, and into whom they enter at death."

"That into which they dissolve—seek to know that; that is Brahman. Regarding this, the name "Brahman" is derived from the root *bṛh*, meaning "to grow. Being endowed with multiplicity while remaining in oneness, or by virtue of its perfecting [all things], it has attained growth and is thus called Brahman.
And so it is:
"Salutations to the Lord who always delights in creation, who always sits facing the face of maintenance,
and who always holds the staff for devouring the three worlds."
And by such [passages] as: "In the mind of universal variety, which is comparable to a level wall-surface," and so forth.
In this way, through recognition, it receives the designation "Brahman."
And for this very reason, because it sustains both [consciousness and matter], there is the designation of the neuter gender for the intellect (*cit*) and the non-intellect (*acit*).
But there is no contradiction in the fact that Śiva’s gender would be neuter because he is Brahman; so, enough of this.
And so says the Veda: "Prajāpati moves within the womb; being born, he shines forth in many ways. The wise behold his source; they abide in him."

3b) All the worlds. I know this great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness. Only by knowing him does one pass over death; there is no other path for going. Those who [worship] the deity Ātapat. He who...
The domestic priest of the gods, who was born before the gods.
And not for the sake of mere brilliance did the gods produce the Brahmic brilliance at the beginning;

they spoke of that knowledge which belongs to the gods. The gods were his will; Fortune was his splendor and Fortune was his beauty. Day and Night were his two wives. The stars were on his side. The Aśvins were his form, pervading all.
The half-months, months, seasons, and years do not touch him; he stands firm.
No one beholds his form with the eye; only he who has been kindled by the heart, by insight, and by the mind, knows him. Those who know this become immortal. Hiraṇyagarbha.
"In the beginning, he who was born from the existent became the sole lord of all that exists. He supported this earth and this heaven.
To which god shall we offer our oblation? and so forth.
And so it is said: "Just as a crystal takes on the form of various colors through impurities, even so does the Lord assume the forms of gods, humans, animals, and plants."
Just as the reflection of the moon moves in the water while the moon itself remains motionless,
so too does this Great Lord, the Self, move through the aggregate of the body, the senses, and the world.

Within that [body], there exists this entire universe— a continuous stream of diverse bodies, organs, and worlds— and the enjoyer therein is Śiva himself, who has assumed the state of a bound soul (paśu).

By such means, this Paramaśiva, the Supreme Lord, whose multitude of qualities has been proclaimed in many ways as the essence of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-sāra*), is established as the inconceivable consciousness (*cintācintya*) of all, the Great Lord who is one's own Self (*svātmā*). Being the very seed of everything and consisting of that [Self], He is called the "Principal Seed" (*bījapradhāna*).

"Having a beginningless, incomparable nature"—thus it is stated in the *Gītā*. Furthermore, [it is taught] by the Sāṃkhyas and others under the guise of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; by the Mīmāṃsakas under the guise of ritual action (*karman*);
and by the logicians (*tārkika*) under the guise of inference (*anumāna*) and so forth.
The beginningless path is Brahman;

and by means of the conceptualization of the gods, the intellect, and the vital breath, as well as through the essence of the sacred teachings, that which is established as the object of valid cognition is indeed [realized] through the very nature of valid cognition. That nature is purely non-avidyic.
The cause of the impurity on the face of the stainless mirror is indeed its own time of soiling; O Goddess, [this is] the laughter of the gods.
And likewise, in the *Muktāvalī*: "Ignorance is the womb from which manifold non-existent things appear as if real."

Arising for a moment, they go to dissolution in the single ocean of consciousness. If the causality of clay and other materials toward a jar is not accepted, how can the causality of ignorance be established by those who possess true knowledge? And so it was said by the venerable Vasiṣṭha:
In that mirror of consciousness, all things are reflected;
as stated by the Blessed One: "Just as there are many currents of its own velocity," and so forth.
Therefore, it is not otherwise than that.

4a) Thus, because it shines forth in many ways and is pervaded in many ways, it is called *virāj*, having undergone manifold transformations. Now, one might ask: how can there be manifold transformation for that which is a single entity? It is because of the very oneness of the One, and because of the non-oneness of the many.
Because it is understood through words; for example, there is the understanding of a single form in such expressions as "this is a cow" or "this is a cow."
"Likewise, look at these cows sitting in the garden."

[The opponent asks: "In this case, since there is multiplicity of the many, how can the multiplicity of the one be understood through this [statement]? To this it is replied: In all Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, Yoga, Vyākaraṇa, and other [texts], the understanding of the multiplicity of the one is established.
For thus it is: To Him who, having transcended birth, perceives the sequence [of cause and effect] and so forth, and who is the knower of all objects;

to Him who is praised by the gods; to the first poet, the heart of Brahman—to Him, at whom the deluded are bewildered; in whom the threefold creation is false, there being an exchange of fire, water, and earth, through His own power.
We meditate upon the Supreme Truth, which is eternally free from deceit. || 1 ||

In this regard, the birth and other origins of this world have been declared in the Purāṇas and other texts; by this, although there is oneness, its manifold nature is indeed established. Furthermore, [He is] "I," who am cognizant of all objects by way of His own essential nature; He who is the first creator of Brahmā and the giver of the Vedas and so forth; and in whom even the wise are bewildered.

"From which speech turns back, along with the mind, not having attained it"—just as there is an illusory transformation of fire, water, and earth, so too the world is false in that Brahman. By its own light, what indeed is established as second? That very one who is thus non-dual.
We shall meditate upon—that is, we shall contemplate—the Brahman which is Truth, Existence, and Bliss, the Reality, the Abode, and the Immortal. We praise it;

that is to say, for the sake of the pacification of all obstacles. Or, as it is said: "In the abodes situated one below the other, which are distinct and numbered, there is but one Bindu, and yet it appears as many in others."

[The number] ending in five is placed on the right; having positioned that number on its own back, one adds it to one side. By such means, the manifestation of multiplicity from a single entity is established.

Having formed a *bindu* and anointed it with the *yugamātra* [measure], one should meditate upon that which is above and below; according to this supreme instruction, once the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) has been realized through the path of the highest teaching, one should contemplate the *kuṇḍalinī* in the form of a triangle.
The three drops, the three corners, and the *sūtti*— the very nature of which is the cognition of the phonemes from *a* to *kṣa* in the form of script.
Because it is the support (*ādhāra*), the nature of that triangle is the path of instruction known as the *Saddhośa*.

Just as there is a single meaning for one [word] through its manifold applications—from the sense of a single *yava* up to the limit of thousands, lakhs, and parārdhas—so too is it with the Sāṅkhya: "Root-nature (*mūlaprakṛti*) is not a modification; the Great One (*mahat*) and the others are both natures and modifications."
There are seven evolutes, and the group of sixteen is an evolute; the Puruṣa is neither a primary cause nor an evolute.
Thus, in this case, the multiplicity of that which is indeed one is established. And furthermore:
In that very same [text].

"From the specific determination of the instruments of birth and death, and from their non-simultaneous operation; the plurality of Puruṣas is established, as well as from the reversal of the three guṇas," and so forth. Thus, in all such passages as those mentioned, the manifold nature of that which is essentially one is well known.

Even poets describe the multiplicity of a single face or of the moon, as in "the lotus-face" (where the face is the moon), or "that which is the face is the moon. In this very way, they describe manifoldness; and it is the same for the moon as well.
Behold the moon-like face, like the orb of the moon, a lotus in the lake of the center of the sky.

By such statements as these, what indeed would poets not say? And so too the grammarians. For example: "The eighteen-fold nature of the vowel *a* consists of short, long, and protracted forms; through the union with the vowels *ai*, *au*, and *an*; and by the distinctions of nasalization. Thus, for a single [vowel].

The eighteen-fold nature of the *kāra* (the sound *k*) and its role as a *saṃskartṛ* (agent of refinement) is well-established as consisting of one hundred and eight forms within the various systems of Pāṇini’s successors, such as Vararuci. For example, regarding the forms *saṃskartā* and *saṃskartā*, [the rule] applies: *samaḥ suṭi*.

5a) For instance: "The aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), the emotional state (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and the cessation of emotion (*bhāvaśānti*) and so forth, exist as a non-sequential whole;

they stand as the objects of ornamentation (*alaṅkārya*) distinct from the ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) such as *rasa* itself. In this context, *rasa* is said to be the life-force of both verse and prose, possessing the alternative name "suggestion" (*vyañjaka*).

Those who know the reality of aesthetic flavor (*rasa-tattva*) maintain that *bhoraṭa* is a synonym for *paryaṅka*. By means of this, the essence of relishing (*carvaṇātman*), which is like the resonance of a bell (*ghaṇṭānuraṇavat*), is to be awakened and heard everywhere;
for without it, there would be an absence of the effect, and thus it must be understood wherever [the flavor arises]. Indeed, it is not lifeless.
"The body has been used up somewhere. Thus should he speak to those endowed with ornaments.
5b) Who is the fashioner? Who is the fashioner? || 1 ||

In that case, one does not perceive even the two forms consisting of three *s* sounds, including the pair of doubled *s* sounds. || 3 ||

The suffix *śara* [is applied] after the three [roots], and *khaś* after *ka*, *dvi*, and *iṣat*. (6)
Then, when the anusvāra itself is doubled for those [consonants] that possess an anusvāra, there are twelve [variants]. 12.

Thus, there are one hundred and eight [mantras] for each single [deity]. The sense is: how could there be two?

Therefore, by this, there are one hundred and eight varieties. The sense is that one should understand here as well how it is that they do not become fewer than one. Likewise, for those whose souls are satiated by the relishing of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and ornaments, even Mammaṭa, Jalaka, and others [describe] ten thousand [varieties] of a single aesthetic flavor alone.

The nature of its own form (*svarūpatva*) is indeed made manifest. [In this case, although the leaf was written indistinctly, it has been written here clearly. Thus, in examples such as "cow" (*gavādi*), there is the distinction of the word-meaning (*abhidheya*). || 118 || [In that very place]
For instance, [the aesthetic experience] is incapable of being restricted to rasa, bhāva, their semblances (tadābhāsa), or their subsidence (śānti), and so forth;
and thus indeed [it has been stated] by the venerable Abhinavaguptapāda himself in the *Dhvanyāloka*.

"Others, such as those called Bhāskara and so forth, have declared the non-existence of that which was previously proclaimed by the wise as the soul of poetry (*kāvyātman*)—the *dhvani*—and [the existence of] ninefold *rasa*. But that [soul]... [and so on].
Here, the soul of poetry is *dhvani*; it is said to be of nine kinds of *rasa*. And that...
The erotic, the heroic, the pathetic, the marvelous, the comic, the terrible, the loathsome, and the furious—these are the [eight] rasas;
the peaceful (śānta) is also remembered as the ninth.
And yet:

He states the essential nature of rasa: "Now, those causes, effects, and concomitants which exist in the world as the permanent moods (sthāyins) such as love (rati) and so forth—if they appear in drama and poetry, they are called excitants (vibhāvas), ensuants (anubhāvas), and transitory moods (vyabhicāriṇas); and when these very factors are manifested by the excitants and the rest, [they constitute rasa]."

"The essence of *rasa* is traditionally held to be the state of being devoid of purpose (*anartha-yī*); such is the nature of *rasa*. Its divisions are one hundred and five. To explain: there are two types of that whose expressed meaning (*vācya*) is not intended to be conveyed (*avivakṣita-vācya*), namely, that in which the expressed meaning is transferred to another meaning (*arthāntara-saṃkramita-vācya*) and that in which the expressed meaning is completely set aside (*atyanta-tiraskṛta-vācya*). (51)" Thus it is said. These are the two divisions of that whose expressed meaning is not intended to be conveyed.

But that which arises from the sequence is rooted in the power of suggestion (*śabdaśakti*); it is of two kinds, namely, based on poetic figures (*alaṅkāra*) or based on the subject matter (*vastu*). Thus it is [as follows]. (5)

Among those, the type based on the power of meaning (*arthaśaktimūla*) is threefold: that which arises spontaneously (*svatasambhavī*), that which is fashioned by the poet’s own creative intuition (*kavipratibhānirmita*), or that which is communicated through a character created by the poet (*kavinibaddhavaktrapratipādita*). These varieties are further divided into two types—either a fact (*vastu*) or a figure of speech (*alaṅkāra*)—resulting in six kinds of suggestors (*vyañjaka*). Among these:
Thus, there are twelve [types] including the suggested (vyaṅgya) varieties of *vastu* and *alaṅkāra*, doubled; however, that which is rooted in the power of both [word and meaning] is only one.

Thus, there are twelve types based on the power of the meaning (artha-śakti-mūla). [12] Thus, those based on the power of both (ubhaya-śakti-mūla) [are added]. [13] Together with the five preceding varieties, they become eighteen. [18]
Since the eighteen [topics] are twofold by virtue of being manifested through words and sentences, there are thirty-six.

36. From among these, one distinction must be excluded because that which is rooted in both powers lacks the quality of being manifest through words. Therefore, there are exactly thirty-five. 35. Consequently, even in a literary composition, it resides within the power of the meaning (artha-śakti).

There are twelve [types] based on the power of meaning (*artha-śakti-mūla*) as occurring within a composition (*prabandha-gata*). Thus, there are forty-seven [in total]. Following that, since rasa and the like exist even in individual words, parts of words, phonemes (*varṇa*), and stylistic arrangement (*racanā*), there are [further types] of the suggested meaning whose sequence is imperceptible (*alakṣya-krama-vyaṅgya*) as occurring in parts of words and in stylistic arrangement.
There are four varieties based on whether they pertain to the phoneme (*varṇa*) or the power (*śakti*), and whether they pertain to the individual instance (*prabandha*).

Thus, there are fifty-one varieties in the Bhāskārī. Of these—meaning of those fifty-one pure [varieties]—by multiplying them with their own fifty-one subdivisions, there are twenty-six hundred and one varieties. Of these...

Furthermore, by multiplying [the previous number] by four—consisting of three types of *saṅkara* (blending), namely: as doubt, as the relationship of principal and subordinate, and as the mutual penetration of a single phoneme (*ekavyañjanānupraveśa*), and one type of *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture)—there result ten thousand plus four hundred and four. Of these:

When combined with the fifty-one forms consisting of the pure divisions, the result is five hundred and forty-one (541). [And so it is stated in the Trika scriptures and other texts: "In the abodes of the number of divisions situated one below the other, there is one dot (*bindu*) even among those previously mentioned..."]

"One should cast the prayer at the end and that [instruction] upon one's own back; thus, with wisdom, one should cast them as a single unity," and so forth in many ways. In this manner, there are ten thousand varieties of a single rasa alone.
Nevertheless, these have been stated here merely by way of illustration, for fear of making the book too voluminous.
Enough with this, for fear of prolixity. And thus, power resides in the *tattva*.

7b) [The syllables] beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, starting from the beginning in successive order, are joined with one another in pairs and triplets; these deities, beginning with *ā* and *ī*, are like sprouts.
"In the Triple City (Tripura), there are indeed names that are internal secrets;
beyond those twenty thousand names of Bhairava’s consort, there is the Supreme Radiance.
By this [verse], the Goddess possesses twenty-one thousand names. Enough of this digression.
By this mere praise and by this mere digression, the orientation has been illustrated.
Now let us return to the subject at hand. Thus, when the one Supreme Lord is established, and having somehow attained His servitude—somehow.

After some time had passed, the Blessed One himself gave this instruction to his own devotees: "Know that the wise who see reality will impart knowledge to you through prostration and through inquiry itself. And then, each of them...
Beholding the Guru as the Guru, and having approached him—

just as one seeking honey [approaches a tree], or as the Self [approaches] through tradition— and by means of the grace of the pure intellect arising immediately from association with him, prostration, inquiry, service, and so forth, [one attains] that which is difficult to obtain within.
Because of the state of being a servant of the Supreme Lord.
By the power of wholesome karma that had matured immediately following hundreds of thousands of previous births accumulated in the past.

A *dāsa* is so called because servitude (*dāsya*) is bestowed upon him according to his desire. Furthermore, by means of the root *dasu*, "to cast down," one casts aside the blindness of ignorance; then, through contact with the rising sun of knowledge, one relishes the attainment of that very immersion (*samāveśa*).
The meaning is: having relished the state of being the Supreme Lord through the contemplation of identity with one's own self.

And he who is our supreme preceptor—[the sense being that we ask him]—having approached with water for the feet (*pādya*), [in this context, the grammatical construction is joined as follows]: by means of the suffix *ṇic* according to the rule beginning with "after roots ending in vowels," etc., having attained—that is, having resorted to—the state of servitude to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) by his own self; for this is the supreme cause.

And having attained [this state], O Supreme Lord, the engagement of worldly speech occurs through a mind that has become identical with the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) [of the deity]; this is the meaning of what was said regarding the utterance of words. And on that very point, it was stated by [the Lord] himself:
8a) Previously, you [scholars] there have indeed led, caused to circulate, and reflected upon this in your *Svasūtravimarśinī*. For instance:

Even though this [realization] comes into the range of one’s own heart as if for the sake of the Supreme Lord himself— belonging to one upon whom the descent of Śiva’s power has firmly descended— nevertheless, what human effort (*puruṣakāra*) can possibly accomplish there? For even that [effort] is [like] blind darkness in that regard.
[Because this [world] is not illusory (*amāyeya*), being of the nature of pure light (*śuddhaprakāśarūpa*),
since it is impossible for it to be an object of error (*pratyapāyatānupapatteḥ*)?]. By this [statement],
how did they previously state this, and how indeed was it stated again?
The statement that [the suffix] *ṇic* occurs after a root even when another [verb] follows, having reached [that other verb], is a mere error.

Nevertheless, since the words of the Lord himself [of the supreme gurus whose very nature is the Lord] are more authoritative, what else can we know? Enough with this unveiling of secrets. And thus it has been stated by the Lord himself:
As stated in such passages as, "At the end of many births, one endowed with knowledge takes refuge in Me," and so forth.

Furthermore, in the *Sūtravimarśinī*, it is stated: "Because that [impurity], which belongs to Māyā and resembles blinding darkness, cannot possibly approach its own opposite, which is of the nature of pure light," and so forth. Thus, enough of this; for these great souls [derive their authority] from none other than the Great Guru.
"Should even negligence be tolerated by those like us? Or rather, what do we know of such a secret practice?

Even the causative *ṇic* affix (*hetumaṇṇic*) is more authoritative; the meaning is that the causative affix following *vāśurā* and others is most authoritative. In reality, however, only the causative *ṇic* is the authority."

"Everything [is established] because the treatise possesses a logical reason. Having said this, I shall now demonstrate that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which is the cause for attaining the attainment of all prosperity.

And all those are the perfections (*sampad*). Their "attainment" (*samavāpti*) is the attainment of that which has the nature of unifying the manifest and the unmanifest—such as blue, yellow, and so forth; it is the cause for that [attainment].

Because the experience arising from its recitation possesses a contracted intentionality within the heart, it is the cause for the attainment of absorption (*samāveśa*) therein; therefore, it is said to be "the cause of that. And thus: "The lights of the lamp of scripture illuminate something [of it] for him."

For it has been stated [in the scriptures]: "She is from the heart," and so forth. And I shall establish that very recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which serves as the cause for attaining proximity to the Supreme Lord. Proximity to the Supreme Lord.

The sense is: "I cause [him] to reach [that state]. Regarding that very Maheśvara who has become thus, there is knowledge directed toward him (*pratīpa-abhimukhyena*). It is by way of direct perception (*pratyakṣatayā*), as in: "This is Devadatta," or "This is Śuklavāsas Vāmanadatta," and so forth; or as in: "This is a jar."
The meaning is: "I establish this through direct perception, and I also illuminate other [matters] by means of that."
This doctrine— that by entering the unsurpassed path,
through the observation, experience, and reasoning of the Pratyabhijñā scriptures,
supreme sovereignty becomes as manifest as a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand— is clearly proclaimed.
This objection is raised with respect to those who are awakened; however, for those who are unawakened, there is no such thing as a lack of [the teaching].
And so it is stated in the Siddhāntārtharatnāvalī: "I experience non-duality as clearly as a myrobalan fruit held in the palm of my hand;
thus, both this life and its manifestation are entirely pacified."
And thus it is well known: "Is it so? [The answer is: "It is so."

Even words of instruction, though they have entered the heart and are intended to restrain it, are powerless against those in whom [passion] has taken deep root. Can the downpours from the clouds, even when clinging closely and without interval, impart moisture to lotus leaves?

By such statements as these, and by the saying, "The path is that which the great multitude has traveled," everyone here has the right [to practice], regardless of whether they are unawakened, awakened, or self-awakened.

Therefore, this doctrine is clearly established: that whatever enters into the state of immersion in the experience of recognition becomes manifest as direct perception. And so it is said: "The jar knows itself as the Self, and I too always know myself as the jar."

"I know through the self that is Śiva, and I know as the self that is Śiva. And in the *Spandakārikā*: "Since the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything because it is the source of all states of being, and because it attains identity with them through the nature of their awareness, there is no state whatsoever in which it does not [participate] in the contemplation of words and their meanings."

"Śiva alone is the enjoyer, existing everywhere at all times in the form of the object of enjoyment"—when one possesses this realization regarding the Vāyu [principle], perceiving the entire world as being of the nature of *kṣiti* (the earth), he is equanimous, disciplined, and liberated while living; of this there is no doubt. Furthermore, these [verses] are found in the *Pratyabhijñā* itself.
The manifestation of entities appearing as present occurs only through their existing internally, even while they appear externally.
Just as before, the object would not be manifest without having the nature of manifestation;
nor could the manifestation be distinct from the self-nature of the object’s manifestation. (2)
If manifestation were both differentiated and non-differentiated, there would be a confusion of objects;
for an object whose nature is manifestation cannot exist as non-manifestation, nor does it desire to be so.
The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of "this," which is [initially] fragmented, is that repose within one's own essential nature; this is the reflective awareness [expressed as] "I am. (4)

Thus, even with respect to an object that is non-different in terms of space, time, and so forth, the cognition whose essence is internal reflective awareness (vimarśa) directed toward a single designation is uncontradicted in its reality.

Some hold that both the causal suffix (*hetumaṇṇic*) and the reflexive suffix (*svayaṃ*) apply here; others maintain that even another suffix may apply, as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) has authority in all cases. Indeed, the repose of the Light within itself is proclaimed to be the state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*).
And that very repose has been described as the cessation of all dependence.

"Autonomy, agency, and primary sovereignty as well"—by such statements as these, it is established that everywhere the non-dual Light, whose body is consciousness, the ultimate reality, unfolds at all times. May there be auspiciousness! (7)

And therein, there is not even the slightest trace of thought regarding the knower, the known, or the act of knowing. Thus, by this [verse], the state of being the cause for the attainment of all perfections (*samasta-sampat*) has been demonstrated for *pratyabhijñā*. And so, the state of being the cause for the attainment of all perfections has been demonstrated for the Supreme Lord.

[The compound] *pratyabhijñāyāḥ* is a genitive *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*. However, if it were a *bahuvrīhi*, it would mean "that recognition for which the attainment of all perfections is the cause. Therefore, by resorting to the *bahuvrīhi*, the blue face and so forth constitute the means (*upāya*) for that recognition.

Since everything manifests as the very nature of consciousness, it is through the knowledge of that [consciousness] that it is attained; thus, this path of instruction is established. By means of the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound, however, the sense is that the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of the Supreme Lord is the external cause for the attainment of each respective [state]. Likewise...
And by the compound *asmad-parameṣṭhi-pādāraṃ*, the form [of the word] is indicated by means of a *bahuvrīhi* [compound], as in the passage beginning with "it is indicated."
Thus, the first meaning of the initial verse beginning with these words is established.

Now, as for the purpose of others: having somehow attained service to Maheśvara—the cause for obtaining all forms of prosperity—and desiring to be of benefit even to ordinary people, [the author] establishes the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of that [Lord]. This is the connection [of the verse]. For it is because...
The sense is that, by virtue of having Maheśvara as one's servant, there is indeed the attainment of all prosperity.
But it is not the recognition of Him that serves as the cause for the attainment of all prosperity.
For some maintain that once Maheśvara’s nature as one's own servant is established, the arising of the recognition (pratyabhijñā) of Him occurs.

And yet, the meaning follows from the mouth of the Guru: having somehow attained the servitude of Maheśvara for oneself, and [having attained] Śiva and so forth; likewise, having attained—that is, having reached—the servitude of Maheśvara. The sense is "having sought to attain."

And likewise, desiring to benefit people, I shall establish that very recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which is the cause for attaining all perfections (*saṃpad*). For it is precisely that [recognition] which possesses the quality of being the cause for attaining all perfections. Furthermore—

And she is the cause of benefit even for ordinary people; indeed, she alone generates the state of servitude toward Him. Therefore, the former teachers maintain that she alone is the cause in all cases. And so it was stated previously: "By those various [means], she is approached..."

Just as a lover, though standing nearby and approached by the slender maiden with various gestures, remains unrecognized as if he were an ordinary person among the crowd; even so, the Self, the Lord of the Universe, though His qualities are perceived by the world, is not recognized, and thus He is not able to manifest His own vast majesty.

That [recognition] has been declared; for that very purpose, this [recognition] is taught as the cause for the attainment of all prosperity and so forth. And because this entire mass of phenomena, having attained expansion by virtue of being a surging mass expanded through light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), [exists].
This world is indeed that which is designated by the term "this"; otherwise, it would not exist, like a sky-flower and the like.
It may be so. Therefore, the surging waves and the like, being established therein and overflowing with its own nature, are indeed identical with it;
thus, there is no such thing as an object of cognition consisting of external movement.
That which, being followed by the state of being a knower, one might think is an external object of cognition—this is nothing at all.

And so it was stated previously: "If there is determination (*avadhāraṇa*) with respect to those very appearances (*avabhāsa*), what is the use of another external object that is logically untenable (*anupapatti*) in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)?"
And thus:
The non-establishment of inherence follows from the impossibility of the manifestation of a whole.

Those who maintain contradictory views— such as those concerning trembling and non-trembling, obstruction and non-obstruction, being colored and uncolored, and so forth, regarding the distinctions of atoms and aggregates— even in the external doctrine of the accumulation of atoms,
since there is no aggregate other than the atoms themselves, if those [atoms] were to join with one another...
That would be merely a single atom. Or else, if one were in one place and another in another, there would simply be many [atoms];
thus, nothing external would be established as being known by its name.

On the other hand, there is either a single atom or many atoms that grasp the distinctions between parts such as the directions. And thus, when these directions are being gathered together, what is "one" here and what is "another" there? Since there is no such thing as a direction-atom (*dig-aṇu*), [the distinction of directions is not established].
"There is nothing external whatsoever in reality"—
thus has this been established in detail by the supreme gurus in the *Sūtravimarśinī*. Therefore,
all this is merely a manifestation of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*) and is of the nature of consciousness (*cidātmaka*).

That which consists of the attainment of light and bliss is indeed called *mud* and *paramaśiva*. And so it is said: "The manifestation of things that exist as appearances, yet are not [externally] existent, occurs through their abiding state itself, appearing externally as if they were objects as they were before. Thus, the object is manifest. (1)

It would [not exist] without having the nature of luminosity. Nor could there be a separate luminosity; for the object's state of being luminous is its very self. If luminosity were distinct [from the object], then there would be a confusion of the object; for the object is luminous by virtue of having luminosity as its essence, and not otherwise.

"It is established. If that appearance of something as if it were external were to lead to an inference [of an external object], then—since consciousness is non-different [from its content]—it could not be the cause of such diverse appearances; nor could the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) serve here as the cause for such diversity. What, then, would be the basis for the diversity of that very awakening?

This very point is certain: entities whose nature consists of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), which are dense with the bliss of light, arise like bubbles and dissolve back into that very same source; thus, they too are causes for recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), as indicated by the *bahuvrīhi* compound. And furthermore:

"Because it is the cause for the attainment of the totality of all perfections through recognition"—this is indeed expressed by the *ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa* compound. Thus, this is the explanation of the first sūtra; and in this way, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is the subject matter of the treatise.
And this is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* by way of implication (*garbhīkāreṇa*). That established point, when proven, whereby other related points are also proven, is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*.

Just as the self is established as distinct from the sense organs and so forth, because of the unified apprehension of a single object through both seeing and touching— this point being thus proven— it is also established that the sense organs are distinct from the self and possess restricted objects and functions.

When the meaning of the initial sūtra has thus entered the path of experience through its purpose, the sense is that success is achieved everywhere, like the attainment of a wealth of jewels from the Rohaṇa mountain. Furthermore,
this opening verse serves as an introductory statement (upodghāta).
For it is thus:
The introduction is for the purpose of encompassing the meaning of all the treatises.
And so it is said:

That wherein the essence of all the scriptures of the Āgamas is determined, even by means of a single word or a portion thereof, is designated as *upodghāta* (the introduction) by those who know it; this was proclaimed by the ancients and should be recognized as such. (1)

That in which the determination of the meaning of the entire scripture occurs at the very beginning of a single discourse, being endowed with all the defining characteristics, is called the "Introduction" (upodghāta). || 2 ||
And its meaning is as follows: "upa" means in the vicinity of oneself; "udghāta" means rising or emergence.
The root *han* is used in the senses of killing and going. || 1 ||
And yet:
"Upa" means having sat down near oneself; "udghāta" refers to the dispelling of delusion regarding the objects of knowledge.
And yet:
"Upa" means having entered into the self; "ud" is understood as being at the beginning of the scripture and as knowing one's own self.

By the prefix *upa*, there is the approaching of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) by the self; and it is said that one "ascends" (*udgamyate*) to the attainment of the Supreme Lord. Furthermore, it is said that those roots which have the meaning of "going" also have the meaning of "knowing. And likewise, it has been stated by the ancients: "The prefix *upa* [indicates] proximity to the self."
The excellence characterized by the sovereign superknowledge (*abhijñāna*) of the Lord, which is like a *ṭaṅka* (a sharp tool), is destroyed; that by which [the mind] comes to rest.

*Upa* means "in the vicinity of oneself. *Ud* means that the delusion regarding the object of cognition (*prameya-viṣaya*) is destroyed, or rather, the reality of the object of cognition is known, precisely above (*ūrdhva*) the scripture.
Or [it means] "by which."

11a) Likewise: *upa* [is used] with respect to the self (*ātman*); *ud* [indicates] that by means of this [knowledge], the reality of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratattva*) is struck—that is, known—vertically through the scripture (*śāstra*). Since those roots whose meaning is "to go" (*gaty-artha*) have the meaning of "to know" (*jñāna-artha*), and because the root *han* (in *upahanti*) belongs to the class of roots meaning "to go" as well as "to strike," its sense here is "to know. This is the intended meaning.
Thus, this first verse serves as an introductory prelude (upodghāta) to the subject matter; enough of this.

Regarding that which was composed as this introduction by the supreme gurus in four verses: having approached the Supreme Lord with the first verse, and having contemplated the Supreme Lord together with His limbs as consisting of His two powers and as consisting of knowledge and action;

Regarding the introduction: it has been taught under this title. Furthermore, we have indeed indicated that the nature of the powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) and action (*kriyā-śakti*) consists precisely in being the state of servitude to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). If the substratum is unestablished, then in the apprehension of its qualities, there is the intention of establishing what was [previously] unestablished.

By way of digression: just as in the case of "This is a Brāhmaṇa," where the object of knowledge is understood to be a Brāhmaṇa characterized by genus (*jāti*), quality (*guṇa*), or action (*kriyā*), so too here [the object] is to be known. Enough with this prolixity;
now, therefore, the subject matter (*viṣaya*), purpose (*prayojana*), and so forth are being stated—for even a dull-witted person does not engage in an activity without having a purpose in view.
It proceeds as follows: by what means is that which has been stated as the purpose understood?
Thus, the purpose here is the attainment of the perfection of entering into union with Him through the acquisition of supreme lordship.
For upon the attainment of the state of the Supreme Lord, all perfections consisting of His outpouring (*niḥṣyanda*) flow forth,

just as a wealth of jewels flows forth upon the acquisition of the Rohaṇa mountain. Thus, the purpose (*prayojana*) and the subject matter (*abhidheya*) herein are the means for attaining identity with the essential nature of the Supreme Lord.

And the title of this treatise is *Pratyabhijñākaumudī*. The qualified candidate is one who is sinking in both [worlds] due to the loss [of their true nature]. Thus, in the Supreme Self—which is self-luminous by its very nature—there is an absence of contact with ignorance (*avidyā*) and the like; however, there is another, namely the individual soul (*jīva*).
And regarding that very uneven ornament, there is the illustration of the uneven ornament (*viṣamālaṅkāra*) which says: "Do not trust."
For it is thus:

Not only is there the attainment of the desired form through one's own voice, but there is also the possibility of what is called "residing in one's own substratum" (svāśrayatā), which serves as an ornament for this [work]. Now, the mantra of the beloved Maṃhikā is clear; having brought it to rest, he swallows it.
Another who desires accomplishment [must practice] that which is dependent upon a support; thus, according to this [teaching],
as in the Mātṛpurāṇa, there is no other [reality] than the one whose nature consists of the knower, the known, and the act of knowing.

The state of being the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and so forth—when does that cease? It ceases when the sound (*svara*) assumes the nature of the "servant" (*dāsa*). Thus, all this is an error; so they say here:
"In ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), that indeed is not to be meditated upon (*adhyeya*); it is the Supreme, acting within its own Self as the agent."

By the words "the Siddha" and so forth, [it refers to] the Supreme Lord who is not [limited by] accomplishment (*asiddha*). But by the words "in this" and so forth, [it refers to] the individual soul (*jīva*) whose nature is delusion (*moha*), even though he is [in fact] accomplished. Because of the non-difference between these two in their mutual worldly transactions, there is a slight distinction; however, [this distinction] must be understood as infinite. [This is because] that which is the state of being an egg (*aṇḍita*) is itself that which possesses it (*tadvān*). Thus it is said.
[And so says the Veda: "Two birds, inseparable companions, dwell upon the same tree; of these two, one eats the sweet fig, while the other looks on without eating.
By this, the nature of master and servant is established.]

By means of the two Siddhas: one is the Prata (the master), and the other is the Dāsa (the servant). Both are established as the Supreme Self and the individual self (jīvātman); the rest has been previously explained. By this statement, [the matter] is manifold in many ways; it will be explained further ahead. And this is according to the path of ornamentation (alaṅkāra-mārga).

The authors of the *Alaṅkāra* have shown this through a distinction. The *Atadguṇa* and *Viṣama* are two separate ornaments. Thus, when another's quality is attributed [to oneself], even if the capacity for it exists, if one does not accept it even though it is new, that is the ornament *Atadguṇa*.

Like the Supreme Self. And as for the illustration: Just as the pure whiteness of a royal swan is not deposited [in the water] and yet is not not-deposited; though the Ganges-water is turbid with sediment, it remains like the moon—there is no destruction even of its own self when eclipsed by Rāhu. It is made [to appear so] by Rāhu.

In the same way, even if the nature of light and bliss were destroyed in the case of the individual soul (jīva), how could there be the state of being a soul? Since the soul’s own self is obscured by the impurity of māyā and time, there is a mutual distinction between these two—the Lord and the soul—due to this disparity in their qualities. Thus, it is said: "Therefore... [The rest of the verse follows].

Resembling the essence of mercury (*rāṅkara-rasa*). May there be auspiciousness! 4 || 4 || And here, [he is] the awakened one, whose heart has the mark of knowledge flashing forth through the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) of the Supreme Lord, and in whom the darkness of ignorance has set.
Thus it is said; for one who is unawakened lacks the qualification [for this practice].
And so it is said:

Even when brought to their awareness, the words of instruction are unable to restrain those whose minds are deeply rooted; do raindrops from the sky, even when clinging closely and without interval, bestow coolness upon lotus petals? Thus it is once again.
And because there is the accomplishment of one who is self-awakened, there is again the application of the cause for accomplishment.
Only one who has awakened to that is called an *adhikārī* (one qualified for spiritual practice).
And so it is.

The words of instruction from Vasiṣṭha addressed to Rāma: "He who possesses the conviction, 'I am bound; may I become liberated,' is neither utterly ignorant nor fully wise; he is one who has authority in this [spiritual] science. Thus is the awakened one. And there exists the relationship of means and end.

The connection [of the treatise] is as follows: here, the means (*upāya*) is the scripture consisting of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), and the goal (*upeya*) is the attainment of the totality of all perfections; this is established. Enough with excessive detail. Such is the meaning of the first verse. Thus.
The first chapter is completed in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha.
May there be auspiciousness for the worshippers of Śrīvidyā, whose consciousness-born [forms] manifest solely through her grace.
Now, those such as the Sāṅkhyas [assert] primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause;
likewise, the Mīmāṃsakas and others [assert] karma as the cause; similarly, the Naiyāyikas and others [assert] the self (*ātman*) as the cause;
and the Buddhists and others [assert] the non-existence of the self as the cause.
The body and so forth.

For even the Pātañjalas and others [regard] the practice of yoga, such as breath-retention (*kumbhaka*) and concentration (*dhāraṇā*), as the cause for [attaining] supremacy; likewise, the Vaiṣṇavas [regard it] through Viṣṇu as the cause, the Śaivas through Śiva as the cause,
and the Śāktas through Śakti as the cause.
"Particles such as the sun, moon, and fire are but sparks of Your splendors," and so forth;

likewise, the Śaivas [assert] Śiva as the cause. Thus, whether something has been explained somewhat coarsely or subtly, having wiped away all that, there remains something called the Unsurpassed Quiescence (*anuttara-niṣpanda*).

The word "that" (*tat*) refers to the supreme, most excellent reality (*tattva*), the seventeenth or eighteenth [principle]. That very same [reality] is now characterized on this second day by its being the cause for the accumulation of power (*śakti*). Now, as for what was said regarding the attainment of all prosperity—

I shall establish the reason for that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). Thus, this very scripture, consisting of recognition, is the cause for the attainment of all perfections. And since recognition is the scripture therein, and since scripture possesses the authority of tradition (*āgama*), it is therefore nothing other than the authority of tradition.

The means of valid cognition for establishing Īśvara consists of the four pramāṇas. Indeed, the four pramāṇas belonging to the followers of Maheśvara, which were previously established, have been specified here for the purpose of understanding through indirect operation. And among those, scripture alone is the authoritative means, because it is the word of a reliable person.
Thus, by this statement regarding the authority of a trustworthy person (*āpta*), the very existence of God (*īśvara*) is established as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

By this [argument], Īśvara is the effect; however, regarding the claim that scripture (*āgama*) is the cause, here scripture itself is what is called Īśvara, while Īśvara—as in the case of a jar or other such things—is the effect. How so? To this he says: Oṃ!
In the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is the agent and the knower, established as one's own self from the very beginning...
Or who could establish either the negation or the proof of a non-inert self? (2)

He is the Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose body is filled with the wheel of powers such as Māheśvarī; his form is the manifestation of perfect consciousness and bliss, non-dual and indivisible, characterized solely by the nature of "I" (mat-kāra). His manifesting body is the "I" (aham).
And he is completely full, his body filled with the power of the universe, which is the reality of his own vibration.
And so it is said:

There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and the stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Following Him alone as He shines, everything shines; by His light all this is illumined. And so it was stated previously: "And that which is this intuitive flash (pratibhā), that is the meaning of the word 'That' (tad-artha)."

"In the Root Scripture itself it is said: 'The cognizer who is of the nature of infinite consciousness, though beyond succession, is veiled by succession; he is the Great Lord. And the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta says: 'That which, being prior to all manifestation and full, first causes the universe to appear as "I".'"

"Then he desires to divide his own digits in order to manifest, expand, withdraw, and remain; I bow to that which consists of the entire nature of the supreme Śiva and Śakti. By such [verses], [the author describes] the solar orb of consciousness...

[This is] the composition. And when that Maheśvara has been established, by the syllable *haṃ* appearing [within Him], through the mere unfolding of the will (*icchā-unmeṣa*), this world—having become the locus of objectivity—is called "the world" (*jagat*) because its nature consists of vibration (*spanda*). It is eternally existent, whether manifest or unmanifest, and so forth.
Form.
And so it is said:
In the beginning, Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
He supported this earth and that sky. To which god shall we offer our oblation with our speech?
He who has eyes on all sides, faces on all sides, hands on all sides, and feet on all sides.

By such statements as these [it is shown]: in this very way, that Supreme Lord is indeed established from the beginning; likewise, He is the agent endowed with the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*), and likewise the knower endowed with the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). And for this very reason, He is within His own self; for the worldly transaction of the "knowable" and so forth arises from the conjunction of the self with the powers of knowledge and action.
It is established. For instance: "I know the pot and so forth; I perform the action and so forth."
Thus, when the Supreme Lord, whose nature consists of both knowledge and action, is established as one's own self, who else could there be—
other than that very same non-inert self— who, while remaining a knower, would abandon the state of being a knower and, having fallen into the blindness of birth,
maintain that "the Supreme Lord" is some other entity distinct from himself? Or rather, [who would claim] that the name "Lord" refers to anyone else?
One might attempt to establish a negation, as the Buddhists and others do, [claiming] that "God does not exist;

if He did exist, would another not perceive Him directly, like a jar? But He does not exist [in that sense]. For this very reason, it has been said: "He is the non-inert Self. Indeed, O God, all those such as the Buddhists are dear to You.
Thus it is said: "Indeed, we are the awakened ones in this world, our fame renowned everywhere;

we are experts in the conceptualization of word-meanings as being mere mental constructs (vikalpa)," as stated in the *Mañjarī*. And they subsist upon word and meaning by means of mere mental construction alone. Furthermore, [as will be shown] later...
Now, having raised that position with the words "the appearance of the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇābhāsa*) and so forth, [it is said]:
"Subsequently, fifty thousand [arrows]—half of half of ten [times] ten—reach the palm of the hand of the Daśāvatāra; for the son’s half-moon [arrow] falls."

Thus, in the Kaśmīrī language, [it is said] "kṛmuṣighāṃta" (or "kaśamīraśuṣayā"). Of those two, there are a hundred or a thousand. And therein, by the mere measure of *jalamakula*, what small gain of ghee is there? By the negligence of the great-souled ones, they defile their own selves.

Thus, no one is capable [of such a task]. For the Great Lord (Maheśvara), who is established from the beginning as the object of knowledge or knowledge itself, is omnipotent and possesses a body manifested with all qualities; therefore, one should perform [the rite] for him alone, because [any other agent] would be non-pervasive.
And so it is said: "From whom the birth, etc., of this [world] proceed, and from whom the wise—though desiring to know Him through their own intellects—are bewildered;
in whom the threefold creation is unreal, like the interchange of fire, water, and earth, by His own power."

"Let us meditate upon the Supreme Truth, which is eternally free from deceit. Furthermore, in the *Uttara-mīmāṃsā*, the definition and other characteristics of Brahman are established right at the beginning:
"Then, therefore, [there should be] the inquiry into Brahman" (*athāto brahmajijñāsā*). By the words "then, therefore" (*athātaḥ*),...

After the Pūrvamīmāṃsā (the section concerning ritual action), in the Uttaramīmāṃsā, Brahman is that which is to be inquired about; this is the remainder [of the sense]. And therein, Brahman: from the root *bṛh*, meaning "to grow" (*vṛddhau*).

Being one, he manifests the universe—which consists solely of his own vibration—in the form of "this. At first, it was merely "the non-manifest" (*avyaktam*); subsequently, having attained the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedya*), it assumes forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth. And this occurs through the power of his sustaining (*dhāraṇā*).
Just as [the world] appears as if it has attained growth through various sounds and diverse scents, so too is Brahman described as being like a city and so forth.

And the desire to know—that is, the wish to understand—that very [Brahman] is what is meant by "jijñāsā. For once Brahman is known, the entire universe is indeed said to be Brahman, because there is no distinction between cause and effect.

Furthermore, because it would follow that there is an identity through non-distinction, and because there is the occurrence of attaining those [powers], as well as the arising of the multitude of qualities such as those various sovereignties;
therefore, Brahman is to be investigated—this is the intended meaning. || 1 ||
And therefore: "The origin and so forth of this [world] proceed from that [Brahman]. (1.1.2)
And from that Brahman, the birth and so forth of this world proceed—this is the ellipsis.
And because:
In the Śrīspanda [Kārikās].
We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers, whose opening and closing of his eyes cause the dissolution and arising of the universe. || 1 ||
In that wherein all this effect resides and from which it has emerged,
there is no cessation anywhere because its nature is unobstructed.
Even as it extends through the various distinctions of waking and so forth,
that which is non-different from them never departs from its own innate nature, even when it appears to have undergone a transformation.
By such [passages] as these.
And thus:
"One should see [it] as having the nature of seeing, for it is not based on the Word alone. (Sūtra 1.1.5)

Since Brahman alone possesses the quality of being a seer (*īkṣitṛtva*), primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and the like are not the cause. This quality of being a seer is seen in the text: "He thought: 'May I become many, may I procreate. For this very reason, primordial matter and the rest are "beyond speech" (*aśabda*); because they are insentient (*jaḍatva*), they are likewise beyond the reach of scripture. Just as that Lord thought: [as described in the cited passage].
Thus, by that [scriptural statement], the Pradhāna and so forth are not characterized as the "seer," because it is said, "the Pradhāna saw."

By the phrase "That which is much" (*bahvasya*) and "This is It" (*iti na iti*), it is shown that whatever exists is Brahman. Therefore, it is determined that the entire universe, including all moving and non-moving beings, is born from the drops of its sovereign power. And [it is] Pradhāna;
Pradhāna is Nature (*prakṛti*), consisting of the three qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas.
Prakṛti is the state of equilibrium; it is not the object of perception. It is also eternal.

And it is the twelfth principle (tattva), situated below the Śiva-tattva. Thus it is said: "Śakti, Māyā, Prakṛti, and Pṛthvī—these are the powers of the Lord, the All-pervading Master. As for that which...

The illustrious Siddha Kapila and others, having placed this Uṣṇīṣa on the right side, proclaim its greatness; that [teaching] is suitable only for them, and not for the unsurpassed scriptures and the like. And those [teachers], Kapila and the rest—

Thereafter, they have entered the path that leads further along the course; like the merging of many rivers into one, through such practice of reality (*tattva*), there remains for them nothing of the notion "this is mine" or "I am this."
Because it is free from error, knowledge arises that is distinct and absolute. || 1 ||

Because of the nature of the aggregate, because of being for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three guṇas and so forth, because of presiding over [the elements], because of the state of being an enjoyer, and because of activity for the sake of liberation, the Puruṣa exists. Just as the flow of milk from the insentient [cow] occurs for the sake of the calf's growth, so too does [the activity of Prakṛti] occur for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa.

The activity of the Pradhāna [is as follows]. For thus, here and there, they speak in such and such a manner; and the sense is that in all cases this is the setting forth of the unsurpassed path. And so the Blessed One said:
"Just as the many currents of water of rivers flow toward the ocean alone,"
In the same way, O Nara,
these world-devas enter you with a force of increased speed for their own destruction,
just as moths enter a blazing fire with a force of increased speed for their own destruction; even so.
The flames of destruction, with their full force increased, blaze forth from your mouths on all sides.
All this— whatever has been, whatever is to be, and whatever exists— is born from that mere unfolding (unmeṣa) alone. And thus, since there is no other born besides him,
he, Prajāpati, moves within all worlds as the embryo, being born again and again.
He shines forth in many ways. The wise behold His source;
in Him all worlds abide. I know this Great Puruṣa, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness. Only by knowing Him does one transcend...

"There is no other path for reaching [the goal] than death; there is no other way by which one may go. "He who shines upon the gods, he who is the domestic priest of the gods, he who was born before the gods"—thus it is stated in the *Tantrāloka*. Furthermore, whatever is known as external or internal, that is of the nature of light (*prakāśa*).

The supreme body of Śiva alone is the measure [of all]. Blue, yellow, the face, the form—Śiva is pure light. In this supreme non-duality, whose essence is light, who else could there be? The relationship of means and end would exist [only nominally], for that is indeed nothing but light. This...

Whether it be duality, this distinction, or even non-duality, the Supreme Lord shines forth as nothing other than the very nature of light. On this ground, pleasure, pain, bondage, liberation, consciousness, and the insentient— all these words are one in essence, like the terms "pot" and "jar."
Or rather, it is one and the same. How indeed could that unmanifest portion shine even while [the manifest] shines? Or, if that [unmanifest] were shining, its duality would be lost.

And if that [object] were not manifest, how could its status as a real entity be asserted? For this very reason, it is established that its nature consists in being a particular manifestation. Therefore, when the doctrine "this is manifestation" has been set forth, those who maintain the theory of distinct cognitions (vibhinnajñānavādins) have been immediately refuted, starting with the proponents of the Sun (Sūrya) and others.
Only luminosity is declared, because non-luminosity is negated.

15a) The word "one" (eka) does not have as its meaning a number that partakes in the distinction between directions or individual entities. The Lord’s power is the Supreme Goddess, for she does not depend on anything else. Nor is this God the possessor of power, since he is not the substratum of anything whatsoever. He is not an object of meditation, because [the triad of] meditator, meditation, and the object of meditation [does not apply to him].

After the dismissal (*visarjana*), he is worthy of worship because of the absence of further procreation; likewise, while existing [in that state], he is not a worshiper, nor is he one who initiates others, nor even one who has received initiation—the Supreme Lord is himself the initiation. Here, there is no [need for] the rites beginning with the stationing (*sthāna*), seating (*āsana*), restraining (*nirodha*), consuming (*aṅgha*), joining (*sandhāna*), and invoking (*āvāhana*), ending with the dismissal (*visarjana*).
"It is appropriate for agent, object, and action; it is neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor is it devoid of both.

For that state is difficult to discern—indeed, it is some indescribable, unsurpassed reality. Thus has it been extensively determined by the venerable Paramaṣṭhin. Enough with much talk. Such, then, is the case.

When the Supreme Lord—devoid of all causal adjuncts—is established, who is capable of asserting whether this Lord exists or does not exist? Listen to this: it is He, O God, who rises in the morning for the worlds; and He is also the reservoir of the waters.

It is heard that [this place] is a mine of jewels forever. Therefore, let alone anyone else, even a perfected being (*siddha*) would not dare to perform either an injunction or a prohibition here; enough of this. And so: "The path to you has been traversed;
your Self is equal in majesty to those two [the sun and moon]. This [world], by the exclusion of what is not that, expresses [you] as such."
The Śruti also says: "By whom is he to be praised? Of how many kinds are his qualities? To whom is he the object?
Whose mind does not fall back upon him as the supreme goal? Whose speech does not [do so]? And so forth. Now, it is said:
Even scripture (*āgama*) does not apply there, for among the four types of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), ending with scripture, [the following applies]: "This is a jar" is a perception;
this is a jar, not the absence of a jar, because it is perceptible, like a cloth and so forth—this is inference (*anumāna*).
This jar is similar to the universal of "jar-ness," because it performs that function.

15b) Thus is the illustration. "O worthy one, what is this so-called 'substance' (dravya) that comes into the range of direct perception? To that he replies: "This is a jar, this is a jar, this is a jar," because of its capacity for functional activity. And instruct him thus: "And this is a jar."

By way of inversion, you might bring the meaning of "cloth" regarding the effect of a "pot"; thus, while the four means of valid cognition strive for their establishment only within the scope of the pot's effect, they do not extend beyond it to things such as distant objects. Furthermore, let those desiring health serve Śivā.
By the statement "serve [it]," the traditional teaching implies that health may or may not result. Thus,

this conventional discourse involving the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), such as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth," occurring in expressions consisting of four or five words and so forth— [from which] speech turns back.

Since that which is unattainable by the mind cannot be established or refuted by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the like, enough with these excessive words; for a great soul should be reflected upon even through negligence—so, enough with this prolixity. And as for those [which...]:

All essential treatises that bring about creation, maintenance, and dissolution arise from that very source; yet how could they possibly endeavor to establish or negate it, given the lack of logical connection and the impossibility of such a claim? And so it is said:
The seat of the Lord is divided into ten, eighteen, six, and eight [scriptures];
the essence of that is indeed the Trika scripture, and the essence of that is the Mālinīmata.
By this [statement], the manifestation of the sixty-four Tantras, headed by the five Brahmās, is indicated; and they too—

How do they manifest that intrinsic nature? Regarding the phrase "from that very manifestation," the use of the ablative case (*bhūtavibhakti*) indicates that it is eternal; thus, the meaning is that it is established from the beginning. It refers to the agent, the knower.

16a) By the designation "the creator and knower is Maheśvara," [He] would attain perceptibility, just as in the case of "this is a jar. [One might say] "this is Īśvara"; for by the very use of the nominative case (*bhūtavibhakti*), He is eternally established as the "creator. And thus, He is known as the creator, Maheśvara.
By such statements as these: for that which is indeed the power of knowledge is itself the power of action.

For action has the very nature of the sprout of knowledge; that which is knowledge is itself action, and that which is action is itself knowledge. Thus, because these two arise like a seed and its sprout, there is no sequence here. Therefore, all this is faultless. And by that, this second...

The meaning is that the verse, too, is indeed faultless. [Objection: But if the Supreme Lord is thus established as the conscious Self who illumines the universe, then why does this manifold variety of the world—consisting of the moving and the unmoving, the stable and the unstable, blue, yellow, and so forth—appear everywhere in the form of "I," which is His very own nature?

Thus, while manifesting everywhere in all states, why does He not come within the path of experience through the senses— through such an experience as "This is the Lord," just as one says "This is a jar"? For, according to [scriptures] such as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," it is He alone who exists everywhere.

"Because it is set in motion," so it is said. But [the author] says: "However, because this [reality] is not perceived due to the power of delusion, even though it is seen, this recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not demonstrated through the manifestation of its power.
