And because there is no distinction from cattle and other animals. For just as cattle and others, upon seeing a man carrying a sword or grass in his hand, approach him or move away from him due to the specific difference in their mutual interaction; and likewise, having seen that very same man carrying a staff, they [behave] accordingly.
What is more remote? They go [to it], because of non-pervasion.

Thus, there is no distinction between living beings and animals and the like; for there is activity when there is pervasion, and no activity when there is non-pervasion. And thus, one whose knowledge has been stolen away by *māyā* [is as follows].
"Those who rely on existence," and so forth, refers to those who have not lost sight of the ultimate truth. And therefore:

"Like a worm in a dance, moving swiftly from one whirlpool to another, they pass from birth to birth and never attain liberation. Thus, by resorting to birth after birth, they do not attain liberation at all. And therefore: "At the conclusion of the ripening of good karma..."

"Rescued by the Treasure of Compassion, they reach the shore and rest at ease in the shade of trees," and so forth. That is to say, having been drawn out from the whirlpool of the river by some compassionate one,
and having reached the shade of trees there, they rest as the sun's rays rise.

Likewise, these [beings] find rest through instruction and other means bestowed by someone or another who is youthful. This is the application of the analogy. Thus, even though the reality of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvara-tattva) is always manifest and appearing as its own form, [it is nevertheless perceived as such], just as in the expression "this very one is the tormentor of the mind" (*manodarta*).
"I do," "I go," "I see"— by such [expressions],
this [Self] is indeed cast into the fire of the sense-organ of sight; through illusion (māyā) and ignorance (avidyā),
it appears like the orb of the moon eclipsed by Rāhu, or like the solar disc [reflected] in a whirlpool.
This [Self] is directly perceived through the great limiting adjunct (mahat-upādhi). Is it that the moon does not exist there, or rather that the sun does not shine there? And so say the Sāṅkhyas.

External objects of cognition are not apprehended due to excessive distance, extreme proximity, impairment of the sense organs, instability of the mind, subtlety, intervention, being overwhelmed, and collision with similar objects. Among these, "due to excessive distance" is as follows: [a bird] flying in the sky is not perceived.
Even though it is present, it is not seen because of extreme distance. What does it intend to do there? It has no wings.
For example, due to proximity: "The collyrium situated in the eye is not seen because of extreme proximity."

As in the case of the impairment of the sense organs: due to blindness, deafness, and so forth, one does not see, nor does one hear. As in the case of the non-abiding of the mind: when the mind is carried away by desire and the like, one does not see, nor does one perceive. As in the case of subtlety: as with ghee in milk. As in the case of obstruction: as with [an object] behind a wall.

One does not see the king's wives and such when they are obstructed by walls and the like; nor [is there non-perception] due to being overwhelmed, as in the case of the milk in cows of the *saurabhī* breed during milking. Or it is like the equal impact [of heat], whereby all varieties of sweetness—such as sugar, candied sugar, and honey—manifest in the sugarcane.

Thus, by this [statement], all [the qualities] are touched upon there; they do not exist as objects of direct perception. However, due to the influence of form and other factors, they remain concealed and are not spoken of; this is the manifest traditional teaching (*pravāda*). And thus, by virtue of being possessed by *māyā*, the person becomes a stained beast (*paśu*) who lacks awakening. So it is said.
In the *Paramārthasāra*: "Just as a king who has gone out to fight...
[Thus,] even though the king is seen day and night, because he has gone outside the palace, he is as if unseen; what contradiction is there in this? For indeed, [one might object]:
"But recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is not even perception; it is merely a deception."
This is certain. It is not so; therefore, it is said: "By means of the manifestation of power, this recognition is demonstrated. Knowledge and action are the two powers.

Like the two wings of a swan, they are well-known. By means of their manifestation—that is, their demonstration through the definition of characteristics and so forth—recognition is shown; this is the meaning of "we shall do."

How is there the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), or how is there action (*kriyā*)? This very instruction is the instruction regarding that [power]. And since its nature is devoid of appearance (*nirābhāsātmatva*), even if a description of its characteristics were provided, it would result in contradiction due to the impossibility of having a substratum and because of logical inconsistency (*vyāghāta*).
And because of the occurrence of defects.
And thus: "Would that conceptual construction belong to the non-conceptual, or to the conceptual?"
If the first *vyāhṛti* were likewise [to require another], there would follow infinite regress, circularity, and other such fallacies.
For that too there would be another, and for that yet another; thus, there would be the fall into an infinite regress.

Even so, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) that establishes no root; and because of the statement "the conceptualization of a conceptualization," there would follow further fallacies such as circularity (*cakraka*). Circular reasoning occurs when the prior depends on the subsequent, the middle depends on the subsequent, and the subsequent depends on the prior—as for example, in the case of [the following]:...

That which exists through conceptualization as a conceptualizer of conceptualization, that indeed is non-conceptualization itself. Furthermore, in the method of describing qualities such as non-conceptuality, there are contradictions such as the unestablished nature of the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*) due to its being without a locus, as for example: "The sky-lotus is fragrant."

The meaning is that one should remain in a state of silence through speechless discourse and so forth, as in the examples "because of being like a lotus" (*aravindatvāt*) or "like a mind-born lotus" (*manojāravindavat*).
Alternatively,
in meditation, one may assume a contraction of the limbs and so forth by remaining silent like a tortoise.
One should remain [in that state]; enough with this extensive elaboration. And as it is said in such passages as, "from which words turn back," and so forth.
Likewise, even the Veda, fearing that your equanimity toward speech and mind might be surpassed by something else, declares this through the negation of all other objects:
"By whom is he to be praised? Of how many kinds are his qualities? To what subject does he belong?"—for such a question falls within the realm of the inferior.

And by [the verse] beginning with "Whose is this bowing? and so forth, it is established that this path of instruction is such that in the description of qualities and so on, there is only the manifestation of the two powers of knowledge and action; it is not the manifestation of those [qualities themselves]. That very point is now demonstrated.

17b) Now, regarding that which was stated: "Even though the Supreme Lord is self-luminous, for one whose vision is obscured by the darkness of delusion, He does not appear at all except through the application of the intellect. And that very point he elucidates with a pair [of verses].
Oṃ! For indeed, the support for those who have become inert is the refuge of the living; knowledge and action are considered the life-force of living beings. || 4 ||

Oṃ. In that regard, knowledge is self-established; although it does not depend on the body of action (*kriyākāya*), it may be perceived by others as well. Through that [perception], the knowledge of another is inferred. And so it is shown:
for all beings, [there is the perception] of blue and non-blue, of places, of large and small, of jars, cloths, slopes, and so forth.
Establishment (pratiṣṭhā). Stability has the living being as its locus; that of which the living being alone is the locus.
For it is thus:
I see; I eat; I go; I hear.
Whatever worldly transaction there may be, such as this and others, that indeed has its locus solely in consciousness.

Because [the sense of] "I" ascends and finds its rest in this very "I"; for without that, the mass of objects of knowledge would be like mere stones, leading to the undesirable consequence that the Lord would be non-eternal. Indeed, nothing whatsoever can be useful if it is devoid of life—this is what follows from such statements as "arising," "this," "that," and so forth.
It is established that its persistence has the living being as its substratum, because it is established that its nature is inseparable from that [living being]. And because [one thinks]:
"I see," "I know," and "I ascertain this."

If there were no cognizer at all who appeared as "I" by way of his own nature, then who could speak thus: "I see," and so forth? Therefore, it is established that this inertness has the living being (jīva) as its substratum; for the conventional usage of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so on, exists only in relation to the inert.

For it is established that [the self] exists as the agent of activity. And for this very reason, there is knowledge: "I know"; and there is action: "I do. Thus, both knowledge and action constitute the life of living beings—those endowed with *jīva*, those possessed of consciousness, and all created things, both moving and unmoving. Life is *jīva*.

Thus, [the self] exists, because otherwise the accomplishment of worldly transactions would be impossible. This entire mass of entities has become dependent upon the body and speech; what kind of reasoning is this, that one should require a substratum for that which is itself dependent? (4)
And in order to demonstrate this very point through reasoning, he says:

Oṃ. In that regard, knowledge is self-established; since it does not depend on the body of action, it is inferred by others as well through its manifestation, and thus non-knowledge is also inferred. This has already been established previously: "I know the jar," "I am doing [it]."
Thus, since [the result] is established in this way, actions are indeed perceived by others and even by other [means].
"Or, 'this one knows, and this one acts'—thus it is established that these are the arguments regarding the body."
Moreover, this conventional usage has indeed been observed by others in the world as well; for example:

Having been dispatched for that purpose by the king's command, he proceeds toward that place. Upon reaching that place, having performed various tasks and duties here and there, he returns once again. And by the act of going there, that respective task [is accomplished].

Having carried out the king's business by means of knowledge regarding its execution and so forth— determining through the method of "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done"— and having returned once more to reach the presence of the king, he informs the king of what was thus performed or left undone, such as the sacrificial altar and other matters; that man, moreover, is one who exerts effort.

"And he is a tiger"—such [expressions] would be the subject at hand. In this regard, this worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*), whose nature is manifest and appearing, is established as a practice of knowledge and action performed by oneself and observed by others. Therefore, in that case, knowledge is self-established (*svataḥ-siddha*).
Thus, everything beginning with "not existing as dependent on the body of action" is established as entirely faultless.

Thus, this is well known as the *upodghāta* (introduction). Furthermore, its definition was previously established by our venerable preceptors (*parameṣṭhipāda*) as follows: "The determination of the meaning of all scriptures which appears therein is celebrated as the *upodghāta*. And likewise: "The word *ud* [is used] for the scripture..."
Thus, "ud" signifies that which is near the Supreme Lord; it denotes the delusion regarding the object of knowledge.

Furthermore, by such statements as "Or is it cognition that is understood? and so forth, these five verses, which have issued from the mouth of the venerable Teacher, encompass the purpose and meaning of all scriptures.

And thus: *upa* signifies the supreme lord’s absorption (*samāveśa*) attained through the firmness of ultimate devotion; *ut* means "arisen"; and *ghātaḥ* refers to the striking away of this entire mass of objects of knowledge (*prameya-rāśi*) which has fallen into the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*). This is the introduction (*upodghāta*). Furthermore: *upa* means "in the proximity of the Supreme Lord."

"Ud" means it arises; "ghātaḥ" means movement. Or alternatively: "upa" means in the proximity of the Lord (Īśvara) and the Self (Ātman); "ut" means excellence; that by which one is struck [toward] or brought to rest [in that state]. 3.

"In the presence of the Supreme Lord" (*upaparameśvara*). Regarding "ud": it is that by which delusion (*moha*), consisting of the mass of objects of knowledge (*prameya-rāśi*), is destroyed—that is, removed—at the very beginning of the scripture. (4) Regarding "ud": it is known in the presence of the Supreme Lord that one's own true nature (*svarūpa*) exists within the objects of knowledge. (5) Because [the root *ud*] has the sense of "going" (*gati*).

By the rule "at the end of *dvā*, *jñāna* means 'object' (*artha*)", those roots meaning "to go" (*gati*) are understood to mean "to know" (*jñāna*); thus, in the expression *striyaṃ hanti*, it means "he goes to a woman" (*striyaṃ gacchati*).

Thus, this introduction having been established by its definition, the path that is the gateway to liberation is proven. And so: "Just as one who attempts to step over the shadow of his own head with his own feet finds his head instead at the place of his feet, so too is this *baindavī* [drop] of Śiva. (1) Śaivī.

By such statements as "the mouth is spoken of here," and so forth, it is established that this introduction (*upodghāta*) is indeed the very door to liberation, through the reasoning that constitutes the essence of the scripture. We too, having become proficient through the practice of experiencing those teachings and having attained the supreme reality by means of that very first verse, [proceed] according to that true path.

With the words "the supreme introduction" (*paramopodghāta*) and so forth, they indicate that we shall proceed [with the exposition]. And for this very reason, even the five verses (*pañcaślokī*) are in harmony with the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Just as there is an experience of the experience of the ultimate reality of all scriptures through the presentation of these five verses.
Thus, with this verse [as the fifth], the "Illumination of the Ultimate Reality" consisting of five verses is complete;
thus ends the second chapter in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Ānanda.
[+ * * *? What can I say? This is darkness upon darkness; this is a great boil upon a tumor.

Speaking thus, we say that by means of the supreme verse (*aty-śloka*), all—beginning with the Awakened (*prabuddha*) and the Self-Awakened (*svaprabuddha*)—have indeed become awakened, having attained identity with and absorption into That (*tādātmya-tadāpatti*).

Having somehow attained the state of servitude to Maheśvara, all those objects of that [consciousness]— which are of the nature of light, which illuminate that very nature, and whose essence is that very nature, being nothing other than it— are established as having the essential form of "the knower and the known," and so forth.

By the verse concerning his own nature (*svātmala*), and then by the second verse beginning with "Maheśvara," which establishes that the agent and the knower are one's own self (*svātman*) as primordially accomplished (*ādisiddha*); and by the four verses beginning with "By that [power], other knowledge is deluded"— no one at all is capable of knowing, whether they be unawakened (*aprabuddha*) or awakened (*buddha*).
Or, by means of the single path beginning with "or [he is] self-awakened" (*svaprabuddha*), there is a certain [teaching] in one way;

and then a certain [teaching] in another way. In this regard, there is great laughter even for those who have attained [the goal], consisting of the presentation of the unreal as real, and the presentation of the real as unreal.
In this regard, there is no authoritative proof for that; rather, in every such case, there is only the state of being a deceiver.

To this we reply: It has been stated by the ascetic (yati) that all are indeed attainers of that state; and it is also declared that the Great Lord is the very Self of all, such that all are indeed the masters of their own selves. This is established through such statements as "the jar knows the cloth" and so forth, as well as "I am composed of all," and so on. All of that [is as follows]:

This is indeed true, not merely a figurative expression. For instance, just as one who has traveled on foot experiences every bit of the path and, upon reaching a foreign land, recognizes it and its surroundings by hearing of them from others; so too [is the case for the knower].

[How] shall we give [this]? And one who makes known that which is unknown to others is called an *āpta* (a reliable authority). This is the determination regarding the other world (*paraloka*), like the root of a tree. Thus, our former teachers also, having entered into the true nature of that [reality], have declared those various determinations; so it is even today.

The verse is established. And therefore, that which is beyond it—that supreme state previously seen by the Seer—is such that no one knows it, nor can anyone speak of it; yet one knows it beforehand when delusion [is removed].

And by the verse: "We have understood it thus: from Śiva down to the earth, the sequence of creation and maintenance is established as being of the nature of Śiva—supremely tranquil, free from conceptual construction, and devoid of the relationship between the object of knowledge and the knower. This is true even for you."
"I establish [the disciples] on the path that is the non-path; may you also attain that which I have attained"—this is auspicious.
Now, [I shall describe] the Supreme Lord, who consists of knowledge and action, by means of his two powers.
Having strengthened [the resolve] therein, those others—
the ancient Buddhas and so forth— placed their turbans and head-covers to the right in order to strengthen their own doctrine, [worshipping] the Supreme Lord who is the form of one's own self.

Like those who claim the solar orb does not exist because it is obscured by clouds, the "Beloved of the Gods" (the Materialists) conceal [the truth] with the body, the senses, the vital breaths, and so forth. Asserting that "the body is the self," or "the vital breath is the self," or "the intellect is the self," or "space is the self"— for them, now:
Having fashioned arms like those of wrestlers and having laid them upon the ground,

he speaks in order to strengthen his own doctrine called Śaiva— which is the nature of consciousness (*cidātman*) and self-luminous— [in order to refute the Mādhyamikas and to establish that doctrine].

[Objection: "Indeed, one cognition has the appearance of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while another, called conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), is accompanied by verbal expression; yet even though these two are manifold, they do not appear here [in this context] to any eternal perceiver, because there is no cognition of 'I' (*ahaṃ-pratīti*)."
This [consciousness] resides within the body. (7) The word "nanu" introduces a question from one senior in wisdom among the ancient teachers.
"Aho! We Śaivas are indeed the knowers in this world, our fame renowned everywhere; we are experts in conceptualizing the meaning of words as being mere mental constructs. And he who—
It is said that the Great Lord is the self of all,
because [the devotees] have minds intoxicated by the taste of the honey and other [substances] he has drunk, and because their minds are fixed on him alone.
If the first [alternative] holds here, then its result is expressed in your own words.

"And these should be disregarded like one who is insane. Then another says: "He who is the seer, he who is the hearer, and he who is the smeller—that is the Self, the Supreme Lord. To that also, [one replies]: "Is it the mind? Or the intellect? Or the ego-sense? Or the body? Or the vital breath?"
Or it is conceived as "space. It is called *cit* because it cognizes; it is the Self (*ātman*), the mind (*manas*), or the intellect (*buddhi*).
It is of the nature of certainty; it serves as a witness in all things, because of the prior determination that "this is the Self."
19b) "This self is supreme bliss. Let that [supreme bliss] itself be the Supreme Lord; what is the use of a self?
Furthermore, if there were something called the "self," why is it not perceived?
Because it is not seen, it does not exist. For that which is non-existent has no manifestation, and for that which is existent, there is no non-existence.
This is because of such statements by the Blessed One as seen above. Furthermore: "That which exists is said to be existent;
that which does not exist is the supreme non-existent. A pot exists on the ground, and otherwise there is no pot.
If the Self were that [pot], it would be perceived in the heart. Since it is not perceived, it does not exist.

Therefore, this worldly convention (*vyavahāra*) is clearly established in the world through two types of cognition: first, that which is called non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*), which possesses the appearance of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇābhāsa*); and second, another which is called conceptual (*savikalpa*), which is associated with verbal expression (*sābhilāpa*). It is by means of these two alone that the accomplishment of worldly convention is achieved. For instance:
Someone having come from afar sees [him] from a distance, thinking, "This is someone with form."

Thereafter, someone perceives something as "this" and determines it to be such. Thereafter, having reached its vicinity, one considers whether "this is that" or "it is someone else. Thereafter, upon reaching even closer, one says with certainty, "This is indeed that; it is not another. Thus ends the non-conceptual [state].

Knowledge; subsequently, because it is devoid of training and so forth, this [being] is grasped by means of conceptualization through the construction of all characteristics, such as "he belongs to such-and-such a caste" and "he has such-and-such a complexion."

[The self is known] by the mind (*manas*), likewise by the intellect (*buddhi*), and likewise by the sense organs (*indriya*) and so forth; thus, this very pair of cognitions, together with the mind and the rest, is the cause for the establishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).
Without this pair, nothing such as the self (*ātman*) and so on is possible, because it would be illogical [and] because it would not be manifest. And furthermore, [it is] like an axe.

20a) For it is thus: because [the self] appears as distinct, because [statements of non-difference] refer to something else, because the discourse on non-duality would result in the collapse of conventional usage, and so forth—by this [argument], it is established that "no self whatsoever exists. Now, those same elder Buddhists...
They respond to the Śaivas by means of mutual dialogue alone, employing the logic of the "lion's glance" (siṃhāvalokita).

Oṃ. Now, if experience were to perish, how could memory, which follows upon it, exist? If the self were the experiencer, it would have to be non-eternal. (8) O Śaiva! If you should say: "According to your [own] view, the self is not eternal; for indeed, when the destruction of experience has occurred..."
Just as when the perceptual cognition "this is a jar" has arisen, immediately thereafter the thought occurs, "The jar that was previously seen by me— what was seen before—
is now entering the path of memory by the power of the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) of that experience"; this is inference based on memory (*smaraṇānumāna*).

And its being known appears [to consciousness], just as in the expression "this is my mother. By this experience, when the previously established [object] is present, there occurs recollection merely through its association with that [experience]. And immediately thereafter, when [the object] is established, who indeed could be the knower of the experience of recollection if the Self did not exist? It is "I" [who knows].
"I know," "I do," "I see"—such conventional usage belongs to the self alone.
Even without that [consciousness], could some embodied subject or the like, being of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), act in this way?
By this, it is established that there certainly exists a Self; thus, even the elder Buddhists are capable of asserting this through mere appearance alone. And so it is said in the *Spanda*:

Even though there is a distinction between waking and other states, that [consciousness] shines forth undivided; it does not deviate from its own innate nature, for it is perceived as such. And so: "In the waking state, sound, touch, and the rest are objects of cognition, distinct due to their variety."
20b) Therefore, being solitary, it does not differ from the nature of oneness with that consciousness.
Therefore, this Self is called the non-measurer, the grasper of the objects of knowledge and so forth. || 8 ||
When this has been thus established, the elders reply as follows.

Oṃ. [Objection: "If the destruction of the perception (*dṛk*) within the Self of Truth (*satya*) occurs, then how can there be memory regarding unseen objects through that [perception] as a gateway? For memory must reside in the very same locus where the original experience occurred. [Response: O Śaiva! Even though Your Self exists, what is the use of that [perception]? For previously, when the experience "this is a jar" arose, and subsequently, upon its destruction—
Regarding the arising [of memory]: when a previously perceived jar has been forgotten, by what cause does its recollection occur?
The inquiry is: by what cognizer or knower, and by what object of cognition?
Furthermore, the elders have said: "Now, O Śaiva, that which is experience is precisely that state. That memory which is 'this is a jar' is of that very same state."
This mother who has experienced [this] enters the path of memory, just as one says, "She is my mother."
For it has been stated that memory arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of previous experience. || 10 ||
And therefore, the elders say:
Oṃ, for indeed, memory arises from the latent impressions of prior experience.
If this were so, what would be the purpose of the permanent self (sthāyin) existing within the womb?

Thus, if it is as stated—that memory occurs at the very same locus where the experience occurred—and this is indeed what is taught; if that path of experience is capable of bringing about effects such as memory and so forth, then what is the use of that [separate] self? And thus, when this is established, it is merely for the sake of conventional usage.
Just as a tumor within the heart is for the sake of great pain, so too is that very thing for the sake of great suffering.

What meaning could there be in such thoughts as "I have been killed by this internal suffering," and so forth? Nothing at all can be done by that self. Rather, the suffering is simply, "But what shall I do?"

21a) And therefore, there is no purpose whatsoever in its existence or non-existence. Just as someone might say, "Space exists," "The gods exist," or "Humans eat," and such statements are to be disregarded like those of a madman, so too is the claim that "the self exists."

"Do not entertain even the slightest suspicion that [the opponent] is capable of ascending to the level of intellectual reasoning. Therefore, they say: "From whatever this [world] arises, from that very same source it [returns]."

Oṃ. Therefore, when phenomena (dharmas) are distinct, since there is no difference in their essential nature (svarūpa), memory is established through mental impression (saṃskāra); thus, the "rememberer" is merely a conceptual construction based on what was previously seen. Consequently, even though the collection of phenomena conforming to that very mental impression exists as distinct from the self (ātman)...

Because there is no distinction in the essential nature of the self (*ātman*), and because there is an absence of any [external] qualifying attribute (*viśeṣa*). Furthermore, once memory is established through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of experience immediately following that [perception],
then just as the previously mentioned definition of the object was merely imagined (*kalpita*), so too is the rememberer (*smartṛ*) merely imagined.
Thus it is established that [the self] is imagined by conceptual constructions. And so says our most excellent teacher:

For through experience, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) appropriate to itself is inferred; and that latent impression establishes a state of being identical to its former form, as in the case of a tree whose branches were once severed and have long since grown back. Now, as for the attributes of the self:
Intellect, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion, effort, merit, demerit,
and mental impressions— these are the qualities of the self. Now,
the elders seek to establish that the self is merely a conceptual construction and is not subject to impermanence and other such attributes.

Because there is no distinction in the essential nature of the self due to the non-superimposition of [external] dharmas, and so forth; yet, even so, that twofold power— consisting of knowledge and action— is dependent on the cause, and in the absence of the cause,
it is dependent on the effect.
21b) Because [it arises] from existence— referring to that pair consisting of cognition and action— he says this in order to render it invalid and to refute it as well.

If knowledge (*jñāna*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cit*), then why would it not be eternal like the Self (*ātman*)? On the other hand, if it were insentient (*jada*), how could it illuminate objects? Knowledge and action are accepted as qualities;
therefore, since they do not exist apart from the Self which is their possessor, it is established that even these qualities do not exist [as independent entities].
Therefore, because it would follow that the self is impermanent through its connection with attributes (*dharma-yoga*), it follows that its two qualities would also be impermanent;

thus, there must be identity between the quality and the possessor of the quality (*guṇa-guṇin-sāmānya*). And because of the non-difference between those two, just as the conscious self (*cidrūpa*) would be impermanent through its connection with attributes, [so too would the world].

There would be the consequence [of over-extension]. Likewise, because there would be no mutual distinction between that [self] and its qualities; and likewise, if it were eternal, there would be the consequence of faults such as [the self being] a universal (jāti), etc.; and there would also be the consequence of the self and its qualities being non-eternal.

Thus, since birth (jāti) exists in this way, how could there be the manifestation of this [self], or of its qualities, given that impermanence and other such characteristics exist? For if it were like a stone, what kind of "consequence of the acquisition of contradictory properties" (viddha-dharmāpatti-prasaṅga) would this be? For in this way, by means of the impermanence of cognition...

If [the self] were insentient (*jāḍyatva*), how could there be the illumination of objects, as in the case of the Self [of the opponent]? For knowledge has consciousness (*cit*) as its nature. If [it] were non-eternal, it would be like an insentient object such as a jar, because it would possess qualities such as merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). By this pervasion (*vyāpti*), one cannot say "I know" or "I do not know."
How could an eternal time be established, since it is insentient like a jar or other such objects? How indeed could that be so?

Thus is the pervasiveness of the elder Buddhists established; for it is certain that they are experts in the conceptual construction of word-meanings as being mere mental constructs (*vikalpamātra*). And so, indeed, we Buddhists are renowned everywhere in the world for our various conceptual constructions of word-meanings.
Since knowledge is thus established, [the author], in order to refute even that activity which has it as its subordinate nature, says:

Oṃ! Even the activity of the body and so forth toward an object consists in its arising in various locations and times; it is not perceived otherwise, nor is such activity possible for a single entity that is unitary and successive.

22a) For instance, in such cases as: "Here indeed Devadatta cooks," "Vāmanadatta is coming," and "The Brahmin with the red turban is going," there is a sequence of multiple actions— such as the rice, the act of ruling (*indana*), and the cooking by fire— and [the agent] is distinct from the nature of Devadatta who has gone to the house, being located in an external place.

The nature of Devadatta is thus obtained as "he is in the house" or "he is not outside," or "he is outside and he is not in the house. Indeed, only this much of an action is obtained, and nothing else, because nothing else is perceived. Nor is that [perceived thing] itself an action. Or [it may be said]: [the nature of Devadatta is thus obtained].

Knowledge belongs to some wise person; it exists in that which is sequential due to having both inert and non-inert natures. Since that [knowledge] is one, yet possesses manifold natures, it cannot belong at all to the inactive Self, because that would entail the contradiction of a single entity possessing manifold natures.

Thus, when the non-existence of the self has been established in this manner, and when both the unestablished nature of the substratum (*āśrayāsiddhatva*) and the unestablished nature of the dependent (*āśrayisiddhatva*) have been proven, he says the following immediately thereafter to further solidify that very point by means of the maxim of "digging a pit and planting a pillar" (*sthaṇānikhananyāya*): || 13 ||
Oṃ. It is observed that whatever is situated in this or that [cause], that very thing comes to be;
there is no other relation than that of cause and effect. For in this way, when this or that lump of clay and so forth exists, that very thing—such as a jar and so forth—comes to be.

Because of necessity, there is nothing else; thus is the pervasion (vyāpti) ascertained. From that clay comes the jar, and from threads comes the cloth—this sequence is established by the principle of the Supreme Lord’s destiny (niyati), and not otherwise.
Nor do flowers and the like, or fruits and the like, arise from clay; nor indeed do they arise from threads.

For [the definition would apply to] jars and the like, or sesame oil and the like; thus there is both under-extension (avyāpti) and over-extension (ativyāpti). Indeed, that which has been stated by you— namely,
that since the occurrence of memory arises from the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience, and since worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is established by this alone,

thus, by the statement that "the Supreme Lord is the conscious body consisting of knowledge, light, and bliss," the Buddhist position is refuted. And by that, one's own position is rendered firm in its conviction.

In each instance, it is like the orb of the sun. Now, therefore, I endeavor to compose this *Kaumudī* on Recognition (*Pratyabhijñā*), having investigated the path of Śiva through the teachings of my Guru and the scriptures. (25)

27b) Now, if it is as you say— that the Self, as the agent of self-luminosity, is pervasive and indeed shines forth in all states and at all times through its nature as the subject and its agency in perception, memory, and so on— then what has been stated [is established].

For it is established that there is some form of error; therefore, once this is proven, he confirms what was stated previously.

"Oṃ. That which is remembered as 'such was seen by me' even through differentiation—that very [act] is the grammatical derivation (vyākaraṇa) of this [Smṛti], because of the traditional teaching (smṛti): 'That which was seen by me in such a way. "That which is remembered as 'it was thus for me,' even through such differentiation—that is what was seen by me; [this is] of this [Smṛti]."

That very [activity] of that self is indeed its manifestation (*vyākaraṇa*); it is a differentiation (*vibhajya-ākaraṇa*), but it is not something other than that. Thus, there is the engagement of the self in experience, recollection, and so forth.
30. Furthermore, he confirms this very point:
he demonstrates that in perception, memory, and so forth, that one [subject] alone functions as the agent of cognition by way of being the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

Oṃ. And that cognition which perceives "this is a jar" or "I perceive this," and which apprehends [the object] as inherent, is also a perception of that [inherent] substrate. (32) "Perceives this jar"—if one has reached the state of perceiving merely the thing-in-itself; or "this is a jar"—by this, the duality...

And that which appears as a manifestation through form, up to that point, is the ascertainment (*avasāya*). And that ascertainment resides in the agent; it is considered to be inherently inherent (*samaveta*) within one's own self, which is the cause and self-luminous, and is joined with the specific relation of inherence (*samavāya-sambandha*) in that ascertainment.

Because it has that as its intrinsic nature; because of the relationship between those two as the grasped and the grasper; because those two are like quality and the possessor of quality, or like action and the agent of action; because they possess a relationship; and because they are bound by the relationship between genus and individual, due to the specific inseparable connection between the locus and the located. Thus it has been stated.
And it will be said [later]: "Now, he alone is the experiencer, the agent, the knower, the Great Lord (maheśvara), all-pervading like the sun of consciousness"—thus he concludes.

"Oṃ! Even when one reflects, 'This was seen by me,' the subject and object are non-different; they shine as two aspects within the cognizer (pramātṛ). For thus [one reflects]: 'Indeed, this was seen by me,' or 'This is that'—even while reflecting within the self whose nature is the 'I' consisting of the threefold structure (tripuṭī)."

As distinct from the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). And for this reason: "this object to be grasped, such as a jar," and "this self who is the cognizer, the subject. Thus, two things appear to the cognizer; these two things are non-different [from him] by virtue of being the grasped and the grasper.

[It is] manifested from its own self. And thus: "The repose of light within itself is indeed proclaimed as the state of 'I' (ahambhāva); and that very repose is said to be [attained] through the cessation of all dependence. And likewise:
"Since the pure knowledge and action of the Lord are indeed [the result of] reflective awareness (vimarśa)," and likewise:
"Otherwise, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) would not be the very nature of manifestation;
for even if an object is colored by light, it would be like an insentient thing such as a crystal," and so forth. Therefore, this is established; such is the meaning of the word "that" (*tat*).
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the *Śrīmat-ṣaḍadhvajñāna-kaumudī* composed by Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha,
through the assistance of the venerable goddess Parā; may there be auspiciousness.
Of those whose hearts have been purified by the recognition of the Lord of Śrī.
Now, all this world that appears— whether existent or non-existent, blue or yellow, gross or subtle, moving or stationary— is nothing but consciousness (*cinmaya*).
Its essential nature is solely the unfolding of the Supreme Lord, which is the very radiance of consciousness.
It is that which is superimposed through the false attribution (*adhyāsa*) upon one's own self; it is ascertained to be like a wave in the ocean.

Is it truly existent within the Supreme Lord, who is one's own self? That which is real manifests externally precisely by virtue of its being real, according to the scriptural statement, "From the Real, the Real is born. For without its abiding within Him, its external manifestation would be impossible.
He says this in order to demonstrate, by means of two sūtras, that it is like the fluid of a peacock's egg.
Oṃ!
The manifestation of existing entities occurs as an external form for those very things that abide within.
Oṃ. Just as before, the object would not be manifest without having the nature of manifestation;
nor could the self-nature of the object be manifestation if it were distinct from manifestation itself.

Oṃ. If manifestation were divided, there would be a confusion of objects; therefore, the object is of the nature of manifestation, for that which is not manifest cannot be established. For indeed, in the case of entities such as jars that appear through direct perception, they are called "entities" (bhāvāḥ) precisely because they exist [as manifest].
Objects are that which have manifestation as their appearance.

For those things situated within the self—which is the directly perceived nature of consciousness—there occurs an external manifestation, like the golden color [within] a peacock’s egg or a metallic essence; this is determined by the principle of *niyati* (the law of necessity), such as [the cognition] "this is a jar," and so forth.

This manifestation, delimited by consciousness (*vidyā*), which consists of both internal and external appearances, has not yet ascended to the status of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) such as a jar; thus, this sequence is established. Furthermore, if it were not so, then [the object] would have been previously known through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Through the knowledge of those who strive [in meditation], it would be as if unknown, because of their mutual pervasion and because of non-pervasion. By what could one grasp what? That effect, being already present within the cause, ought to become manifest externally, just like the fluid within a peacock's egg.

O Lord, it is indeed established as the final doctrine that gold, copper, blue, and so forth—whether produced from mercury or otherwise—are externalized through their respective manifold diversities. Furthermore, that which is called "manifestation" (prakāśa) is not distinct from the object itself, because of their mutual inherence (samavāya). And since...
It is established that luminosity is the very nature of the object. For in this way, it is non-different from its own self;

the meaning is that it is one and all-pervading everywhere. If, on the other hand, it were different from the thing, then there would be a confusion of objects: [one might say] "Bring the jar," and [another] "Bring the cloth."

In such cases as "Bring the cloth," [if one were to say] "Bring the clay," and so forth, even that which consists of knowledge would not be understood. By this, it is shown that the object (*artha*) is also of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*);
for by what cause could manifestation itself not be established?
For the point is this: in the absence of a knower for that which is to be known, by whom would it be perceived? It would be like a stone.

Therefore, that which is within the Lord of the Universe is certainly one's own self; moreover, it exists neither outside nor inside, for such a retinue is beyond reproach. This is because it has been stated: "That which is within is without. And thus say the Sāṃkhyas: "Because what is non-existent cannot be produced, because there must be the grasping of a material cause, because everything cannot arise from everything..."
Because that which is capable produces only what is possible for it, and because the effect exists within the cause, the effect pre-exists [in the cause], and so forth.

Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because it is not perceived, and because it is external; and because inherence is established between them mutually, there is no production from any state whatsoever, due to the absence of power in a single entity.

O Lord, because an agent who possesses power acts only upon what is possible to do; for one performs only that which can be performed—just as clay produces a jar, or threads produce a cloth—but clay does not produce a cloth, nor do threads produce a jar, and so forth. Furthermore, it is because each effect arises from its own specific cause.

Just as clay is the cause for earthenware and gold for golden objects, therefore the effect, being already existent within that cause, ascends to the state of manifestation even externally. If it is argued thus by the proponent of external objects (*bāhyārthavādin*): "The object of cognition is distinct from the external object, [and this distinction is] indicated by the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)."
Let that which is external be, in reality, the nature of valid cognition (pramā) non-different from awakening;
yet it appears as having a distinct nature through jars, cloths, and so forth, being accumulated by the web of shimmering conceptual construction.

What is the use of this [external object] which, in reality, is outside the form of your own conceptual construction? Those who advocate for external objects (bāhyārthavādins) have been successively refuted by their predecessors. Now, having raised the doctrine of external objects once more, [the author] will later refute it as well by means of its representation as a mental image (ālekha).

Having eliminated the two-fold aspect of the self, this entire [universe] is indeed composed of consciousness alone; it manifests externally while remaining within the body of consciousness, which is the very nature of Paramaśiva. This declaration is made clear here by the group of three aphorisms, demonstrating that there is no such thing as "external" at all.

Oṃ. If that sudden appearance were external, it would lead to inference; however, for consciousness which is non-differentiated, there can be no causality for diverse appearances. Nor can the awakening of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) here serve as the cause for such diversity.
Furthermore, what is the cause for the diversity in that awakening? (3ab)

If [the opponent argues that] by means of conceptualization (*ullekha*)— such as "I am having such-and-such an appearance at this time," "I am doing exactly this," or "I know," or "I am going in this way"—
one might infer an external object; yet, for consciousness which is non-different [from its content], there can be no manifold appearance.

How could a causal appearance, being merely accidental, lead to the inference of an external object? For it is pleasing to the heart only by virtue of being a mere delusion. Nor can the awakening of latent impressions (vāsanā) lead to the inference of an external object; for that too occurs only in the form of a mental representation.
How could a mere delusion, like a mirage, lead one to infer [the truth]? For example, O Bhīma, he might say: "I have no means of livelihood here; I am going by the path to the king's gate.
Having arrived there, I will announce my own desire for the kingdom to the king, and the king will grant it."
I take half of that portion, which moves along its path with the speed of a horse.

Having mounted it, I shall go to a foreign land as long as I have strength; having won there wealth measured by a *lakṣa*, I will send 20,000 [coins] to my home, 20,000 to my teacher, 20,000 to my wife, 20,000 to my friends, and 20,000 [to myself].

[These include] ornaments, garments, jewelry, and so forth. Thus, by whom were these latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and the like—both stable and unstable—produced? [They are produced] due to the absence of any specific substratum. And what is the basis for such diversity? Nothing at all. Therefore, even for those two—the spontaneous latent impression and the awakening—[there is no cause].
Because this [external world] also spreads outward by means of a form imagined within its own self, it becomes identical with that [consciousness];
and having attained the state of being the knower, it is always described as "full of joy" (*sollāsa*).
It has been stated that "without that, there is no accomplishment. Therefore, it is said: "That which is situated within me appears as if outside."
It reveals that very essence; nor is there anything external by means of this—such is the intended meaning. || 3 ||

30b) Immediately thereafter, when the mind has thus resolved, he demonstrates that this entire universe is nothing but self-luminous consciousness; therefore, whatever occurs regarding the existence or non-existence of external objects of cognition, it is understood as being identical with that [consciousness].

Oṃ. It might be argued: "When practical activity (*vyavahāra*) is established and determined within those very manifestations (*avabhāsa*), what is the use of another external object that lacks logical justification? O proponent of external objects!
[This refers to] within the manifestations—which are essentially reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—and when practical activity is established and ascertained within those very [manifestations].

There exists an internal discourse within the manifestation (*avabhāsa*), and it is also manifested externally through such [expressions] as "this is a jar," "blue," "yellow," "red," or "this. When this has been thus determined, there is no external [object] that could account for it; rather, it is by means of what is manifested as "this is illogical" (*ayuktam*)—not by means of logical reasoning (*yukti*). For by that [reasoning], it is not [established].

"Something" [is said] because it is not established by reason; thus, these words, blunted in their claim to the existence of external objects and bound to the performance of a futile task, are unfit for any purpose—enough with these mere sounds. And therefore:

Oṃ. Indeed, the Lord is the very nature of consciousness; by the power of His will, He manifests the multitude of objects existing within Him externally, just as a yogi manifests a collection of things without any material cause. Now, it is also stated in the scripture: "This self-luminous conscious Self manifests the multitude of entities residing within."

As previously stated, by its own will, it manifests this [universe] even externally in the form of "this is the remainder" and so forth, through its residual state. How is it without material cause (*upādāna*)? It is without the causal conditions of inherence (*samavāyi*), non-inherence (*asamavāyi*), and instrumental (*nimitta*), as well as other external requisites. How is this? Just like a yogi; for he too—
He remains in the state of yoga.

31a) The Lord, the witness of the universe, the creator and protector of the universe, causes all this world to unfold and also causes it to close; indeed, without any external material cause or accumulation, he manifests this entire universe—which resides within himself—outwardly. (And so it is said:)

"Salutations to that Śūlin (the Wielder of the Trident), who, though boundless like Nārāyaṇa, weaves the variegated picture of the world upon a wall-less canvas by gathering the materials of his own diverse powers—salutations to Him who is worthy of praise for His singular skill. What is this?
Is it an acceptance of the soot-like darkness of a mere verbal bombast? Enough! 39.

Now, if this is so, then among the four types of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), that which is well-known as inference (*anumāna*)— which makes known what is not perceptible by means of what is perceptible, such as fire being made known by the perception of smoke— is itself the superior means of knowledge.
"In all the treatises"— thus he replies, explaining that very same [reality] as being both external and internal.
Oṃ. Inference is not desired as having an object that has never appeared [to consciousness];
for external things such as seeds and the like are indeed non-apparent.
Furthermore, the appearance of an external object could never arise from another appearance; therefore, this [inference] does not [grasp its object].
Nor is there establishment [of the object] through inference (40). Inference is sensory;
it does not apply to what has not previously appeared, such as smoke, with regard to an object like fire that is beyond the senses.
This is not desired—that is, it is not a valid means of knowledge—because the operation of the senses and so forth occurs only toward what has already appeared.

But in the case of non-appearance (*anābhāta*), an increase certainly occurs on the days of the Guru (Thursday) and the Moon (Monday). It did not happen there due to the force of fate (*daiva*). In this very way, even when the self is unmanifest (*anābhāsātman*), activity is not desired by means of the *ku* syllable and so forth. [One might say]: "Because smoke is seen here, fire exists; there, it was not."
How, then, does the operation of inference proceed? Even in the case of a seed and so forth, the external object is not merely a non-manifestation;

rather, it is precisely the manifestation of the internal reality. That a sprout necessarily arises from a seed is indeed perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Therefore, the manifestation of the external is [in fact] the manifestation of the internal reality.

By the statement "this is a jar," [the external object] would not be established, because of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*). Nor is its establishment as an external thing possible through inference, since [inference] does not operate regarding supersensible (*atīndriya*) objects and the like; rather, it applies only as far as the range of the eye extends.
Since the pot is the object to be apprehended and the engagement of inference is what occurs, how can this inference and so forth be the cause for the engagement with that which is beyond the senses?
31b) Furthermore, the sense is that external objects are not established even by means of inference. || 40 || 41 ||
Now he concludes.

Oṃ! From the Lord, there is indeed the manifestation of the multitude of existents established within His own Self; without that [Lord], the reflective awareness of desire (*icchāmarśa*) does not proceed. Therefore, from the Lord, the manifestation of the multitude of existents established within His own Self occurs externally as well. And... [the sentence continues].

Therefore, without that [reflective awareness], deliberation indeed proceeds; for what is called "deliberation" (vimarśa) is the impulse to do something or not to do it. And because they know the reflective awareness of manifestation to be its very nature, otherwise the object would be mere light.

Even when colored by another, it would be like an insentient object such as a crystal (43). For they know that the power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) is the very nature of manifestation, which is essentially consciousness; otherwise, even if the object were illuminated, it would indeed be nearly insentient, like a crystal or similar thing.

This is the certainty. Herein is the intended meaning: the Self, which flashes forth internally as "I" and possesses the nature of both consciousness and non-consciousness, becomes reflected externally through the operation of its power of self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*). It manifests in such [cognitive acts] as "I know," "I act," "I go," and "I perceive."
"Having been projected [into] his own ritual actions and the like as 'worthy' or 'unworthy' through the operation of *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), he acts.
Therefore, it is indeed said that the innate power of *vimarśa* belongs to the Self; for without it, there would be the undesirable consequence of being like a stone. Thus, this being established:

Oṃ. For this very reason, this [subject] should make itself the knower while remaining distinct; however, it does not fragment its own sovereignty by being oriented toward the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). And for this very reason, that which is the object of knowledge is also its very self, because the doctrine of external objects has been refuted. And for this very reason, this Self...

Maheśvara, dividing his very own self, makes it an object of knowledge and causes it to appear as an external object through its state of differentiation from himself. However, when he is free from doubt, that object of knowledge does not exist even in the slightest degree; it has not been, it is not, and it will not be, for it lacks any ontological reality.

Furthermore, the independence of this self would be shattered; it would perish. For through association with that [object], there would be attachment to it, and by means of that, through the repeated realization of identity, there would be identification with its nature.
Consequently, the attainment of its own essential form—the very nature of the self—would be lost. This is indeed established. || 47 ||

And likewise, our supreme preceptor [Abhinavagupta] has said: "I bow to that non-duality which, from the stainless Fullness, first manifests as 'I', and thereafter projects its own manifold digits in their various branches;
it is the state of the expansion and contraction of its own essential nature, the very life-force of existence."
"Everything has Paramaśiva and Śakti as its essence," and so forth; for this very reason.

Oṃ. By means of His sovereignty, the Lord—having fashioned Himself from the non-dual Self through volitions such as "I am Īśvara" and so forth—engages in worldly activity. Therefore, the sovereignty of the Self being established, He manifests Himself as unliberated through that very sovereignty.

The Lord Maheśvara, by His own will, through the nature of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*), having fashioned [the world] with the thought, "I act thus," "I go thus," "I become great in this way," and "I cause my own Self to manifest in this manner," [declares]: "I am the Lord; I am Śiva; I am eternal."

By means of [the realization] "I am Śiva" and so forth, he desires to sport with the *cakras*. Thus, his will—which is the manifestation of the accumulation of power (*śakti*) whose essence is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—is set in motion; in this regard, the Supreme Lord alone is the cause. (48) In this way, there are five powers belonging to this Supreme Lord.
He shows that from freedom comes freedom.

Oṃ. Due to the difference in the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of "I-ness" and so forth, this Self is distinct from that [limited self]; for this creation exists solely as the object of its "I-reflection," like an action under the power of the agent. Herein lies the intended meaning.

"I am Śiva; I am the individual soul (jīva); I am Brahman; I am Viṣṇu; or I am Maheśvara"—by such expressions as these, there is nothing other than this form of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and so forth; there is no other essential nature.
I am Śiva, indeed Śiva; I am Brahmā, indeed Brahmā; I am Viṣṇu, indeed Viṣṇu.
However, because the nature of "I" remains inherent in each of those instances, the sense of "I" is not lost.

Just as when there are various distinctions such as bracelets, earrings, garlands, armlets, and rings made of gold, only the gold remains and not the earrings or other forms; even so, upon their arising, [the Self] would remain as its own specific nature, "I am. And thus: "Of various kinds of colors..."
Just as a stainless crystal assumes the form of gods, humans, animals, or trees, so too does the Lord;
thus it is stated in the *Paramārthasārasaṃgraha*. Therefore, even in this case, it is precisely the "I-ness" (ahantā).
In the ultimate sense, [consciousness] has only the immediately preceding condition and nothing else. And in that regard, what is it like?

Just as with the action [of the root *hu*], it is like this: in examples such as *juhoti*, *juhutaḥ*, and *juhvati*, there are only distinctions of one, two, or three [agents]; however, there is no distinction in the act of offering (*havanakriyā*) itself. And it is established that this [act] is common to all cases. [Objection: But if this is so, regarding such a supreme consciousness (*parāciti*)...
He explains how conceptualization, discursive thought, and so forth are not other than its own nature:

Oṃ. Māyā is that by which the entire range of objects of cognition, distinct from the Lord, is measured (mīyate) and correctly measured (pramīyate) through ignorance, conceptualization, determination, and so forth, appearing in diverse forms such as jars, blue, non-blue, and the like; thus it is called Māyā. And so it is said: [Verse 50]

"Maya, like a puppeteer, brings about subjugation; the Omniscient One is the Lord. But another, being under the sway of ignorance (avidyā), is manifold due to its various forms. Thus, the individual soul (jīva) is said to be consciousness (cit) itself when under the sway of ignorance; and by virtue of that very state of being subject [to it], that consciousness—
It has as its domain distinct objects of cognition, through such variety as "this is a jar," "this is a cow," and so forth.

And it is designated by these very names: "knowledge" (jñāna), "volition" (saṃkalpa), and likewise "determination" (adhyavasāya). It is spoken of by these names because, through the superimposition (adhyāsa) of those [attributes] upon it, it has come under the sway of ignorance (avidyā); this is the intended meaning. [Objection: But if this is so, then regarding experience...

In states such as volition and recollection, because they consist of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and exist with a nature characterized by differentiation (*śūlatva*), let there be the movement of consciousness (*citi*). However, in that state of pure experience alone— which is free from verbal expression, internal discourse, and the like, being an objectless and partless state— there would indeed be only "this is something."

And in that regard, how does this [consciousness] function? For if it were not to function, one would say, "I did not perceive anything," and thus the non-functioning of consciousness would occur. How then could this Self be all-pervasive, the witness of the universe, and indeed woven through everything? Thus, by refuting [the contrary], he demonstrates [its nature].

33a) Oṃ: How could there be the arising of reflective awareness (vimarśa) even at the moment of direct perception? [Otherwise], how could activities such as running toward something be possible, devoid of synthesis (pratisaṃdhāna)? For one who has come from afar and perceives something seen from a distance as "this is something," even in that case...
It must be stated that there certainly exists that which is called "reflective awareness" (vimarśa), because without it, mere experience would not be established.

Immediately thereafter, the sense is that this very consciousness (*cit*), which possesses the power of reflection, persists here as well—designating [the object] as "this is that" through the expression of genus, quality, action, and so forth—and strives to experience it by means of the phrase "and it is maintained. However, in the opposite case: "Having been commanded by the king, he runs for the sake of that task."

If [the cognition] at the moment of reconnection is devoid of verbal expression and the like, how can the exclusion of that [expression] and so forth be established? If this were the case, then there would be no cognizer possessing reflective awareness therein.

And so it is said in the *Spandakārikā*: "Whether extremely angry or exceedingly joyful, or reflecting 'What shall I do?', or running toward a distant goal—one reaches that state where Spanda is established. Now, since the Supreme Lord's nature as the universal agent is established, that which belongs to Him is indeed [Spanda].

"It shines externally; and this 'I' illumines [it] by its very own nature. Regarding this, he states the reason for why it illumines things such as jars in the form of "this" (*idam*), that is, in the form of their specific appearances: * *bahirābhāti* (It shines externally). * *bhāsayati cāyamahaṃ svarūpeṇaiva* (And this 'I' illumines by its very own nature). * *ityatra ca yadidamiti rūpeṇa ghaṭādyākāratayā bhāsayati tatra kiṃ kāraṇamityāha* (And regarding this, he states what the cause is for the fact that it illumines in the form of "this," namely, in the form of the appearance of jars and so forth).
Oṃ. This determination that "this is a jar" is the power of the Supreme Lord, which, like the Self, appears as something beyond name and form; it does not appear as a mere "this-ness."
Oṃ. Pure consciousness alone, in accordance with the differences in space, time, and objects of perception, appears as a succession of cognition, memory, determination, and so forth. (53)
That determination which is intensified by name and form— the ascertainment "this is a jar," the certainty "this is a jar"— is indeed the power of the Supreme Lord;
it shines as Śiva, its own essential nature, through its inner selfhood and not as an external "this-ness."

The sense is that it appears as an object of cognition (*vedyatayā*). However, when there is merely a distinct state of being an object of cognition in accordance with space and time, there is memory of cognitions; the sense is that determination (*avasāya*) and so forth appear as having transitioned [into that state].
33b) "This is a jar," "This is a cloth," and so forth—these are distinct objects of cognition.

In that regard, there is conformity to place and time, because such [cognition] is possible in any place or at any time. Therein, what is called "knowledge" consists of the form of experience such as "this is this," and so on; and prior to that—

That recollection is [the thought]: "That which was previously experienced by me is indeed this very same thing. And therein, the determination is the ascertainment; thus follows the path of worldly convention. It is precisely this that appears as having a sequence, but in ultimate reality, there is no sequence, nor even—
Only sequence remains; that which is called knowledge, the supreme reality known as Brahman, is the ultimate principle, and thus nothing appears to possess sequence.
And so it is for the proponents of consciousness (Vijñānavādins): "The object of cognition is that which has the appearance [of the cognition]; apart from that, there is no other object."
Furthermore: "The apprehended form and the cognition [of it]—these three are not therefore made separate."
Because, through such [statements], a single cognition alone appears as having a threefold nature, there is nothing else. // 53 //
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha.
May there be auspiciousness for the devotees of Śiva; now, [regarding] the Great Lord within one's own self...

He explains through three verses that the two-fold nature of "I" and "not-I," which is the very essence of Supreme Bhairava, shines forth by its own inherent nature; thus, there is never any loss of that essential nature.

Oṃ! That reflective awareness which, though its essence is light, has speech as its body, is not a conceptual construction; rather, it is rightly called a determinative cognition because it excludes duality.
Oṃ! Indeed, the manifestation of two distinct things—such as a jar and a non-jar—would only occur through the Light itself;
there is no manifestation of anything else that is separate from it.

Oṃ. That [cognition] belongs only to those who possess the capacity for such intuitive manifestation (*pratibhā*), because it excludes everything that is not that [object]. Indeed, this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "this is a jar" is said to be a determination of that [object]. And as for the internal perception "I," such as "I act," "I know," "I sleep," "I... [and so forth].

In such expressions as "I am going," that which is called the reflective awareness of "I" (aham-avamarśa) is precisely of the form "I" (aham). This [I] is characterized by pure sovereignty (svātantrya), is the full consciousness (cit), consists of the nature of the subject (hantā), and has as its inherent nature that which manifests everywhere. And for that [I], there is no "I am going."

By such [expressions] as "I do" and so forth, through contact with great limiting adjuncts (*mahopādhi*) and the like, there is indeed multiplicity. And by that, one might be able to know that one has fallen away from one's own true nature. For this [Self], whose essence is light, is always [so] according to the characteristics stated [in the passage] beginning with "from the stainless, full [light]."

It is the luminous body of consciousness; for this very reason, it is the body of speech. Its ultimate reality is the form of the supreme *parā-vāk* which is dissolved within, meaning its essence is pure consciousness.

For non-silence (amauna) is indeed what is called conceptual construction (vikalpa). Rather, it is the determination of both [the self and the non-self]. The intended meaning is that the determination of the nature of "I" and "not-I" is what is called [conceptual construction]. He states this very point:

The manifestation of both the distinct [entities], the jar and the non-jar, is indeed their illumination by means of this [cognition] "this. It is the manifestation of light itself, and not the manifestation of any other separate, differentiated entity; for it is impossible for anything other than that [light] to possess luminosity. Thus it is said.

Siddham. And thus: by the measure (*mātrā*) and the measurer (*pramātṛ*), who possess the manifestation of that [reality], there arises the cognition "this is a jar, not a cloth. Furthermore, the delusion regarding what is not that [reality] is destroyed because everything has that as its true nature (*svarūpa*). And the ascertainment (*niścayana*) of that is the act of making it certain; this is what is called "distinct knowledge" (*pṛthag-jñāna*). [The word] "jar" [is used].

Thus, because there is no exclusion (*vyapohana*) of "that" and "not-that," this conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) "this is a jar" exists through their mutual interpenetration. This too is indeed the reality of Maheśvara;
it is not something other than Him. As for the external world, this conceptual construction "this is a jar" is established.

Therefore, what is called "sequence" (krama) is entirely subsumed within that [Self], for this Self of everyone is non-different from its own nature as "I. Now, one might object: how can there be the superimposition of "not-I" upon the Self, which is the very nature of the pure subject as "I," since such a superimposition would be useless?
He says this, shattering the mere delusion that thinks, "How is it that he is thus? and "How is it that he who is thus could be otherwise?"—it is nothing but delusion.

Oṃ. That which, having abandoned its state of being the mind through Māyā, shines forth as indeed non-different [from itself], yet appears as if differentiated within the body, the intellect, or the vital breath by means of an imagined nature; that reflective awareness as the subject, expressed as "I," arises from the exclusion of other [objects] and is nothing but a conceptual construction born from the appearance of an external counter-correlate. (57)

Herein lies the intended meaning: the reflective awareness of "I" (aham-avamarśa) is twofold—pure (śuddha) and pertaining to māyā (māyīya). Among these, the pure is the nature of consciousness as it shines forth; the impure, however, consists of the body, the vital breath, and the senses.

In the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, [the Self], having abandoned its manifesting nature (*prakāśamāna-svarūpa*), abides in the form of the subject (*pramātṛtā-ahaṃ-rūpeṇa*) and functions by making that subjectivity its primary concern through the conceit (*abhimāna*) of being that subject.
"I alone am the body and so forth," or "I am the objects of cognition, both blue and non-blue."

"Possessing the conceit of being a knower" (pramātṛtvābhimānavān) means that, having abandoned the state of being the mind through the method of falsely identifying with it, [the Self] appears as a separate manifestation as the knower within everything from the body up to the ether—
such as "I am the embodied one," "I am the vital breath," and so forth.
Because it excludes [the notion] "it is something else," that is indeed a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), produced by the appearance of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*).

"I am the embodied one, not the vital breath; or I am the vital breath, not the intellect; or I am the intellect, not space," and so forth—this is the state of being the counter-correlate to another. In that regard, the Ājīvakas, by virtue of [observing] the production of qualities through cooking, transformation, and so on, maintain that the body is the self because it is unstable.

And they think thus: consequently, the followers of Kaṇāda and others consider the intellect (*buddhi*) itself—which serves as the locus for knowledge, pleasure, and so forth—to be the self (*ātman*). Furthermore, some among those who know the Upaniṣads consider the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone to be the self, as it is the substrate of hunger and thirst. And others...

The Sāṅkhyas and others who propound a void Brahman declare that the Self is the principle of space (*nabhas-tattva*), which— being devoid of the entire aggregate of all objects of knowledge— is like the sky due to its emptiness and possesses the nature of the great element of ether, yet they regard this as the subject (*pramātṛ*).

This is the intended meaning here: the subject (*pramātṛ*) who, by virtue of being under the power of *māyā*, abandons the state of pure consciousness (*cittatva*) and resides in the body, the intellect (*buddhi*), and so forth—that subject is also nothing but a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because its activity consists in the exclusion of other things (*anyavyapohana*) and because it is dependent upon a counter-correlate (*parapratiyogitva*). By this, [the status of] that which has the form of the "I" of the intellect (*buddhyahaṃ-rūpa*) is not [established as ultimate].

There is no doubt whatsoever regarding purity, impurity, and so forth; however, it should be understood that due to the influence of contact with *māyā* and the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the conscious and unconscious, there occurs the superimposition (*adhyāhāra*) of this or that [attribute]. 57.
Moreover:

Oṃ. Even that conceptual construction of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) which consists in the joining of previous appearances and so forth—occurring at some time within a single manifestation—is appropriate only when [the subject] appears as distinct [at different times]. [For example: "I who was a child am the very same I who am now young," or "He who was young is the very same one who is now old. Such is the joining of previous appearances and so forth.

Sometimes [the notion] may arise with respect to the body and so forth due to the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience; and that too has been called "conceptual construction" (*kalpanā*) when there is a distinct appearance. By this, since the Lord himself plays as one who is limited by *māyā*, what room for objection is there? Thus, everything is faultless. || 58 ||
35a) Now, he concludes this very same point previously stated by means of another reasoning through the sense of four verses.
Oṃ. Thus, even in the realm of conventional practice, the Lord, having entered the body and so forth, may manifest by His own will external objects that were already shining within.
Oṃ. Thus, whether in conceptualization, or in the process of its removal, or even in knowledge, it is certain that the internal manifestation remains ever-present.
Oṃ. However, in the case of innate knowledge whose nature is external manifestation, it exists in the form of a prior experience within recollection and other such mental states. (62)
Oṃ! There exists only the natural state within conceptual construction, which moves through the vowels;
for it appears as whatever configuration is intended within the sphere of the intellect.
Therefore, for that reason, the Lord— relying upon the body and so forth,

and engaging in worldly discourse such as "I act" and "I know"— may manifest by His own will, through the opening [of His power], the entire flood of objects existing only within Him, outwards. Therefore, regarding the experience of this Lord:

Therefore, it is certain that the internal manifestation remains present even within recollection, then within conceptualization, then within the process of exclusion (*apohana*), and within the definitive cognition or knowledge such as "this is a cow" or "this is not a horse."

And because of that manifestation as something external, in the experience "this is a jar," the previous experience remains and is as if established within the memory, such as "this is the very thing I saw before" or "this is Devadatta. Therefore, the multitude of objects resides within the Lord.

Since it is manifested even externally, it is established that this entire collection of objects, while being manifested, is of the very nature of non-dual consciousness and is therefore essentially identical with light. Consequently, that [consciousness], which consists of prior experience, resides within a conceptual construction that moves according to its own will— that is, one that functions by its own free choice.

In the conceptualization of a jar and so forth, there exists that which is innate and natural: "This is Devadatta," or "This is Vāmanadatta," who was invited to the great sacrifice and other such rites.

Because of the manifestation of the intended configuration through such [means], it is revealed within the stainless intellect; and for this very reason, that very Maheśvara-tattva pervades everywhere—
in all experience, recollection, and so forth— by way of its essential nature as "I am" (sad-aham).

"35b) It reveals that which resides within its own self even externally. Thus, the sense is: "In this way, I, characterized by consciousness, am one who illuminates both the internal and the external through my activity (vṛtti). 62.
Now, by means of this [text], the Light-natured One manifests outwardly that very object which was already situated within; knowing it thus, one attains recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and,
having tasted it, realizes that all is indeed the nature of the recognition of the Lord (*īśvara*).
