Showing that [the goal] is accomplished without effort according to the principle of *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*— namely, that one indeed becomes one who has fulfilled all duties— he says:
Oṃ, for this very reason, because of the manifestation of whatever is desired through its clear delineation, knowledge and action are clearly established as inherent in every living being. (63)
And this is the meaning here: in the phrase "of every living being," the singular number is used to indicate a class (*jātāv ekavacanam*). As in:

"The cause for the emergence of that [poetry] is the examination of the world, the sciences, and the treatises on poetics, as well as practice through the instruction of those who know poetry. Here [the singular is used].

Regarding the "arising" (udbhava), that is, the composition, of that poem (*kāvya*): these very [factors] are the cause (*hetu*), expressed here in the singular number, and not by the plural designation "causes" (*hetavaḥ*). For this reason, even here, by the phrase "of every living being," it is meant "of others who depend upon life. To illustrate: one has gone out from the house.
Seeing the village youth with his hand holding a fresh, brightly blooming cluster of blossoms, the complexion of the young woman’s face becomes increasingly pale as she gazes at him;
observing this, Devadatta reflects: "Is she one whose eyes are like lotus petals?"
"Born with a soiled face. From this it follows that he was not endowed with qualities such as natural beauty;

thus, seeing him young, she became infatuated. Therefore, it is known that the implied meaning (*vyaṅgya*) is: "You have not come to the house for the fourfold rendezvous," [as indicated by] the soiled face. By this, [the state of being] *malinamukhā*...

"Thus having understood [this], one engages in the activity of one's own duty. By this, it is established that for every living being, both knowledge and action are accomplished by their very nature—even in the case of all animals and so forth. Thus it is everywhere.

Knowledge and action are established by their very nature. Even a beast, having gone out from its house onto the path or into the forest, or into water and so forth, knows whatever edible things such as grass it encounters and consumes that alone;
it does not consume things such as dry wood or thorny grass. Therefore, knowledge and action are indeed established even for it.

By this [statement], it is established that even for a bound soul (*paśu*), knowledge and action are established by their very nature. Therefore, for whom would this pair known as knowledge and action not be established? This is the sense. For this very reason it has been said: "Knowledge and action are clearly established for every living being. Why? Because, as previously stated, they exist according to one's desire.

"Because of the manifestation as a comprehensive synthesis. Thus, in this *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (conclusion established by the context), the sense is that the meaning of the scripture, which consists of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), is not unestablished for us through supreme inference;
rather, once that [scriptural] meaning is established, its subsequent... [follows].
Even other matters are established [by implication]. This is the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on a supporting argument). For example:

"The Supreme Lord, whose own nature is consciousness, does not engage in worldly recollection and so forth. This is in accordance with the meaning expressed by such statements as, "I know," "I act," and so on.

For when that [Lord] is established, other entities following Him are also established. It would also be established that Maheśvara is both the agent and the knower. Thus, it is proven that this entire living being is endowed with knowledge, action, and so forth. 63.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the *Śrīmat-Pratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha.

36b) Now, since these Buddhist elders previously raised the darkness of doubt regarding the question, [we reply that] there is no experiencer of self-experience and so forth, because such a thing is not perceived. And what is this [experiencer]? Is it the body, or the vital breath, or the intellect?
By the words "or like the sky," and so forth, he has merely fashioned a stain upon his own face. Now,
having dispelled that stain of their doctrine, he reveals himself through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) and for the sake of removing the great doubt [of others].

Oṃ. That which appears as this manifestation, colored by the sequence of objects yet itself non-sequential and infinite in its nature as consciousness—that cognizer is Maheśvara. Since this Maheśvara, whose nature is unsurpassed luminosity, has "I" (aham) as the essence of his self-reflection, he is indeed that very [Maheśvara].

The conscious self, which is the bliss of absolute freedom, is called "awakening" (bodha); for it has already been established previously that it is always of the nature of pure consciousness alone, persisting everywhere even in experiences such as perception and recollection. That very consciousness is of this kind; it is that very [consciousness] which constitutes each respective object.

The jar and other objects, consisting of reflections, are made to undergo diversity; yet she herself is of the singular nature of the reflection of consciousness (*cidābhāsa*), distinct from both contact with and non-contact with those [objects]. For this very reason, she is called the "successionless, infinite form of consciousness" (*akramānantacidrūpa*). And for this very reason, she alone—since...

The "knower" (*pramātṛ*) is that whose nature is the cognition of identity with the triad consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; he is called the Great Lord (*maheśvara*) because he is of the essence of those [three]. Furthermore, their relationship is one of mutual pervasion. And so it is said in the *Tantrāloka*: "Of the single Lord of Consciousness..."
The internal intuition (*pratibhā*) is the body [of consciousness]. It is either gentle or otherwise, and it is measured;
thus they worship the wheel of the waves of consciousness. Internal intuition is the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*).
That [intuition] is "measured" because it is delimited by various gentle or fierce forms and so forth. And this very [point is as follows]:
He demonstrates by analyzing: "From this [state], nourishment arises"—thus has this Goddess Saṃvit arisen.
From meditation that is mixed with discursive thought and yet free from [external] activity,

the Lord of the Image (Bimbeśvara), who is Bhairava as pure consciousness, is worshipped by those seekers of knowledge who desire both worldly enjoyment and liberation, through both limited and unlimited [states]. Those who...

"For the wise know that nothing whatsoever exists as an object of worship apart from awakening; even they, when discerning awakening, regard [all things] as non-different from awakening," and so forth. Likewise, elsewhere:
This self is the supreme bliss; this consciousness is self-luminous.

This consciousness is self-luminous, meaning it is self-manifesting because it is not an object of cognition (*avedyatva*), whereas in the case of its opposite, such as a jar and the like, there is perceptibility (*parokṣatva*). Wherever there is non-objectivity, there is no perceptibility; wherever there is perceptibility, there is [objectivity].

Self-luminosity [is established] as follows: like consciousness (*saṃvit*). Wherever there is no non-mediatedness while being unobjectifiable, there is no self-luminosity; for example, a jar—this is the negative instance (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*). Thus, this positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) has been previously established.
This is conventional usage; for instance, [the statement] "consciousness is the self" and so forth, because consciousness itself is apprehended in such a manner.

And likewise: "There the sun does not shine, nor the moon and stars; these lightnings do not shine, much less this fire. Everything shines only after Him as He shines; by His light all this is illumined."
All this shines by means of speech. And so says the Veda: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning;
once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists.
He supported the earth and this heaven—what god shall we worship with our oblation? Thus it is said.

Thus, the cognizer is Maheśvara, who is established as previously described; he is the supreme Śiva, the omnipresent meditator whose nature consists of meditation and the object of meditation. He is proven to be the cause of the thirty-six principles beginning with Śiva and ending with the Earth, and the source of all powers. Now, [the following is stated]: 64. Now...
By means of the pervasion between the object of knowledge and the knower, their mutual relationship is demonstrated through a connection that is like the joining of hands.

"Oṃ! That [recognition] is established when various entities, through the gateways of their distinct cognitions, come to rest within a single subject; it is in this state that such recognition becomes possible. And since, due to their internal nature, there is now a unity of the subject, the external pursuit of entities occurs; thus, here, between the object and the subject, there is a mutual..."
The connection is with the destination; and that very thing is the connection known as the reunion with kinsmen.

The state of being known is their bondage, occurring sequentially for the two groups of entities; the sense is that there is a mutual relationship of bondage between those two. For when entities such as jars and so forth are established within the subject (pramātṛ), they proceed [toward him].

37b) Indeed, there is no need for the removal of another [concept]. For those who know this, the mutual relationship between [the notions] such as "this is a jar" and so forth is indeed easy to understand. Therefore, this [principle] is established as being appropriate for the wise, pertaining precisely to the internal distinction between the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the knower (*vedaka*).

The sense is that even externally, this sequence of the perceived and the perception transcends [the external world]. Now, he demonstrates how, in the absence of this [internal sequence], there could indeed be no mutual relationship between the two:
"Oṃ! Of objects that are completed within themselves through the sequence of space and time, there is a simultaneous manifestation..."
Otherwise, how could there be such a coordination?

(66) If this were not the case, then how indeed could there be what is called "coordination"? For if it were independent of that [object], there would be the undesirable consequence of its activity being independent; whereas if it depends on that, there is its dependence for activity.

Those who know this say it is simply by way of a logical consequence (*prasaṅga*). Therefore, that which is to be accomplished through a single manifestation, and which is to be accomplished solely by the consciousness of the Supreme Consciousness (*paracit*), is worthy of being established. What is the connection (*samanvaya*) or relation?
None whatsoever. [This applies] to objects such as various pots and the like, as well as to space and time.
They desire the sequence of the sacrifice in this manner. Of what kind of beings? Of those who are self-perfected.
In their own form; that is, for those who have reached completion within the internal nature of their own self.

The connection is as follows: "For what [entity] could there be a concomitance (anvaya) by way of being distinct from those [three] modes? Therefore, one [mode] exists in space, another exists in time, and another exists in sequence. Furthermore, regarding space, time, and sequence, this [concomitance] is accomplished solely through the cognition of objects that possess intrinsic natures (svabhāva).
Otherwise, the sequence is different. In the absence of that [sequence], it continues until its own completion; this is how the connection with the word "ka" (who/which) is to be understood. || 66 ||

Now, is the relationship between objects—which possess a sequence of space and time—accomplished by a simultaneous manifestation? For indeed, in the processes of inference, smoke is the cause of fire; where there is no smoke, there is no fire either. Thus, through the intention to express the non-difference between the cause and the effect, the cause itself [is the probans].

"One should cause [the disciple] to hear that which possesses a cause"—with this, he asks: "What is the use of this further, most trivial worldly transaction consisting of the identity between the object to be known and the act of knowing? Thus he speaks.

38a) Oṃ. For perceptions and non-perceptions that fall upon various distinct parts [of an object], a simultaneous appearance must be established; otherwise, what kind of coherence could there be? Here, when a jar is perceived, a cow is not apprehended; and immediately thereafter, stones and other things [are also not apprehended].

One perceives [the cause] by direct perception itself, thinking, "These are cows. Therefore, if one who is blind or deaf does not see a jar, then they likewise do not see cows and so forth either. Thus, through both direct perceptions and non-perceptions, the relationship of cause and effect is established.

[This relation] is mutual; and it arises solely from a single cognizer. It arises solely from the Self, because [the cognizer], as the subject, is everywhere of the nature of consciousness. Otherwise, how could there be a mutual cognition between smoke and other such causes and their effects, which are established in the preceding [moment] as being grounded in their own respective parts?
Because it is possible [to establish it] in that way. And thus: "That [is for those] who fall into distinct parts. In this manner, it is established:

if the comprehensive unity (*samanvaya*) were not to be accomplished by a single appearance, then what kind of comprehensive unity could there be among perception and the other means of knowledge, which fall into distinct parts? By whom [could it be seen]? By no one.
For it is established as follows: "This mountain possesses fire, because it possesses smoke; whatever possesses smoke possesses fire, like a kitchen hearth;
and whatever does not possess fire does not possess smoke, like a great lake. For in such cases, what indeed is the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) between smoke and fire?

"Because its nature consists of both manifestation and non-manifestation"—by this [statement], since there are distinct parts, nothing whatsoever is logically tenable apart from the cognitive aspect of the subject (*pramātṛ*). The sense is that it has been stated: "Otherwise, what would constitute a coherent synthesis? Therefore, only what was previously stated [remains valid].
To provide further confirmation, he says: "Oṃ! That very self-awareness which exists in mindfulness is the means of valid cognition regarding the arising of one's own nature."
If there is the possibility of a prior experience, that very [consciousness] is the means of proof, and nothing else.
Thus, it is exactly as stated before: whatever consciousness exists in a prior experience, such as "this is a jar," and so forth.
That very [cognition] occurs in memory later, as in such cases as "this was seen by me," and so forth.
Thus, it is established that the worldly transaction between these two— the bound and the binder— is designated as their mutual relationship.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha.

Now, there are also other conventions such as the sublated and the sublator, light and darkness, and others established previously by the proponents of existence (bhāvavādins) and composed by the masters.

"What is the purpose of one's own self, which consists of awakening? For the perception of cause and effect and so forth occurs through the conventional usage of the sublated and the sublator; therefore, enough with this self in the form of a 'knower' (vedaka) or an 'I'. Thus reflecting, he [the teacher] first [addresses] those who have become such."

Having accepted [the opponent's position] merely through their discourse, does he subsequently examine even their view from the standpoint of his own doctrine? He states that both external and internal worldly transaction cannot be established without a single cognizing subject (pramātṛ).

Oṃ. Even the relation of the sublated and the sublator among contradictory things rests within the self [of consciousness]; knowledge does not arise as one [independent entity], because they are fully established within a single cognizer (pramātṛ). In the case of "this is silver" regarding mother-of-pearl, there is a sublation of the silver and so forth by means of the qualities of the mother-of-pearl, such as its whiteness; and that [sublation] belongs to the cognizer.

Without dependence [on something else], it is not established. Silver does not exist in mother-of-pearl, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [silver] being produced even in mother-of-pearl. Here, the very fact that it is mother-of-pearl is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The cognition of silver is not [produced] by non-cognition and so forth, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of mutual contradiction. Thus...

Therefore, because the two cognitions reside within their own respective portions, there is a contradiction in their being mutual causes and effects; for where is the mother-of-pearl, and where is the silver and so forth therein? And where is that whiteness?
Due to this mutual contradiction between these two, the cause here is the state of a single cognizing subject (*pramātṛ*).
The point is that even there, without a foundational basis (*sambhāva*), there can be no comprehension of the knowledge regarding mutual contradiction or non-contradiction.
Thus, in that case as well, the application of the conventional distinction between the sublated and the sublator does not arise by itself;
rather, it is the single cognizing subject—the self whose nature is consciousness—who, being himself the witness (*sākṣin*), [establishes it].

Now, even if [the object] were otherwise established merely by way of conceptual construction, it would not be established without dependence on a cognizer; for there can be no establishment without a cognizer. Demonstrating this as well, he says:

O you who propound non-existence (*abhāvavādin*), if you say: "Just as the cognition of the absence of a jar in a secluded spot is valid knowledge, so too is the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl the awareness of its invalidity. (70)

The knowledge of the bare ground is: "There is no jar on this ground. And just as there is the cognition of the absence of the jar—the apprehension of the absence of the jar—due to the ground being bare in its solitary state, in exactly the same way, the cognition of the mother-of-pearl is also solitary.
The cognition of silver is the cause for the absence of the cognition of the [actual] form; however, that [absence] does not exist. And because:

Oṃ. The nature of a jar cannot be established for that [place] merely through the cognition of a pure location. Nor is the absence of something here, even if it were capable of being perceived by its form, the same as the nature of a jar. This is not a rule: that by the cognition of a pure location, such as "there is no jar on this ground," [the jar's nature is thereby negated]. Therefore...

The nature of being a jar would not be established. What is our objection? Even in the case of "there is a jar here on this ground," even though the jar is perceptible, it is simply the absence of the jar [on that spot]. This is because the gross jar and its parts are possible as distinct from one another in their own respective natures. Nor is there a mutual [identity] between the jar and the location.

The relationship between cause and effect exists because they possess distinct constituent parts (*bhinnāṃśatvāt*). For example, through the cognition of a clean spot on the ground, there arises the notion of the absence of a jar; likewise, this occurs through the cognition of a clean thread as well.
This is indeed due to their mutual distinction of constituent parts. By this [it is established].

The knowledge of the pure, the impure, and the gross is exactly the same; thus, the point is that even by this [distinction], the relationship between the object of cognition and the cognizer would not be established without a single subjectivity (pramātṛtā). || 71 ||
He now demonstrates that very point.
Oṃ! The ground of reality is eternally secluded, because all phenomena are established within their own self-nature.
How then can that cognition, being distinct [from its object], establish the non-existence of that [object]? (72)

The ground is always indeed empty, because entities such as jars are established within their own selves; for the jar and the locus of the ground are established within their own respective parts, such that one says, "This is the jar," and "This is the ground. Nor does the cognition "this is a jar" [negate] the nature of the ground.

This is because there is no cognition of their mutual identity. Furthermore, the cognition "this is gross" does not constitute the cognition of a jar, nor is that [cognition of a jar] identical to those two.

Therefore, this is logical: the ground is eternally secluded because entities reside within their own essential parts. For that very reason, how could the cognition of that [ground]—that is, the cognition of its grossness—be the non-existence of a jar distinct from itself?

The proof: it would follow that non-existence is the cause; thus, there is never the existence of a mutual relationship of cause and effect between the two. Nor does anything at all follow from mere non-existence alone; to this he says:
Oṃ. However, for a blind person, the touch of light and so forth is soft;

therein, one may establish their own cognition of its nature as being non-material (aghaṭātmatā). For the blind person, whose self is distinct from light, because of the absence of eyes, that mass of light— [Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the function of the mass of light.]

The touch of being slightly warm and so forth [is perceived] through the functioning of the tactile sense organ (*tvagindriya*). And by that [functioning], its nature as a jar also becomes manifest, since it possesses touch.

This [argument] is not necessary for him, nor does it exist; for touch, such as heat and so forth, does not establish the nature of a jar. Moreover, in that case as well, the conscious subject (*pramātṛ*), who is all-pervasive, indeed knows by means of that cause, namely touch and so forth. However, in this context, touch alone is not the cause.

"Because they possess distinct natures due to being established within their own respective parts," as has been stated and will be stated again [in verse 73]. "And even so, nothing such as a purpose or benefit is attained," they say.

Oṃ: Just as a *piśāca* might exist within the light even though it is not visible [to that light], so too that which is invisible within the interior of the earth must be prohibited in every respect. Here, there is the establishment of a *piśāca* on the surface of the earth, just as one says, "A *yakṣa* dwells here in the Vahavaṭa."
However, it is not necessarily the case that a piśāca does not exist there simply because it is not perceived.

Because the speaker lacks the capacity [to deceive]; because the probandum is established by means of the authority of scripture, which is the authority of all authorities; and even if a piśāca were there though not perceived, the point is that here it is indeed perceived through the establishment of the authority of scripture.

40a) Just as in this case, a negation such as "there is no jar on this ground" can be employed in linguistic usage, so too one cannot employ the linguistic usage "there is no piśāca on this ground. This is because it would result in a logical absurdity (prasaṅga) that contradicts the words of a reliable authority (āpta). However, a jar [is perceptible] even in direct light.

It cannot be negated by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because this light near the jar does not abide within the jar due to the latter’s limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Therefore, that which is distinct from it must be negated in every respect.

Even if a *piśāca* were to exist in the midst of the world or even within the earth itself, its existence would not obstruct the state of being "non-light. Therefore, it is simply not something that can be negated; the point is that by this [argument], there is nothing whatsoever established as a reason for one another through the presence of a logical reason (*hetu*).

However, if there were only one single cognizer (*pramātṛ*), then everything would be established everywhere; so what is this conventional usage of negation? For by that very usage, having set aside what is established as its own nature, it would resort to another appearance, like a snake [superimposed] upon a rope; thus, there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) here. Indeed, this is not the case for that which is uncreated (*akṛtaka*).

For the pervasion (vyāpti) is that whatever is produced must depend upon a substrate. Therefore, even in this case, it is the established conclusion of all systems that it is only the Light itself, appearing as the cognizer, which manifests the object to be manifested; this is the certainty of the final doctrine. Now, [regarding] even those who maintain the theory of non-existence (abhāvavādins)...

Having refuted the opponent's view— held by some that the darkness of the sky is like the grime of smoke or dust— by means of the very fact that it would stain one's own face, he concludes the establishment of his own position by applying it to the subject at hand.

Oṃ. In this way, the cognition of mother-of-pearl, which has as its form the absence of silver, would not be a communicator of the invalidity of the initial cognition of silver; for it is established that the cognition of the mother-of-pearl is established as having a white nature.

Furthermore, the cognition of mother-of-pearl as having the nature of the absence of silver would also be established; and in that case, the invalidity of the initial cognition of silver would be established.

It has been stated that [things] possess mutually distinct natures, and this will be further explained later. Thus, it is established that this entire worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) would be impossible to accomplish without the existence of a cognizer (*pramātṛ*). || 78 ||

40b) Objection: If there is no cognition of silver in the case of mother-of-pearl and the like due to mere error, then let there be a cognition of silver in that very place through the means of inference. For instance: wherever there is whiteness, there is a cognition of silver, as in the case of the objects of the nine treasures.

The cognition of gold and so forth arises through the perception of white, red, and other colors. Wherever there is no perception of white or non-white—such as in the case of a forest fire and the like—there is likewise no perception of gold or non-gold.
Where such [color-perception] does not exist, it is also absent; for example, in the case of objects such as cowries or mother-of-pearl shells.

Thus, since linguistic usage proceeds on the basis of inference, why is the cognition of silver even in the case of mother-of-pearl not a cognition that is apprehended by another cognition? Nor can it be argued that here there is merely a state of being restricted to its own subjective aspect, for that would contradict your own doctrine. To this, they reply:
Oṃ! Even for one who has established the Dharma, there can be no sublation by means of inference.

But that [knowledge] which is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is logical, as it arises from the cognizer alone. As it was said regarding the "nine treasures" (*navanidhi*) and so forth: "We do not consider that to be false. In inference (*anumāna*) and the like, when the existence of the reason (*hetu*) in the subject (*pakṣa*), the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), and the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*) is present, there is inference and so forth.

This is a matter of conventional usage; however, it does not apply in cases such as "this is silver" with respect to mother-of-pearl, because in the absence of a subject (pakṣa), there can be no similar instance (sapakṣa), and in the absence of that, there can likewise be no dissimilar instance (vipakṣa).
Just as when the root is absent, there is an absence of branches, leaves, and so forth, this [conventional usage] is merely a delusion.

And it is established that because of the manifestation [of consciousness], there is an absence of objects; and because of the absence of those [objects], there is an absence of the subject. For this very reason, since the substratum (dharmin) is not established, there can be no sublation even by means of inference. However, in the case of that which is manifest, whose nature is eternally existent, permanent, all-pervading, and the single form of the universe—

When one's own self is established, even that sublation is unestablished; yet it is established—such is the command of the Supreme Guru. This conventional usage is established as the experience of one's own self. Without this, no reasoning whatsoever exists, nor is there anything but the perception of mere delusion; thus it is established. || 77 ||
41a) Now he concludes all of this: "All."

Oṃ. Thus, within the all-pervasive [Lord] who is inlaid with the appearance of objects that are extremely distinct from one another, worldly transaction—whether characterized by impurity or purity—is experienced. (78) "Thus" means in this aforementioned manner; "extremely distinct objects" refers to entities such as blue, non-blue, and so forth. By these, he is "inlaid."
In the pervasive and all-encompassing Lord Ādiśa, who is called Vāk and is the supreme reality within one's own self, [he who is] stained [is situated].

"This is a jar," "this is a cloth," and so forth; whatever there may be, such as "I am stainless" and so on—whether pure or impure, gross or subtle—all that is experienced in that very [consciousness]. This is the intended meaning here: and Śakti...

The possessor of power (*śaktimān*) and power itself (*śakti*) are said to be two categories of reality. By the statement, "His powers are the entire universe, while the possessor of power is Maheśvara," he who is known as the Knower (*vedaka*)—the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), whose essence is power—is indeed that very one. And that which is called his power is also [that same reality].

The meaning is this: because they are included within the one [consciousness], they are of the nature of consciousness (cit-svabhāva); thus, even externally, they expand as the mere arising of the flash of consciousness (unmeṣa-ccha-jā).

Therefore, being of the form of the mere flash of the nectar of consciousness, they are indeed of the nature of pure consciousness alone; there is no such thing as an object of knowledge other than that. And so it will be stated further on.
Externality is held to be the limiting adjunct (upādhi) for the appearances of existence and non-existence.
It is not because of the non-existence of a self, since those internal [factors] exist as real entities, as expressed by the words "always existing" and so forth.

Therefore, what was said is indeed logical: "In the all-pervasive [consciousness] which is inlaid with the manifestation of diverse objects, worldly transaction—whether stained or stainless—is experienced. Thus it is established.

In this world, which appears like a reflection in a mirror, nothing whatsoever is perceived as "the object of knowledge" or "the knower," for it is merely a delusion; the sense is that this is well-established, as in the cases of a city of Gandharvas or a mirage in a desert. Thus, this [nature of reality] is proven.
The knower is one's own self, the Great Lord; it is established that Śiva alone is the omniscient agent and the experiencer. Thus [ends the section] composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha.
The ninth daily lesson in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* is completed.

41b) Now, as for what was previously stated— that this conventional usage is experienced as being either with stain or without stain, and so forth— it is thus like an illusion (*māyā*), appearing through the sequence of being manifest or unmanifest, while the resonance (*dhvani*) is otherwise.
Oṃ. Sometimes appearances depend solely on the immediate perception of the sense organs;

otherwise, they appear differently in states such as blindness or dense darkness. This is the manifestation of existence and non-existence here, occurring upon the attainment of specific conditions such as blindness or deafness.
The experiences of the experiencing person certainly occur as direct perceptions,
such as "this is a jar," "this is a cloth," "this is blue," "this is yellow," and so forth.
"Because of the absence of great defects such as mental or physical deafness," so it has been stated in some places.

Otherwise, it is different in other cases. Due to the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of blindness, deafness, or partiality, those very experiences become objects of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet they may also become non-perceptual in some instances.
They go from being perceptible to being imperceptible. For example: "What do you hear? "I hear, but very faintly. "What do you hear? "Nothing at all."

The same applies even in cases such as thick darkness (*andhatamasa*). While running for the sake of some task during the day, one sees everything and proceeds; yet, when darkness has arisen, one does not see anything at all. This is due to the increase of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of *tamas*. By this, this alone is the distinction in experience. As for the experiencer (*anubhāvaka*), however—

Such is its own purity: that which is the object of the light of day by day, and likewise the object of darkness by night—even when the entire universe is immersed [in it]—it is of such a nature as to be self-luminous, self-manifesting, eternally unobscured, and all-pervasive; therefore, in that regard, there is no [defect].

"Somewhere there is a loss"—this means that neither duality nor plurality exists; thus it is established. Now, demonstrating that the experience which is of the nature of experience—that is, consciousness—is free from the delusion of difference, he says:
Oṃ! [This applies] when there is the existence of a particular object-appearance and its corresponding object in some instance.
It occurs within conceptual constructions that pertain to objects yet to be, currently being, or already having come into existence. || 80 ||
I remember that which was experienced by me through the yoga-pot; and in the future, I shall experience that very same thing.

In such passages as these, the experience itself is what pervades the three periods of time; yet there is no difference in that experience, nor in the experiencer (such as a jar, etc.). However, the point is that in states such as deep sleep and the like, there is indeed a distinction due to the influence of great limiting adjuncts (*mahopādhi*). But surely—?

Let the mutual distinctions among jars, cloths, blue objects, wind, and so forth be established, since they are not unperceived due to their being directly perceived (*pratyakṣatayā*). But as for that which is manifested internally, how can there be such variety in its manifestation? To this he says:

Oṃ. Even though the manifestation exists within objects that are causes of pleasure and so forth, such as the face and other [limbs], it remains as it is because it has transcended [those objects]. Regarding those objects which are causes of pleasure and so forth, such as garlands, sandalwood paste, and necklaces, [one thinks]: "I am the one with the face; I am resting."

By such statements as these, although the manifestation [of consciousness] exists within the causes such as the mouth and so forth, nevertheless, as before, there is no stability therein because of its internal nature. For instance, when there is the occurrence of suffering and so forth toward harmful grass, thorns, and the like due to a word such as "this," one thinks, "I am suffering. Nevertheless...
Not as before; because it has been experienced at some time or other, or because it has not been experienced.
But since entities such as jars are well-known everywhere and at all times, they are established as having a nature that appears and is manifest in all states and at all times.

Because it is not applicable to the face and other [parts], there is no such mode of experience [as that]. Now, he says that where the face and so forth are experienced through the process of "outlining" (ullekha), their state remains exactly as it is: mukhādau tadanupayogānnatādṛganubhavabhaṅgiḥ || 82 || atha collekhena yatra mukhādayonubhūyante | tatra ca tathaivasthitirityāha || 83 ||

Oṃ. When the face and so forth are being intensely delineated by conceptual construction (vikalpa), its state remains exactly as it was, because it is clearly perceived [as such]. For in this way, when the face and so forth are recognized through the delineation of conceptual construction, they are perceived with clarity; thus [it remains as it is].
The connection is that "stability also is likewise, as before"; the intended meaning is that there is nothing at all [to be established]. || 83 ||
Thus, when it has been established that the universe always and everywhere exists within [consciousness],
he states by way of conclusion that even externally there is nothing at all that appears as something distinct from the existence of jars and so forth.

Oṃ. For appearances of existence and non-existence, externality is held to be the limiting condition (upādhi); it is not their lack of self-nature, since they always exist internally. And this is the meaning here:

The internal existence of all things— consisting of both consciousness and matter, such as the blue sky, the wind, and so forth, which are variegated by the diversity of the universe— is manifested externally as well. Indeed, external manifestation cannot be conceived without internal existence, for in the absence of a cause, an effect cannot arise.

"Because of the connection between the cause and the effect when there is a cause"—by this pervasion (*vyāpti*), and by intending to express the non-difference between the cause and the possessor of the cause, this is established. The sense is that "externality" is well-known to exist only when there is an "interior. And for that very reason, their existence as something external [is established].

"By the words 'this is a jar' and so forth," they say, "that [object] is indeed non-existence (asattā) itself. Its establishment occurs through mere superimposition (adhyāsa), like a city in the sky seen by one who is deluded, or like a painted city; thus, no external name appears as having any intrinsic nature (svarūpa). And this has already been explained at great length previously.

Therefore it has been said: "Then, for those internal [entities] that exist, [it appears] as 'existent'. And for this very reason it has been said regarding entities such as jars, by means of expressions like "this is a jar," and regarding non-entities such as [the absence of] cloth, by means of expressions like "this is not a cloth"—referring to those appearances (*avabhāsāḥ*) which are the act of appearing (*avabhāsana*).

Through direct perception, there is the cognition [of objects] by means of expressions such as "this" or "that," and the externality of those appearances of existence as well as appearances of non-existence,
which is expressed by "this" or "that" and so forth; let that be called the limiting condition (*upādhi*), and not the essential nature (*tattvarūpatā*) itself.
Regarding them, it will be said and has already been said: "Once that is established, this state [is attained]."

The externality of entities that exist internally is also well-established, as proven by the case of the seed and the sprout; likewise, the state of being silver in mother-of-pearl and the state of being gold in brass are established through such examples.
43a) Because that which is non-existent cannot be produced, because there is no destruction of the material cause (*upādāna*), because everything could otherwise arise from anything,

because the efficient cause produces only what it is capable of producing, and because the effect exists within the cause— thus do the discerning Sāṃkhyas maintain that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkārya*). And for this very reason:

Oṃ. Because they are internal and because they are one with the cognizer, even their causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), which is based on differentiation, is [the same] despite external appearance, due to the difference in their diverse manifestations. (85) And because these [objects] are internal and because they are one with the cognizer, their causal efficiency is not based on differentiation; however, when external existence is present, [it appears otherwise].

The connection is as follows: that [consciousness], by being the cause of the appearance of diverse objects of purposeful action based on differentiation, is not [diverse] in itself. And for this very reason...
Oṃ. This manifestation is a conceptual construction; it too is external and appears as something distinct.
Internality consists in identity with the subject; therefore, difference from that is indeed externality.
(86) For it is established that internality is identity with the subject; thus, difference even from that is called externality.

However, that which appears as "this," "that," "this one," and so forth within the domain of conceptual construction—even though it is internal, it is spoken of as being external and distinct; thus, everything is thoroughly established.
Therefore, they say that its manifestation and so forth occur solely through the majesty of the Lord of All and by His will alone.

Oṃ. The manifestation of the act of delineation (*ullekha*), the face, and so forth, occurs through an external nature by the will of the Lord, just as the world of the senses and the elements exists as the perceptible form of the Overseer (*adhyakṣa*). This being so, whether it be internal or established as external, it is [manifested] through light (*prakāśa*) and so forth, or through delineation (*ullekha*) and so forth.
And [it is known] through pleasure, pain, and so forth; and by such expressions as "I am the primary agent" or "I am suffering.
And that [agency] arises solely from the will of the Lord, through various functions such as "seeing," "touching," and "smelling.
Just as the form of the letter *ma* is seen in the midst of the letters *kṣa* and others. I have seen it.
Whether heard, smelled, tasted, or touched, and so forth—in this way, whatever is performed by the free Self, that very thing is performed by Maheśvara. || 87 ||
Therefore, he concludes the previously stated point in this very way.

Oṃ. Without that unity, there would be no worldly course of cognitions. Because of the unity of light, there is that oneness; it is clear that he alone is the one subject (mātṛ). "Tat" means for that reason. [This applies] in cases such as experience and recollection.

The unity of awakening is this very experience; for that which is memory is indeed that same [awakening], and that which is memory is precisely what was present before. By this, the cognizer who is grasped as both the awakened and the unawakened is said to be one; and he is indeed pervasively continuous everywhere. And thus:

"Even though the distinctions of waking and so forth unfold within that which is non-different [from it], they never deviate from their own essential nature, for it is perceived as such. Thus it is stated in the *Spanda*. Therefore, due to the oneness of light (*prakāśa*), unity alone is established everywhere, like a city reflected in a mirror. And because without that [light]...

It is certain that for him there is no engagement with the worldly ways of knowledge—that is, the conventional practices of the world—nor even the adoption of their activities. Thus, it is established that the previously mentioned definition of awakening, which was indicated later on, has been stated with full attention. || 88 ||
Therefore, it is established exactly thus.

Oṃ. That very [Lord] is Maheśvara by virtue of being determined as the nature of reflective awareness (vimarśa), because the pure power of knowledge and action of the God consists of nothing but reflective awareness. Indeed, that very consciousness which possesses the power of reflective awareness is necessarily called Maheśvara; he is called "Maheśvara" because he is great and consists of supreme sovereignty (naiśvarya).

And because the knower [of reality] discerns the self-nature of manifestation, even an object that is illuminated—even if it were like an insentient crystal or the like—would become manifest. This very thing is what is called its "discernment" (*vimarśana*): "I am one; may I become many. "He thought: 'May I become many.'"

"May I be born"—thus arises the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) through the contemplation of "I. And from that [arises] the reflective awareness: "I act," "I go," "I know. He who possesses that power is victorious. And by means of this very reflective awareness, creation and maintenance [are accomplished].
He is capable of performing dissolution, concealment, and grace, as well as non-performance and performing otherwise.
And for that very reason, He alone is indeed what is called *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), because His knowledge and action are pure, like His own essential nature, and stainless.

Knowledge and action—these two indeed constitute knowledge and action. For, through reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), one thinks, "I know this," and "I do this. Thus, the Lord, whose very nature is pure, possesses the powers of knowledge and action within his own self in manifold ways.
For the purpose of accomplishment, when one's own implements are considered [sufficient].
Thus, by this [realization], all this power of cultivation is [attained]: "This is known by me:

'This is a jar. And consequently, one knows that it performs the activity consisting of the removal of water, and one performs each and every such mere activity. In this way, it is the very nature of that self.

The two called knowledge and action are established; and they are established by themselves, from their own self, through direct perception. Having known "this is a jar," one knows "I am doing [it]," or indeed, "I am doing [it].
Thus, the sense is that this entire universe consists of nothing but knowledge and action.
And thus, when Maheśvara is established as the primordial agent and knower, as one's own self, from the very beginning;

By such statements as these, and by the concluding passage ending with "since the pure knowledge and action of the Lord are indeed [His] reflective awareness (vimarśa)," the intended meaning is that this scripture is woven together through the encapsulation (*sampuṭita*) of knowledge and action. And with this very same purport, [the teaching was established] even at the outset regarding the Supreme Lord.

Regarding the word *siddhe*: by the passage beginning with "when the agent, the knower, and the self are [established as one]," and ending with "and subsequently, because of the identity of the subject (*pramātṛ*), that oneness is clearly established as the single reality of the cognizer," the sense is that when that very [oneness] is established, the two principles of Śiva and Śakti are established as one. And [as for] Śakti...

The meaning is that by the statement, "The possessor of power (śaktimān) and power (śakti)—these two are said to be the categories; his powers are the entire universe, while the possessor of power is Maheśvara," the duality of Śiva and Śakti alone is established. Furthermore, at that time, this entire Veda is indeed a covering (varaṇaka).

The intended meaning is as follows: This is the underlying point here. Just as one who attempts to step over the shadow of one's own head with one's feet cannot have the head located at the place of the feet, so too is this *bindu*-kalā. Having thus investigated the secret of the vowels (*svara*) by means of the secret of the vowels, [the] secret...
The sense is that the revelation of the secret is to be contemplated by the mind alone. May there be auspiciousness for all the worlds. [89] From the beginning.
Thus ends the tenth daily lesson in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by the illustrious Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha.

Thus, this chapter on Knowledge has been brought to completion in the *Vivṛtikaumudī* by the venerable [author], who— by the light of the dust from the feet of Taruvara, which dispels the darkness of delusion and blindness, and by the abundance of the surging waves of consciousness-bliss— is resplendent.
Of the auspicious one, it is most unsurpassed.
Oṃ! Thus, according to the capacity of the intellect, this excellent commentary on the *Jñānādhikāra* has been composed by Bhaṭṭāraka Ānandanātha. (1)
It is sweet and straightforward in form, known as "The Awakening of the Child," and it possesses the power to draw forth the supreme goad of the Goddess from its various hidden meanings. (2)

Thus, she whose essence is auspicious and uniquely skilled at agitating the blind darkness of those who speak improper Prakrit, whose mind is filled with compassion for the ignorant who are burdened by the weight of refined Sanskrit speech— 3.
This stream of the supreme nectar of the illustrious Awakened One has indeed rendered the salt-water lake of the unawakened into a lotus pond;
by the virtuous, it has been made a necklace for their own speech, while for the unawakened, it remains a noose that creates delusion.

This labor of commentary has been undertaken by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka as well, with the desire to savor the essence of the ocean of consciousness wherein the descent of power (śaktipāta) has occurred. (5)

Thus, this section on Knowledge (Jñānādhikāra), whose form is the radiance of the power of knowledge, [is written] by the glance of Śrīvidyā for the pacification of the multitude of obstacles upon the earth. In the year marked by the qualities and Munis (1363),
likewise in the month of Nabhasya (Śrāvaṇa), on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight— on a Thursday— at the time of midday.

Thus, with the dawn of Maghā, this chapter on Knowledge has reached its conclusion. In this manner, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) has been examined by means of the previous [chapter]. Now, the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) is examined by means of the subsequent [chapter]. May there be auspiciousness for all the worlds!
May the hosts of beings be devoted to the welfare of others; may faults come to peace, and may people everywhere be happy. May there be auspiciousness for the practitioners.
45a) Oṃ, homage to the sandals of the venerable Vidyā! Homage to the feet of the most excellent Śrī Guru!
Oṃ! Having paid homage to the supreme knowledge, to Śrī Sambhu, the supreme Śaṅkara, and having praised the Lord Guru Gaṇapati, the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims; || 1 ||
Having thoroughly churned and repeatedly entered into the domain of knowledge,
and having then completed it by means of the traditional scriptures known by those learned in the ancient treatises;
Therefore, by means of the relationship between part and whole and through their constant association, we shall now,
by the command of the Guru, reveal the sequence of the section on ritual action.
Once knowledge is established, even ritual action is considered necessary prior to that.
Once that [power] has arisen, knowledge and action are there established by the sequence of necessity.
Now, the form of action—which was previously described for the purpose of understanding both action and non-action—is being explained;
we shall now set forth the continuous sequence of the section on action (kriyādhikāra).

Oṃ. For this very reason, whatever was stated—that action cannot belong to a single [entity] because it is sequential, and so forth—is refuted by the demonstration that it does belong to a single [entity]. (6)

And as for what was previously stated by those of other views and others— beginning with the question of how the one Supreme Lord can have a connection with sequential action— that has already been refuted; the sense is that it has been cast far away.

This is because, subsequently, through the manner of mutual questions and answers, the very nature of consciousness—the Supreme Lord who is one's own self—is established. This has already been stated, and it will be stated again.

Thus, as for the objection that "how can there be a relation of one with many?", that is not so; it is established that this is untenable. Now, once it is established in this way that the Great Lord is indeed one, [it follows that] action is produced from His own nature through the process of assuming various times and forms.

"How can there be a connection between one established [entity] and many? Even so, that same contradiction would recur once again. Thus, nothing at all has been achieved. To this it is replied: "Once Maheśvara himself is established as one, there is no contradiction whatsoever; and his fundamental state remains as unity."

45b) Because there is no contradiction between diversity and multiplicity; just as in the case of trees and so forth. When the "tree" is established at the root, the establishment of the multiplicity of branches and so forth within that tree is already established.
Now, in the venerable Mālinīvijayottara: "That power of the Creator of the world which is said to be inherent, O Goddess, is taught to be His very nature as Will. (1)

Listen to how even that which is one attains multiplicity: it should be known with absolute certainty that "this is thus, and not otherwise. Here, the knower (*jñānin*) is said to possess the three powers of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).
When all this becomes known in this way, then at that very moment, he becomes sorrowless, just like that.

What do they perform here? It is my [view]. Thus, just as she is of two forms, the Sovereign (Īśvarī) again proceeds through manifold divisions according to the power of the *mātṛkā*, like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*). Therein, first attaining the state of being the Mothers (*mātṛ*), she is divided: into two ways and into nine ways by means of distinctions.

The meaning of what has been revealed by such passages as "the fifty-fold Mālinī" and so forth is [found] in the venerable *Mālinīvijayottara*. And that which was previously established as the Siddhānta has indeed been accomplished.
Just as in the case of grammar and so forth; and just as the various divisions of ornaments [are distinguished] from the science of poetics.

The eighteen divisions of the letter *a* and so forth— thus, as previously established, one [entity] has many divisions; likewise, as previously stated by the passage beginning with "so too of Brahman," even for the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*) alone, there is a distinction of infinite actions.

The meaning is that there is no fault in the construction [of the argument]. This has indeed been established previously by the passage beginning with "the preparer" (*saṃskartā*), because it was subsequently demonstrated with certainty that there is only one [reality] whose nature consists of both consciousness and non-consciousness.
Therefore, it is this very one who, assuming a wheel of manifold powers, thinks "I am."

"Because of the support [provided] by ascending to the locus of 'this-ness' (idantā). By this, the sense is that this non-successive (akrama) [reality] possesses the two powers called knowledge and action, which are [otherwise] sequential (krama). [Objection:
But how can that [succession], which is contradictory to the nature of the Supreme Lord who is non-successive, exist in the Blessed One?
Regarding "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*): because it would entail the consequence of mutual pervasion, it would be like saying "one should sprinkle with fire."
Regarding what was stated—"How can that which is non-sequential possess sequence through conjunction and so forth?"—he says:
Oṃ! And that sequence arises from the power of time (kāla-śakti) in relation to worldly activity;
therefore, it is eternal and sovereign, like that of the Lord. || 2 ||

In that regard, when the Lord, by mere vibration, is capable of manifesting the universe through the power of unfolding (*unmeṣa*), he first causes the pair of powers consisting of knowledge and action—
which, though possessing a single mutual nature, appear as distinct forms— to shine forth in a differentiated manner.

Then, due to contact with the Māyā of this Lord, that pair of powers consisting of knowledge and action—which is called ignorance (avidyā) and is governed by necessity (aniyatī)—is said to be "gross" because it is preceded by necessity. And its very state is described as "succession" (krama). For this very reason, it has been said:

Succession (*sakramatva*) occurs through the conjunction of the power of time with action that is governed by worldly necessity (*niyati-śakti*); for instance, by means of temporal forms such as "it was," "it may be," or "it exists. However, this does not apply to the eternal and immutable power of primordial matter (*prābhavyā*).
This [power] belongs to the Lord; it is His. Of that subtle [power], [it is said]: "having made [the world] day.
Just as in the case of the Lord, that sequence [of manifestation] is such that it is not limited by space, time, form, and so forth. || 3 ||
46a) Now, in the context of the section on action (kriyā), [the author] defines time and the other factors through their relationship as primary and subordinate elements (aṅga-aṅgibhāva).
Oṃ. Time is the movement of the sun and other celestial bodies, or the birth of various flowers and so forth;
it is characterized by cold and heat, and in reality, it is simply that sequence.

In that regard, time is completed by means of such things as those established by fixed necessity (*niyati-śakti*), such as the sun and the moon, the mango, jasmine, *kuṭaja* flowers, and so forth; cold and heat, and the various manifestations of pleasure and pain. Thus, the sun [is associated] with the day and the moon with the night.

In the months of Padma, Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and so forth; Mallikā flowers and others in Śrāvaṇa; Kuṭaja flowers in Jyeṣṭha; and the playful charms of women in the spring season and so on; coolness during the northern solstice and heat during the southern solstice—such is the sequence that is called "time."
And that very [power] is also called the power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 3 ||
Now, the sequence of time and the other factors is being determined.
Oṃ! Both the distinction of succession and its absence exist because of the presence or absence of manifestation;
however, the presence or absence of manifestation is brought about by the Lord through the manifestation of the mind.

A jar, a cloth, blue, yellow, and so forth—the distinction that serves as the locus for such differentiation is called "succession" (*krama*). And that distinction arises from the existence or non-existence of appearances; for instance, when one says, "There is a jar here on this ground," and "It is not here. In this way, that very [distinction] consists in the existence or non-existence of appearances.
As for what is called "differentiation": the existence or non-existence of appearances is caused solely by the mere will of the Lord Maheśvara;
it is established that it is not otherwise. 4.
He demonstrates that very fact of its being a manifold appearance.
Oṃ! By means of the diversity of forms, this Lord manifests the succession of space;
and by means of the manifestation of the diversity of actions, He manifests the succession of time as well. (5)

The "form" (mūrti) of an object is its essential nature. Through the diversity of that form, there arises a spatial sequence (deśakrama), such as: "this is a house," "this is a courtyard," "this is a marketplace," "this is a mountain," "this is a forest," and so forth; by means of this, it manifests spatial succession. Likewise, [it manifests] action (kriyā).

And through its manifold variety, it manifests the succession of time. That which is the sequence within that specific form or location is called "action" (*kriyā*). Through its manifold variety, it also manifests the succession of time within reality (*tattva*). [Thus one thinks: "It was done by me," or "I am doing it."
And by the words "I shall do" and so forth, he also manifests the sequence of time through the power of intention; thus, this concludes the exposition of the power of action (kriyā-śakti). || 5 ||
Thus, demonstrating that the manifestation of the three [powers] everywhere consists of the activity of sequential appearance and that this is subject to time, he says:

Oṃ. Even the differentiation of appearances everywhere may be devoid of temporal succession; however, the appearance of [objects] such as the void (*śūnya*) as distinct from the manifesting subject (*mātṛ*) occurs not simultaneously. And that which is the differentiation of appearances everywhere is, as previously stated, subject to the sequence of time—this is the meaning. But furthermore:

The appearance of the void and so forth is distinct [in each case]: in the body, in the intellect, then in the vital breath, and in the imagined space. The reflective awareness "I," which functions as the subject, is not different from that which was previously described by the words "it is indeed conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) and so on—namely, the appearance of the void and the rest; it is merely a differentiation of that very appearance.

Nor does it appear simultaneously to any other cognizer; that is to say, not to one's own self, which consists of uninterrupted consciousness. And because there is no contact with that [other cognizer], it is like a lotus petal in water.
Therefore, he says exactly this:
Oṃ! Even the succession of spatial locations appears within objects to the limited self of the Mother [the subject];
however, for her, it is her own self that appears as her own self through the manifestation of the fullness of being.
To that very limited self, the cognizer such as Śūnya and others, the succession of space and so forth appears.

The infinite [Lord]—that is, the Supreme Śiva who is one's own self, whose nature is immeasurable—shines as full entities consisting of the wonder of the fullness of the I-consciousness (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) by virtue of His own self. This is the meaning. || 7 ||
And he concludes in order to confirm that which was promised in sequence.

Oṃ. However, the power of manifestation is accomplished for the knowing Lord in this way: by the will of the Supreme Lord alone, the distinction between consciousness and the object of consciousness appears.
Whatever action He performs, such as "He does this" and so forth—all that is solely by the will of the Supreme Lord.
And likewise, consciousness, the objects of consciousness, and so forth—all that is also His will alone;
for without it, no one whatsoever is capable of even cutting a blade of grass, yet by His will alone, everything is possible.
Whatever comes to be, that indeed comes to be; the meaning is that what is not so does not come to be. || 8 ||
Thus ends the first chapter in the section on Action within the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭārakānandanātha.
47a) Now, other relations and so forth, such as action, though they may have single or multiple objects, are indeed real;
that is to say, they are firm and stable, being useful for the objects perceived.

Because these [objects] are useful in every respect, they cannot be discarded; therefore, the meaning is that while these are true, other things such as a double moon and so forth are not true. Indicating this very point, he says:
Oṃ. Action, generality, inherence, substance, space, time, and cognition—these existents, by virtue of their stability and utility, are held to have a single substratum. (9)
These [categories], beginning with generality (sāmānya), are considered useful for [the accomplishment of] effects; and therefore, they are real.

However, the intended meaning is that [the substratum] is considered to have both a single and a manifold basis. To illustrate: in such cases as "Caitra goes," "the rice grains soften," and "the fuel burns," the entity Caitra and the others possess both a single and a manifold form. In those instances, Caitra and the others are distinct according to their respective locations, times, and forms.

And Caitra, though possessing a manifold nature, appears without abandoning his singular form as "this is Caitra. That very object of manifold nature is what constitutes action; and because it appears in that very way, it is ultimately real. In this regard, Caitra is the single substratum, while the [various] aspects are the manifold substrata.

Rice and so forth, or the appearance of two moons and so on, are considered to have single or multiple substrata based on their stability and utility; by this [principle], even actions such as cooking are indeed accomplished. Thus, this is appropriate for the purpose of the utility of action.
The meaning is "liberated. || 9 ||
Thus, after the ritual action, he explains the general rule.

Oṃ. In that regard, there is one internal reality which, having attained the state of being perceivable by the senses, reaches a state of multiplicity through [differences of] place, time, and intrinsic nature. || 10 ||

The single reality is indeed one essence, consisting of both the insentient and the sentient. That very [reality], by not being reached through mental modifications such as "this is a jar" and so forth—which are perceivable by the respective sense organs—attains multiplicity.
Subsequently, it becomes that very [multiplicity] again, due to the persistence of its own nature in terms of space, time, and other conditions. (10)

Thus, he says that the mind alone performs the conceptualization of external and internal, gross and subtle, non-conceptual and conceptual, and so forth, as well as [the conceptualization] of karma and the like, because these follow in sequence.

Oṃ! Having these two as their objective support, this internal mental after-cognition (anuvyavasāya) produces conceptual constructions of action and so forth, consisting of the activity of the subject. 11.
Thus, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), whose nature is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and who is characterized by moving both externally and internally,

performs conceptual constructions such as action (*karman*) and so forth, which consist of the activity of the cognizer. Being present as the one who subsequently reflects (*anuvyavasāyin*) in all activities and the like, he encompasses both the external and the internal.
Thus, that which has ceased [from such states] is called "once-returner" (sakṛdāgāmin). || 11 ||
Now, he also clarifies the connection that follows in due order:
Oṃ. The non-existences, whose light is distinct and grounded in one's own self, [reside] in the single cognizer.
It is the locus of the cognition of relation, characterized by mutual inherence and identity of form.

Having shown the general principle, he speaks while demonstrating the relationship: "For entities such as jars, though variegated by the diversity of the universe, are grounded solely within their own essential parts. For a jar is simply a jar; 'this is blue' means it is simply blue; and 'this is yellow' means it is simply yellow."

And that which is "this is red" is indeed only red; it is neither yellow nor blue, nor is the red white, nor is the blue red, and so forth. Thus, entities such as jars and the like are established in their own nature and reside solely within their own nature, because this has been stated previously. Likewise, they are of an isolated appearance.

Even those things that appear clearly as "this is a jar" or "this is a cloth," and so forth, possess unity through their mutual interconnection within a single subject—the Self—which consists of consciousness; for they are characterized by partaking in that [unity]. As for consciousness itself, it is established by such reasoning as: "Consciousness both knows and acts," and so on.
Whatever one knows or does while being of the nature of the ultimate reality,
that very relationship between knowledge and the object of knowledge is itself their mutual interpenetration.
For identity is not possible between knowledge and the object of knowledge, nor between the object of knowledge and knowledge.

For instance: "This jar is known by me. In this way, within a single cognizer, that very resting in the "I" which is the nature of the object of cognition is itself called the mutual relationship, and nothing else. And yet... [text fragment] ...the cow.

By means of this [formula]—"ā || na || ya ||"—one strikes the hour, strikes the hour. Words such as "asahoḥ," "cāritā," "nigāmānayet," and so forth do not constitute a sentence, because of the absence of proximity (sānnidhya).

By this [it is shown that], in the absence of proximity, there is an absence of fitness; and in the absence of that, worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*) does not arise. Consequently, the entire world would be like blinding darkness, and nothing at all would remain. For this very reason, [one says]: "Devadatta, bring the cow. O! [Thus ends the section.]

"Devadatta! You! Bring the cow!"—thus, through proximity and through the capacity [of the words], since the production of fitness occurs everywhere, this relation established as the cause of worldly transaction is proven. || 12 ||
Now he demonstrates the universal (sāmānya), which follows in the sequence.

Oṃ. Conceptual constructions take as their objective support both the uniformity of things that appear as universals and substances even externally, and also the difference between individuals and their parts. (13)

Just as "cowness" (*gotva*) is the state of being excluded from non-cows; when this universal "cowness" is thus established, it is then stated by the phrase "this is cowness" that everything from childhood to old age is cowness.

Furthermore, by this [universal], it is stated that "cowness" consists of all colors, beginning with white and ending with black; thus, there is a single form [of the universal]. And yet, through the medium of individuals, one speaks of "a white cow," "an old cow," or "a black cow"; thus, even through the difference of individuals, [the universal remains one].

Through the complete establishment within its own self-aspect, conceptualization constitutes a single differentiation; thus, the expansion of the power of action occurs through this relationship of part and whole. || 13 || End.
Oṃ! The synthesis of the causes is the object of the reflective awareness of action.
The cognition of "long" and so forth arises from the connection with the existence of the delimited and the delimiting.

In this context, the object of deliberation (*vimarśa*) is called "action" (*kriyā*). Deliberation such as "I am doing it" or "it has been done by me" is action. Alternatively, the coordination of the causal factors (*kāraka*), such as rice and so forth, is called the act of cooking. Furthermore, [this occurs] by depending on a foundation of such limited extent.

"This pot stands"—by this [cognition], that very relation is the objective support (ālambana) of which there arises the cognition of direction, such as "east" and so forth; for "east" and the like are indeed limited to such an extent.

By this, the scope of the investigation is established: that the coordination of the factors of action (*kāraka*) is the action (*kriyā*), as in the case of rice and so forth possessing the action of cooking. Alternatively, the state of being [the object] is the cognition of the connection between the killer and the slain, and so forth. 14.

Thus, by means of various single and manifold forms such as action and so forth, there exists for the cognizer a correspondence of actions which constitutes worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). To dispel the delusion that this is an error, he says:
Oṃ! In this very way, the accomplishment of the mother’s purpose will occur for one who seeks the fulfillment of her aims;
therefore, there is no such error regarding the object that possesses both difference and non-difference. (15)

In this very way, for the cognizer who seeks purposeful action, there arises the thought, "I know the jar. This is because the knower exists; for it is the nature of an object that its establishment depends upon him. Pervading everything is this very self whose essence is his own being, consisting of both consciousness and non-consciousness: "I know."
Even one who knows, thinking "I see," "I hear," and so forth, is indeed called the agent.
For those seeking the fulfillment of a purpose through these [objects], the accomplishment of that purpose is immediate.

This occurs by means of an object consisting of both difference and non-difference—namely, by means of the jar as non-different from itself, and yet different from other things such as [non-jars]. Therefore, the implication is that this is not an illusion. || 15 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, on Action, in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭārakānandanātha.
Therefore, it is established that cognitions such as those involving action, relation, and so forth, do not have the nature of error.

49a) Thus, the cognition [arising] from an action through its connection with a universal and so forth is not an error; therefore, by means of these two [verses], he confirms that it is indeed valid knowledge (*pramā*).
That by virtue of which a thing is determined as "this is such-and-such"—that is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It too arises through its own manifestations. Being essentially reflective awareness (*vimarśātman*), it is unimpeded in its measurement of an object that is non-different in terms of space, time, and so forth, and which is the referent of a single designation. (17)

This [object], such as a jar, would exist; it is measured by such [means]. That which exists and appears as "this" and "that" is a real entity (*vastu*) established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as "this," "that," or "of such a kind."

And by this [statement], "O dear one, consciousness (cetas) has arisen as a new dawn," it is meant that the mass of consciousness (cidghana) has arisen like a wave; and that very [mass] is essentially internal reflective awareness (vimarśa), having the nature of awareness,
because it was stated previously that the inherent nature of manifestation is reflective awareness and nothing else.

And in that regard, when there is a single designation, as in "this is a jar" and so forth, valid cognition (*pramiti*) is a cognition whose nature is luminosity; it is necessarily accepted by everyone that its object regarding the entity such as the jar is unsublated. And thus, in the *Spanda*: "Even amidst the distinctions of waking and so forth, it flows forth as non-different from That."
The meaning is that, as expressed by the words "it is not perceived from its own nature," the self which is the perceiver is indeed all-pervasive. || 18 ||

Thus, in that case, just as the means of cognition (pramāṇa) and so forth are manifold because they do not cognize external objects, that [cognition] itself indeed partakes in multiplicity. And yet, there is no real distinction in that cognizer; this he states in two verses:

Oṃ. Just as there is no difference in the reality of things according to their actual nature or their linguistic derivation, so too is the appearance of an object unified when it is established through synthesis.

Just as smoke, a person, a lamp, the moon, a creeper, and so forth, though distinguished by differences of place and time, are differentiated according to their respective appearances, [so too is the one consciousness]. (19)
By the principle that "where there is inclination, there is rule," appearances manifest according to one's inclination, or according to one's need, or according to one's proficiency;
thus they appear as manifold through diversity, yet also as a unity while abiding in multiplicity.
For it demonstrates its very multiplicity,
just as the circle of clouds at the evening twilight is manifested with various diversities such as red, blue, yellow, and so forth.

Elephants, chariots, horses, infantry, chariot-drawers, riders, sword-bearers, shield-bearers, and so forth—these appear as various distinct manifestations through diverse arrangements; yet this occurs even in the absence of causes such as the eyes or darkness. Likewise, there is the singular act of eating, which is universally recognized as one and the same everywhere. In that regard:

According to one's inclination, according to one's need, and according to one's proficiency, there is a diversity of appearances (*rucy-ābhāsa-bheda*) even with respect to a single object of eating; it appears as manifold. For example: one person eats rice, another eats khecarī and so forth, and another eats cakes and the like.
One [may perceive] meat and so forth; another, vegetables and so forth; one in a certain manner;
and another in a different manner—thus, when a single object is established through a synthesis [of perceptions], they indeed differ according to the diversity of their appearances.
And yet, the previously mentioned [visions], such as the fire-mandala, the long tube-like form,
the upward-pointing human figure, and the smoke, moon, and creeper, are indeed distinguished by various specific appearances (*nirbhāsa*).
Now, he describes them in another way as well.

Oṃ. In the same way, [words] such as "jar," "substance," "gold," and "brilliance" produce effects that are not distinct from their respective appearances; they are the locus of verbal expression. (20)
And likewise, for one named Ghaṭaduvya, for the purpose of fetching water;
for another, for the purpose of traveling; for another, for the purpose of crossing a river;
for another, for the purpose of [fetching] something due to the absence of a jar; and for another, for the purpose of removing dirt. And so it is.
Gold as well: by someone for the sake of a bracelet, by someone for the sake of an earring, by someone for the sake of a ring, by someone for the sake of another, and so forth.
Likewise, brilliant blue, yellow, and other [colors]: by someone for the sake of clothing.

Such various appearances (ābhāsa-bheda) as "belonging to someone else" and so forth are considered to produce distinct purposes; however, the domain of *dhvani*—the operation of sound—is empty [of such distinctions], for its activity proceeds by means of that [emptiness].
