The sense is this: nevertheless, due to the differences among those appearances, there is a restricted causal efficiency (*niyatārthakriyā*).
Thus he speaks by his own power.

50a) Furthermore, because appearances that are non-different manifest through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), there is a restricted purposeful activity for those things situated in their own respective locations.
Oṃ. Just as the rays of light from various lamps in an ocean of flowing currents have a non-contradictory appearance and a single purpose, so too is the cognition of unity. || 22 ||
"This is a jar," "this is a cloth," "this is blue," "this is yellow"— in this way,
whatever appears as this manifold universe is merely restricted purposeful action (*niyatārthakriyā*).
For the sole purpose of a positive injunction is its unfailing efficacy in producing restricted purposeful action.

It remains so. And when all this denotable [reality] is established upon the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameya*), yet is experienced as distinct from that which is established by experience— that ultimate essence which is purely consciousness (*cinmaya*), whose sole body is self-luminosity— then it exists in a state of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Because everything shines as being composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*), even that which is devoid of differentiation and whose function is restricted to a specific purpose is [included] within this [consciousness]. And he demonstrates that very point: just as in the case of lamps and other sources of light, [the light] exists within another light.

Just as there is a cognition of unity among collections of lights that are separated by other lights— since it is precisely through the cognition of their unity that they are established by the number "lamp"— so too, because there is no such apprehension of them as being thus [unified] despite their being diverse and distinct due to the manifold variety of jars and other objects, it is the same in this case. Thus...

And [this occurs] with respect to the ocean and so forth when they have come together, as well as with respect to streams. And thus, for those things which appear without contradiction, there is a single cognition, such as "This is a lamp," where the illuminator is everywhere; or "This is the ocean," or the cognition of the unity of streams, which has the object as its domain.

The point here is this: it is established that through the manifestation of a cognition of a specific difference, there is an indefinite causal efficiency; and through the cognition of a specific non-difference, there is likewise an indefinite causal efficiency. || 22 ||
50b) But surely, according to the Buddhist doctrine, that very self-effacement remains firmly established;

and as for the fact that the causal efficiency of things is inherent and occurs necessarily, does that not imply the existence of some Self, called the Supreme Lord, who is the experiencer? Thus indeed:
Thus he said:

"Oṃ. In that case, regarding fire and so forth which are not distinct [from their causes], there is the state of being the object of meditation by way of cause and effect; and therefore, the nature of the object and so forth is considered to be one with the means of valid cognition. (23)

"Where there is smoke, there is fire, as in a kitchen; this mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke. In this way, when [the property to be proven] such as fire is not yet specified, one may state: "Earth possesses fragrance;
wherever there is fragrance, there is earth-ness," or "it possesses a non-cold touch."

In cases such as "the waters," there is a relationship of cause and effect, as well as qualities such as heat. Furthermore, the person (*puruṣa*) is either the meaning of those respective words or the underlying substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*). This is accepted because [the self] is established from the very means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) as being of the nature of self-luminosity (*prakāśasvarūpa*), for without that [luminosity], nothing could be established. Thus it is said.

[It is] established: "I know," "I do," "I go," "I sleep"—such is the activity of agency. The sense is that all of this is under the control of one's own self (*svātman*) due to the connection between cause and effect. Therefore, [it arises] from the One alone.
For it has been stated: "Because of the means of valid cognition. || 23 ||
And for this very reason, he said:

Oṃ! Even for one who desires [an object], there would be an immediate engagement with the particular (svalakṣaṇa)—which is distinct from the mother, the country, and so forth—by means of inference. || 24 ||

In that regard, there is an immediate activity toward the mother, the father, or one's own self; and even in the case of a cognition whose object is a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) or the appearance of a particular characteristic, there is an immediate activity because its object is connected by an innate relationship (*svābhāvikasambandha*). This is likewise the case with inference (*anumāna*). For what is called inference is not [something separate].
It is thus established that something must exist as a cognizer.

Furthermore, it is not possible for the cognizer to be the illuminator even by means of its own self with respect to particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and so forth. Therefore, it is established that this Self, which is of the nature of the cognizer, is the experiencer in all cases; this is sufficient. 24.

Now, he demonstrates that once the state of being a single cognizer is established through the proof of multiple experiences based on the persistence of multiple cognizers, that very singularity of the cognizer remains unrefuted.

Oṃ. [The manifestation of objects occurs] through their being distant or near, through their being imperceptible or perceptible, through their being external or internal, or otherwise, by means of the manifestor.

Oṃ. Even in a shadow, because the face appears [therein], oneness is not precluded due to what is called a single unifying reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). In some cases, it is [perceived] at a distance; in others, it is very near, like collyrium situated in the eye. [Thus,] its being beyond direct perception (*parokṣatva*) [is established].

[The term] "name" (nāma) [is used]. It is included within the Vedāntic view, like Brahman. And there is immediacy (aparokṣatva), as in the case of "this is a jar. There is also sublation (bādha), such as the affliction of thirst and so forth, as well as internal mental affliction. Likewise, there is the non-existence of the manifestors, such as blindness or deafness, in the eyes and other [senses].
Thus, the connection is as follows: even though there is a shadow of differentiated appearance, the unity of the subject—the experiencer who is his very own self—is not obstructed.

And so it is: "Just as in a mirror-image, a variegated array of cities, villages, and so forth appears as if undivided, yet it appears as if divided both from one another and from the mirror itself. Therefore, it is exactly thus.
Oṃ. Even purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) regarding things that are not produced by a creator is determined by their inherent nature;

otherwise, such action would not occur. [For example,] "Bring the jar," "Take the jar"—such purposeful actions belong to jars and the like which are not produced by a creator. Rather, [they arise from their own nature].
If the experiencer were to cut it off, then that [experience] would not be established by itself; rather, the Supreme Lord alone is the cause in every case—thus this teaching is established.
Therefore, it does not become otherwise through the breaking of a jar or similar events. || 29 ||

[Objection: But was it not stated in that [text] that "the restricted causal efficiency of entities arises from the difference in their manifestations"? How then [can this be so]? [Response: He says: "Because of the cessation of silver and so forth, which appear as perceptible in mother-of-pearl and the like."

Oṃ. Even when there is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of identity with silver, silver does not exist in the mother-of-pearl; because the location of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is inconsistent, as in the case of the double moon, it is otherwise [in the sky]. Herein is the intended meaning (*bhāva*):
just as a jar exists in a state capable of being engaged with or withdrawn from, such is not the case for the existence of silver and so forth in the mother-of-pearl.

In that regard, through delusion, [an object] appears like a snake in a rope, or like water in a mirage and the like; however, this appearance arises solely from delusion. Its persistence is not suitable for direct experience, whereas elsewhere it is so. Thus stands this worldly convention: there is the delusion "this is silver" regarding mother-of-pearl, and subsequently, when that experience occurs...

Subsequently, there arises the cognition "this is not silver. For just as the cognition "this is a jar" pertains to all three periods of time and is characterized by non-deviation, whereas this [present cognition] is by nature an error caused by mental delusion regarding qualities such as whiteness; thus, those who know the truth hold that it is not a valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*).

And because of the connection with the location of that limiting adjunct (upādhi), just as the sky appears large even in the case of a double moon, so too it is always thus [in the case of the Self]. 23.
Thus, showing that the entire creation, variegated as it is with the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth, is entirely the Supreme Lord acting with intent, he says:
Oṃ! Thus, in a single cognizer, the distinction of entities through qualities such as sound and their non-distinction through universals and so forth are both logically established.

Because the genus "jar" is non-distinct everywhere, and because there is distinction through [particulars] such as sound and so forth; therefore, due to this distinction and non-distinction of entities, it is thus logically possible for difference and non-difference to coexist in a single thing without contradiction—this is the intended meaning. || 23 ||

52a) Now, at the beginning of this illustrious treatise, by means of two verses starting with "The Self, the Supreme Lord, is established as the agent and the knower from the very beginning," [the author] establishes that the Self— the Supreme Lord— is the witness of the entire universe, transcendent to all, and the essence of the illumination of everything, since the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth do not apply to Him.

Regarding that which was previously stated— that one's own self is the Supreme Lord, whose nature consists of both awakening and non-awakening, and whose mental activity is essentially reflective awareness (vimarśa)— the author now speaks again in this very manner to demonstrate how this same realization is to be accomplished through the practice of encapsulation (saṃpuṭīkaraṇa).

Oṃ! In the primordial subject, whose form is eternally manifest, who is the Lord of ultimate reality untouched by contradictory states, and who resembles the even surface of a wall upon which the variegated painting of the universe's diversity is depicted—what proof is there for the ninefold manifestation that partakes in all cognition? [It is] not set in motion...

In the previous [section], it was stated that solely by virtue of the state of being the head (the supreme), the worldly transaction of "power" (*śakti*) and "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is set in motion. Herein lies the intended meaning:
just as this Self is the essence of all manifestation, yet there is no other manifestor of it in that same manner.

Someone [objects]: Because it is impossible for light to have another light as its essence, and because one would fall into faults such as infinite regress, what indeed could be called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—such as inference and so forth—which partakes in all cognitions? It is nothing at all as a cause, [being] one's own self.

Thus, by this, there is the expansive stain of a darkened face; yet, therein, not even in the slightest degree can anything be altered by modification, for it is the foundational surface upon which the painting of the world’s diversity rests,
and it is untouched by the contact of mutually contradictory states.
And likewise, in that which exists as the ultimate reality; and likewise, in the subject who is endowed with a multitude of qualities such as sovereignty;

and likewise, because it is established in both the Purāṇas and in the body as being ever-manifest; or rather, manifestation does not exist for the sake of providing the cause for the worldly transaction of the universe's manifold variety.

"Where there is smoke, there is fire"—this is well known by the name of inference; what, then, could it prove in that case? Oh, what skill in worldly logic! And as for the one who is the cognizer of all this—O God—what other cognizer or the like could there be for him, since no such thing is perceived when he is established? Thus it is settled. Now, in that regard..."

That treatise called Pratyabhijñā which has been composed by you is established upon the basis of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). *Pratyabhijñāna* is the knowledge that arises through direct confrontation (*pratīpam ābhimukhyena*), known as the valid cognition of scripture (*āgama-pramāṇa*).
By means of the quarter of the treatise known as Pratyabhijñā, direct knowledge indeed arises.

Thus, that too is incorrect, because [the two] are not obtained there. So he says: "It was stated previously, and now he speaks again: that which exists as this pair of powers consisting of knowledge and action—that alone is the concomitant property of that [reality]; and by that very [pair], this universe of existing things attains its manifestation."

Because of its connection with linguistic usage (*vyavahṛti*). Therefore, by showing that "through the perception of that [word], there is the perception of that [meaning]," the Teacher demonstrates the subject matter of the treatise known as *pratyabhijñā* (recognition).
Thus it is established that when that [word] is known, there is the comprehension of the knowledge of that [meaning]. And so it is said: "By means of power (*śakti*)..."

This is recognized through the act of manifestation (*viṣkaraṇa*). Furthermore, it is from that [manifestation] that the conventional usage of "Īśa" and so forth is set in motion by the radiance of power (*śaktiprakāśa*).
Therefore, in this case, where [the usage] has not been previously set in motion, it is merely due to the force of delusion; [the usage of] "Īśa" and so forth occurs within the radiance of power.

Ordinary worldly discourse (*vyavahāra*) proceeds [only] because of a state of delusion, O Lord; it was not previously set in motion. However, by means of the manifestation of the dual powers of knowledge and action, the discourse beginning with "Īśa" (the Lord) is set in motion. Thus, the nature of impurity (*mala*) has been established in great detail.
Because there is no connection between the subject under discussion and that which is beyond the scope of words or designations; therefore, it is heard in scripture:
"From whom [all words] turn back, not having reached Him, together with the mind—He who knows that Brahman as bliss has no fear from any quarter," and "He has transcended the path."

Even the Veda, fearing that its own nature might be reduced to the status of those two [the individual soul and the world], speaks with trepidation: "By whom is he to be praised? Of how many kinds are his qualities? To whom is he an object? Whose mind falls into the trap of following after your foot? And who is not struck with wonder? (23)

Thus ends the third daily lesson, titled "The Determination of its Results, Objects of Knowledge, and so forth," within the Section on Action (*kriyādhikāra*) of the *Śrīmatpratyabhijñākaumudī* composed by Bhaṭṭāraka. From the beginning, [the total count is] 120.

Now, having established that the Supreme Lord alone is the agent and the knower— His own self characterized by perfect consciousness, existence, and bliss, and none other— he once again demonstrates His very agency.

Oṃ. This very one, by virtue of His infinite power as the agent, manifests these entities according to His will; this is His creative activity (*kriyā-śakti*), and He is the Supreme Lord. [He manifests] entities such as jars and the like, through His infinite power of agency and so forth.

It manifests through the state of being accompanied by the *cakras* (the wheels of energy), emerging from within its own memory (*svasmṛti*) into an external form. It makes [the object] perceptible through such expressions as "this is a jar," by means of the activity of the unfolding of its own will. And this very [activity] is celebrated as the power called *kriyā* (action).
And this very lack of compassion is described as the supreme power of Īśvara; moreover, this lack of compassion is said to be the innate power (*svābhāvika-śakti*) of Īśvara. And thus:
We praise Śaṅkara, the source of the manifestation of the wheel of powers, whose opening and closing of his eyes cause the dissolution and arising of the universe. || 1 ||
In that wherein this entire universe resides and from which it has emerged,
there is no obstruction anywhere, because its nature is the unobscured reality.
Even when there is the fluctuation of states such as waking and so forth, that which is non-different from them expands;
it never departs from its own innate nature, for that is what is perceived.
In the *Spanda* [Kārikās], beginning with these words...
53b) Even for one who is not inert, the power of agency is indeed perceived from the perspective of ultimate reality.
Just as a blind man sees a jar and so forth, and likewise, there is the creation of various grains such as rice and barley from a seed; and so it is.
From the inert [water], which takes the form of water, the birth of living beings occurs through the various activities of the moon—such as its shining and its waning and waxing.
Thus, why is it said that the one called Īśvara is the "agent" (kartṛ) because he possesses the power of agency? For even for another [who is not the Supreme Lord]...
"Because that power belongs to the insentient and so forth," he says.
Oṃ. The power of the insentient is its sapidity (rasā), while the existence of the sentient is its state of being;
for it is from this that the reality of agent and object, as well as cause and effect, arises. (24)
Even if an insentient thing such as a seed possesses the capacity for agency and so forth,

it is nonetheless due to the manifestation of that [capacity] within itself which serves as the cause for its respective activity; it is not, however, by virtue of itself, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence of activity occurring even after the form has ceased, nor indeed is such [activity] observed.

Sometimes, somehow. Therefore, it is logical: that power of agency which belongs to insentient things such as seeds, and the existence of that which exists, resides in that very thing; and therein lies both the state of being the agent and the state of being the object.

The relationship of cause and effect, as in that of the sprout and the seed, exists; and the intention is that the Supreme Lord is their creator. Thus it is established that the subsequent state is to be brought about. || 24 ||
And since this is so:

Oṃ. For those who maintain that what is non-existent is non-existent, the attainment of the true nature of existence is the purpose; and thus, even for that which exists, its further non-existence is sought through the attainment of the goal. || 25 ||

Oṃ! In this world, the relationship between cause and effect revolves through various stages; its state of being perceivable by both types of sense faculties arises from the power of some [unmanifest] principle. (26)
That which is non-existent is non-existent—whether it be the horn of a hare and the like, or a jar and the like, whether stable or unstable.
In that case, the non-existent entity is seen as having the nature of being my object, just like a jar or similar things.

However, for an entity that already exists, there is no further existence; once its attainment is achieved, there is no purpose or utility, because once the purpose is accomplished, [further effort] would be redundant.

For this very reason, the causal relationship of all things in the world belongs solely to the power of that certain Lord who revolves within; and the state of being perceivable by both sense organs occurs precisely because [the object] exists as both an internal and external form, thereby being perceivable by both sets of organs. However—

The intended meaning is that [the world arises] solely through the power of the Supreme Lord and not by itself. For this very reason, it is said that the Supreme Lord alone is the internal and external cause. || 27 ||
Oṃ! Thus, this single activity exists both internally and externally with its successive stages;
it has been explained as belonging to the Enduring One, who possesses a dual form despite being one.
Oṃ. That which is internal with respect to something else is its external effect;
and the dual state of external and internal is said to exist in relation to the subject.
Oṃ. Therefore, the cause is like a mother; and while that [cause] abides as a twofold manifestation, the effect abides as one alone. Thus, the activity of the one is appropriate. (28)

Thus, for the one Supreme Lord alone, who is capable of enduring both internal and external movement through His dual nature, His sequential power of action (*kriyā-śakti*) has been established. Likewise, the twofold state—both external and internal—is dependent solely upon the subject (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, it is the subject alone [who constitutes this duality].

The Supreme Lord alone is the cause in both states [of being and non-being]; therefore, activity is appropriate for this one subject alone, and not for anything else, whether it be insentient matter or a sentient being—this refutes all other doctrines. Consequently, it is logical that the Self, as the agent and knower, is established from the very beginning.
By the words "Maheśvara," and so forth. || 29 ||

And likewise in another way: "Oṃ; for this very reason, even in the case of a soaked seed, the Supreme Lord is the desired cause. It is not at all logical for anything other than Him, such as the seed itself, to possess causality. (41)
The meaning of this has already been explained. || 41 ||

But let it be granted that the object exists; for instance, when a potter, having gathered clay and other materials, himself produces the jar and so forth as the object to be grasped—nevertheless, what is the need for that agent (pramātṛ) or for another cause, namely the Supreme Lord? To this, he says:
Oṃ; for indeed, just as a potter produces a jar from that clay and other materials through a specific arrangement and a sequence of refinements, so too [does the Lord]. (41)

This is the meaning here: the potter is the efficient cause (nimitta) because he produces the clay and other materials from the pot, which is the effect; he causes them to arise—that is, he brings about specific refinements through those refinements of the clay and so forth—solely for the sake of establishing the Lord.

Just as the Lord, presiding over his own primordial nature (prakṛti) composed of the three qualities (guṇas), generates the various objects of knowledge in due order—this is the meaning—it is exactly so even in that case; however, there too, the Lord alone is the efficient cause (nimittamātra). For even a potter [acts] solely through the intellect, which is a manifestation of consciousness.
Because the accomplishment of each respective possible form occurs through that [cause], and because it is established without that [cause]— as was already settled previously—

it is for this very reason that the Supreme Lord is held to be the efficient cause (*nimitta*) even in the case of the sprout. Therefore, since the relationship of cause and effect, of the instrument and its result, and so forth, is established everywhere, He is the efficient cause by virtue of being the cause.

And as the witness, the Supreme Lord alone is the cause. Thus it is said: "By the syllable *ī*, the Pradhāna and other such principles are not the cause; therefore, [the cause] is Brahman. And so says the Veda: "From whom there is no other higher, who was born and entered into all the worlds."

By such statements as these, the question arises: how do the various latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) of the yogi produce [cognition] through volition and so forth? Thus, once again, the discourse regarding a cause other than the Supreme Lord has reappeared. To this point as well, he says:
Oṃ! Even for yogins, by the mere force of their will, things such as jars are produced from subtle atoms;
each one is stable and performs its own specific purposeful action. 42.

For this very reason, even yogins do not possess any causal power like that of Īśvara. Furthermore, if [it were the case that] the creation and dissolution of yogins occur through their own volition alone, without the refinement of clay and other materials— just as a potter and others [act]— then by that very fact, the yogins would also be of the nature of Īśvara.
By means of that very support, those [objects] are then brought forth; indeed, they do not arise for the yogi without that support.

For it is well known that the identity with the Supreme Lord has been accomplished as his own essential nature. By the power of His will, this [occurrence] of yogis—such as a jar or the bringing of water—[takes place].
Even that which arises as a jar or the like, which accomplishes a specific purpose, exists solely for the sake of the Lord;
thus, in that case as well, the Great Lord alone is indeed the cause. (42)

Is this relation of cause and effect, or the state of being a cause and its effect, found anywhere else? Even in other doctrines, he asserts that the Supreme Lord alone is the cause, and not anything else such as the insentient and so forth.

Oṃ. When the existence of a yogic emanation is ascertained by another means of valid cognition, it must be either an effect, a logical reason, or an essential nature; therefore, it is rooted in origination. (43)
Oṃ. Form arises from the manifestation of the singular fire of each respective subject;
even from that which is imperceptible, there is a new manifestation of earth and so forth through the sovereign [deity]. (44)

Oṃ! His activity is unfailing, for it proceeds from one who has conquered others and is not dependent on other subjects. That manifestation is the supreme [state] because it arises from the sovereignty of the Lord of that manifestation. 45.
For instance:
"Even that causal relationship expressed as 'in this, that exists' is not tenable for insentient things that lack mutual dependence. (46)
If it is asked how this is so, it is explained as follows:
Oṃ, for those who are solely established in their own self and devoid of contemplative inquiry [there is no attainment].
This sevenfold meaning is applicable even to the terms "existence" and "non-existence. If one asks, "How so? [it is as follows:]
Oṃ! Even though cause and effect possess a mutually reciprocal nature, they are indeed one; for there is no difference, as their mutual nature is not distinct from one another. 48.
And so it is said:
Oṃ! Through the differentiation of the single self, she follows the sequence of action and time;
likewise, she exists as such through the state of devouring the leaves. 49.
This is the meaning here: non-existence.
When the determination that [the world] is a creation of the Yogin is established, then just as in the case of clay and a jar, there is the production of an effect from a cause;

and even in that case, the desired proof is achieved through the existence of a cause for the cause. However, the intended meaning is that the Great Lord alone, whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is indeed the cause. And so it is said: "He who has gone to the forest... [text fragment].
In cases such as a cold mountain slope, fire is inferred through the non-perception of smoke;

[the inference is]: "This mountain slope is pervaded by fire because it lacks smoke. And this effect [as a reason] is non-deviant, because of the mutual pervasion [of cause and effect], whereas in the case of fallacious reasons, that pervasion does not exist.
Even in cases such as the potter’s kiln, where there is an appearance of smoke emerging externally due to heat and so forth,
there exists another dominant factor that makes it known— namely, "it is hot"— established through mutual pervasion,
the relationship of cause and effect, the relationship of the signified and the signifier, and so on.
And even in that case, it is established that Maheśvara alone is the indicator by virtue of being thus perceived. Likewise, elsewhere [it is said]: "Where there is smoke, fire also exists."
Thus, even by way of pervasion (*vyāpti*), that specific distinction belongs to those who are devoid of dependence. Its establishment is from itself;

likewise, because of prior pervasion, there is no proof of mutual pervasion. For the pure one, this is the cause, or rather, this is the effect. This is because, in the case of cause and effect, they possess a mutually inherent nature.

When [the identity] is established, there is likewise oneness; however, in the case of difference, there is no mutual nature [between things]. This is because the conventional usage of knower and known, and so forth, would exist either perpetually or only occasionally, depending on whether it is restricted to its own self.
Thus, when there is a division within a single essence, the sequence of action, parts, and so forth, occurs accordingly.

Even if agency consists in being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmattayā*), what of it? The point is that once the Supreme Lord is established as the agent and the knower, everything is entirely resolved. And so, previously:
The stability of the world would perish, were it not for Maheśvara, who has made the internal fire his own and possesses a universal form,
being the singular embodiment of consciousness and endowed with the eternal power of knowledge, memory, and the withdrawal of memory.
56a) Now, in order to conclude all of this, he demonstrates that the Supreme Lord alone is the cause,

the agent, the one whose nature is both consciousness and non-consciousness, the experiencer, and the established witness; and he shows that [the world] would perish if it were not sustained by His very essence.

Oṃ. Furthermore, such [a distinction] is not logical for that which is insentient, because of the contradiction between difference and non-difference; however, a distinction of appearances is compatible within the single conscious self. 50.

For there is no distinction whatsoever between the insentient and the sentient, either through difference—as a staff is distinct from a jar—nor even through non-difference—as a jar is not distinct from itself, nor as a staff is not distinct from itself. The appearance of difference arises in contradiction to this [non-distinction], such as "jar," "cloth," and so forth; [this applies] to all things.

The sense is that [the object], being distinct from that which abides as a mere portion of its own self, is the cause of the knowledge of that which is distinct. However, since the experiencer—the supreme Self, the one Consciousness—is established in all, and whether it be the knower or ourselves, all this is necessarily under His control; thus, even this logic is not contradictory. For when the sun has risen, for everyone...
Because the causes, such as lamps and so forth, are inherent in those [objects], and because in that case the feet have not yet been reached.
Because he is established in that [state] everywhere and at all times, he is the Great Lord (Maheśvara) who is the cause; thus is this teaching established.

Thus, although the oneness of consciousness is established in all cases, here it is by way of its formal nature (*rūpatvena*). For the universe, which is endowed with existence, the proof of its own nature is precisely the differentiation of its manifestations (*ābhāsabheda*).
And that [differentiation] is impossible without the reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) of oneness characterized by the will-to-create (*cikīrṣā*).
"Without the conceit that 'I am doing it'"; this was shown by the passage beginning with "He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate,'" and he demonstrates that very point as follows.

Oṃ! Even in the case of the real world, there would be unity through the oneness of consciousness despite the difference between appearance and [the object]; for without the reflective awareness of the unity characterized by the desire to act, no action occurs. (51)

In the case of two appearances that are distinct— such as a jar and a non-jar, or blue, yellow, red, and so forth— there is no accomplishment of action without the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) "I am doing this."
Because she exists within that interval, the simultaneous existence of the wind in her and of her in the wind is mutually established.

And by this very act of discernment (*vimarśa*), the characteristic of medical treatment (*cikitsā*) is established; it is the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and immediately following that is action (*kriyā*). Thus, the meaning is that this pair of powers consisting of knowledge and action belongs to the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) and is indeed established for the sake of the maintenance of the world’s play. Likewise:

And previously [it was stated]: "For every living being, knowledge and action are indeed clearly established," because they are established merely through the conventional usage of "I know" and "I act. By this, the pair of powers of knowledge and action is [established] according to the principle of the section on knowledge and the section on action.
The meaning is that it is established. || 51 ||
And then, he clarifies that very point.
Oṃ! Thus, through the nature of the world appearing as jars, cloths, and so forth, [the Lord] desires to abide; and indeed, causality, agency, and action are likewise [His]. (52)
The world appears through various manifestations such as jars, cloths, and so forth, by means of this [cognition] expressed as "this."

It is precisely the will of that Lord; and that alone is causality. Causality exists everywhere, and agency likewise exists everywhere, possessing the qualities of an agent. That alone is action. For action is said to have the nature of the unfolding of knowledge. Therefore, from that Lord, there is the initial expansion.

From that arises knowledge, and from that, action is said to proceed. Relying upon this triad of powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action, the Supreme Lord himself— whose universal form is manifested by his own radiance— appears in divided forms through the conceptualization of the knower, the means of knowledge, the object of knowledge, and so forth.

It causes the universe to manifest. Likewise, seek to understand that from which these sounds are born, by which they are produced, and by which, once born, they live; that into which they dissolve and into which they enter—that is Brahman, the great source of the universe. It is that which devours the universe and faces in every direction.
With hands on all sides and mouths on all sides; I know this great Puruṣa, of the color of the sun, beyond darkness.
I alone existed in the beginning; there was nothing else, neither being nor non-being, beyond me.
57a) "Afterwards, that which remains of this collection—that is my 'I'. For there is no other born besides him who has entered into all the worlds. And likewise in the *Tantrāloka*:
Furthermore, whatever exists here—whether external or internal, and whatever is considered a means—that is merely the nature of luminosity, the supreme body of Śiva alone. (1)
Blue, yellow, the face, suffering, and light—these are merely Śiva. In this supreme non-duality whose nature is light, who else could there be? || 2 ||
Whether this is duality consisting of difference, or whether it is non-duality—this Supreme Lord shines as nothing but the very form of light. (3)

The meaning of this is as follows: pleasure, pain, bondage, liberation, consciousness, and insentience—these words have a single referent, just like the words "jar" and "pot," and they all signify one and the same thing. (4)

Even in that which is luminous, how can there be a non-luminous part? Or, if it were luminous, how could its lack of luminosity be asserted? Furthermore, while that [luminosity] is manifesting, how can it be called a "real entity"? (5)
Therefore, since this light is established as being one,
those who maintain the doctrine of distinct cognitions— beginning with the Buddhists— are indeed refuted.
Only luminosity is expressed, because non-luminosity is excluded;
the meaning of the word "one" (eka) is not number, as it does not partake in distinctions such as numerical quantity or individual differences.
The Great Goddess is not power alone, because she does not depend on anything else;
nor is this God the possessor of power, because he does not depend on anyone.

The object of meditation is not to be meditated upon because of the absence of a meditator, due to the exclusion of both the meditator and the object of meditation; it is not an object of worship because of the absence of a worshiper, nor is there a worshiper because of the absence of an object of worship.
There is no practitioner of mantra, nor is there such a mantra, nor is there a master who is the father of mantra;
there is neither initiation, nor one who initiates, nor even the Great Lord who is initiation itself.
In this state, which is devoid of agent, object, and action, there is no standing, sitting, cessation, joining, bringing forth, and so on, ending with dismissal.

Neither non-existent, nor existent, nor both existent and non-existent, nor yet devoid of both; for that state is difficult to discern—it is something ineffable, the unsurpassed. Enough with this excessive elaboration, which has been revealed by the Great Guru through his contemplation. Thus [ends] the Śrī...
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the section on Action within the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī*, composed by my venerable teacher Ānandanātha.
The section on ritual action is completed.
Oṃ! May there be well-being for all creatures.
57b) Oṃ, homage to the venerable Lord Viśveśvara, the supreme deity. Homage to the venerable Guru.
Now, therefore, the chapter on the Āgamas is commenced.

Oṃ! I bow to Giriśa, who is the very self of the power of Supreme Śiva; he who is the source of the stream of nectar flowing from the stainless radiance extending from Śiva down to the Kṣitīśvaras; he whose essence is that which constitutes the sphere of destiny; and within whom reside the conceptualizations of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and concealment, appearing as their manifestation. || 1 ||

Thus, by the passage beginning with "the appearance of the particular characteristic" (*svalakṣaṇābhāsa*) and so forth, the Buddhist doctrine and others have proceeded like a dense darkness of blindness. Therefore, in order to initiate the section concerning those doctrines, [the author] says "by the permanent self" (*sthāyinātmanā*) and so forth, provided that such is the intended meaning contained within your own statement.
When the darkness of that [opponent's] doctrine has been made firm by the "logic of burying a post," and then,

for the purpose of refuting that doctrine, having refuted it with the words "If the Great Lord were not one who has internalized the infinite forms of the universe," and so forth, he (the opponent) is subsequently perceived as one who has already accepted the very point previously established.

By means of the word "Sat" and so forth, having solidified one's own essential nature as "Aham"— which is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— during the rising of the fierce sun; and from that, [one realizes] the two powers consisting of knowledge and action, which are of the nature of sovereignty.

Having condensed the five topics, and having clearly demonstrated the nature of the two powers— that both knowledge and action are established for every living being, and so forth— and having subsequently [discussed] knowledge in the section on knowledge and action in the section on action;
Having thus directed [the mind] toward each respective object according to its specific intention, now follows, in due order,

the section on the scriptures (*āgama-adhikāra*) concerning the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*)— from Śiva down to the earth— which have been described as the supreme and most excellent, according to their defining characteristics and essential purport.

By means of demonstrating that the two powers characterized as knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*kriyā*), which are established following the previously established Śiva-tattva, belong to the *ātura* (the one in need of grace) alone,
that pair of powers is declared to have its characteristic established; such is the nature of that power-tattva.

The definition previously stated is established. By means of that [definition], in the passage beginning with "the knower is he, the Great Lord," the author states this in order to demonstrate that the knower— the Great Lord Śiva— is indeed established as Śiva, renowned by such a name and possessing the aforementioned characteristics.
Oṃ! Thus, the internal and external activity, following the sequence of action and time, belongs only to the Mother; for knowledge and action are mutually inseparable from her. || 1 ||

Action, whose essential nature is an outward-flowing activity both internal and external, manifests as "I am thus," "I do this," or "this has been done," whether its internal or external operation extends outward. This outward extension is, for example: "I cook," "I act," or "I alone know this object."

That very [expansion]—thus, whatever expansion occurs externally or internally, even as it follows the sequence of time—that is indeed of the nature of action and knowledge, for without those two, realization is not achieved. And in those two, there is only the Self (*ātman*), whose manifesting form flashes forth within as "I. It is not...

And [this applies] to the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. Because the intellect and the rest possess sovereignty, freedom from distress, and the accomplishment of all that was to be done; whereas [the self], being by nature predominantly insentient, is like a stone and so forth. Therefore, they are neither mutually separated nor mutually conjoined.

The connection is that knowledge and action belong to this [subject], because he alone acts and he alone knows. By the word "end" (anta), the two-fold nature characterized by the Śiva-tattva and the Śakti-tattva is established; such is the connection. || 1 ||
58b) Now, as their turn has arrived, he defines Sadāśiva and Īśvara.

Oṃ. However, at the beginning, that reality known as Ātman arises from the intensification of internal piercing; whereas, through the state of externalization, it subsequently becomes the Supreme Lord.

This is the process: that internal reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which, by virtue of being kissed by the power of internal knowledge (*antar-jñāna-śakti*), takes the form "I am the agent" as its own nature; that very reflective awareness is the principle (*tattva*) known as Sādāśiva.
And that [same awareness], when appearing as the external self, is expressed as "I do this."
"Those who know [the truth] say that the nature of reality (tattva) is the very essence of the Lord in the form of gross reflective awareness;
by this it is shown that all this is indeed composed of knowledge and action, and His will alone is the cause everywhere. || 2 ||
For it is thus:
Oṃ! This Īśvara is the opening of the eyes externally, and Sadāśiva is the closing of the eyes internally.
And in the case of co-referentiality, this applies to the two cognitions "Being" (in the *sadvidyā*) and "I am this" (*aham idam*).

The manifestation of that very Lord externally is known as Īśvara; this is through the state of being (*bhāva*). Internally, the manifestation is Sadāśiva, whose body consists of the cessation of emission (*hānimeṣa*); this is due to the cause of the state of being (*bhāva-hetutayā*).
Furthermore, the connection is that both of those [Īśvara and Sadāśiva] are dependent on Him, and are indeed produced from Him, namely Īśvara and Sadāśiva.

And because these two cognitions— "I" and "this"— share a common substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such that the state of being "this" rests within the locus of "I," there exists between the cognitions of "I" and "this" the *sadvidyā* (the knowledge of Being). *Śuddhavidyā* (Pure Knowledge) is the repose within one's own Self.

It is established that the purpose of the cause is the attainment of its own nature by this entire world, just as black gram attains the state of the *sambikā* plant and as a banyan tree attains the state of the seed-vessel. || 3 ||
Now, what is the nature of this knowledge? Therefore, he said: "And from this very [source]."

Oṃ! Just as through the observation of wealth, one perceives that all entities—which exist in a state of differentiation yet are endowed with being—have consciousness as their essence; [so too is this]. || 4 ||
Oṃ. Here, the state of "otherness" (*aparatva*) of entities arises from their appearing as "I-consciousness" (*matātmatva*);
whereas the state of "supreme-ness" (*paratā*) arises from their being veiled by the "I-sense" (*ahantā*). Indeed, that is the intermediate state (*parāpara-daśā*). Herein lies the intended meaning:
Because, in the case of resorting to external existence, there would follow its non-difference [from the Self], and because there would also follow its difference [from the Self]—
such is the definition of Śuddhavidyā.
And she is well known as both the supreme and the non-supreme.

59a) It is well-known; for this very reason, it is *śuddhavidyā* (pure knowledge). Its essential nature (*svarūpa*) consists of pure knowledge because its "I-ness" (*ahantā*) is unobscured. And that which is the first stage mentioned therein as the sixty-fourth is the supreme nature (*parasvarūpa*).
Abiding in the form of peacock-egg juice, the essence of the *vaṭadānikā* plant, and the essence of *māṣa-aśambikā*,
she is celebrated as Śrīvidyā by the most excellent practitioners.

And I, having turned away from the inauspicious principle (tattva), [perceive] that which is immediately subsequent: the Śakti-tattva, which is supreme, pure, transcendent of the universe, and whose very nature is that [Śakti] herself. Because she is endowed with existence (bhava) and because her nature is that of "wishing" (aṅkana), she is celebrated as "Śakti"; for by her power, she is capable of being designated as such.
That power, being free from the state of equality with the two [aspects], is called *śuddhavidyā* (pure knowledge). || 5 ||
Now, by emphasizing the essential nature of these two great ones,
[the author] demonstrates that very duality which has issued forth externally, as it follows in due order, through the twofold nature of that [duality] itself.

Oṃ! Even for the agent who is of the nature of consciousness, the power of Māyā—which consists precisely in the cognition of distinctions among non-existent things—is indeed capable of being known, just as [it is known] by the Vidyeśvaras. || 6 ||
Established in the principle of *vidyā*, they are all-knowing and all-doing; thus they are the *Vidyeśvaras*.

Even though *māyā* consists of the power of the awakener (*bodhakartṛtā*), its perception as distinct is called *vidyā*; for even this power of *māyā* is indeed *vidyā* because it leads to transcendence from *saṃsāra*. And those who abide therein—

It is established that [they are] Mantreśvaras and Vidyeśvaras. Furthermore, it is the power of Māyā itself that is called "Vidyā" merely by appearing as a reversal of its own essential nature. And this very point is stated with the intended meaning of another verse. (7) For instance:

Oṃ. Of that whose nature is sovereignty, the power of knowledge (vidyā-śakti) is the illuminator when it exists as the state of the bound soul (paśu), while the power called māyā, on the other hand, causes concealment. 8.

That which is called *avidyā* (ignorance) is the state of the transmigrating souls (*saṃsārin*) regarding their own self’s sovereignty, characterized by the relationship of the known and the knower. By means of this, one does not know one's own true nature; thus it is called *avidyā*. Furthermore, that which causes the concealment of that very sovereignty is called *māyā*. For this very reason...

Regarding "paśyabhāveti": that which is known as "this is blue," "this is yellow," and "this is white"—from that [arises] the reality (tattva), and from that, that very same self is known through differentiation; that is *vidyā*. It is called *vidyā*.

And thus, that cognition which occurs in such forms as "this is blue," "this is yellow," and "this is white," and so forth—because of its lack of knowledge regarding reality (tattva), and due to the absence of the realization of the sovereignty of one's own self and so on—its power unfolds; this is called "sāmānya" (the universal). By this [it is explained].
The meaning is that the essential nature of the two principles, Māyā and Avidyā, has been determined.
He clarifies that very concealment.

Oṃ. When that which is of a single essence appears as differentiated—whether it be the void, the intellect, or the body—the power of Māyā manifests within the non-Self. (3) When entities appear as differentiated, such as the body and so forth appearing as the subjectivity of "I," then it is established that this is the unfolding of the power of Māyā.

When the non-self, the void, the intellect, and the body are perceived through the sense of "I," and when there is a distinction expressed as "this is this" and so forth— even while that which is of a single-flavored nature appears as consisting of the flavor of duality— there arises what is called "māyā," which has no other support.
The sense is that, having taken its stand, it throbs even more intensely. || 3 ||

And therefore, because the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is distinct from the confidence born of the state of being "one who has come together" (*samāyāvī*), it is said that the subject (*mātṛ*) is pervaded by the pentad beginning with time (*kālādi*). And he demonstrates that very point:

Oṃ. And that cognizer who is [perceived as] empty and so forth, distinct from the object of cognition—the cognizer who is the object of knowledge and is enveloped by the pentad of time and the other factors. || 9 ||
And therefore, because of its illusory nature (*māyāvitva*), when there is an object of knowledge (*prameya*) distinct [from the subject],

it is said to be enveloped by the five branches within the gross form of *māyā*— namely, Time (*kāla*), Knowledge (*vidyā*), Limited Agency (*kalā*), Attachment (*rāga*), and Necessity (*niyati*)— and thus interwoven and bound.

And since he is incapable of even bending a bowstring bound by that [power], what need is there to mention [his inability] regarding such things as revealing his own true nature? The sense is that this has been established previously. || 9 ||
60a) It was previously stated that the immeasurable *nava-caya* is enveloped by the five beginning with time (*kāla*). To the question "Of how many kinds is it?", he says:
Oṃ! That which consists of the twenty-three principles, comprising both the effects and the instruments, has as its single undivided nature the Pradhāna, the root cause. (10)

Among those, distinguished by their gross and subtle natures, there are five known as sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; these are designated as "effects" (kārya). The subtle ones, known as the "subtle elements" (tanmātra), are the "causes" (kāraṇa). || 5 ||

And their effects are those known as earth, water, fire, air, and ether—these are the five gross elements. Likewise, there are the five organs of cognition known as hearing, touch, sight, taste, and smell; and similarly, the [five] organs of action known as speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
The five organs of action, the mind, the intellect, and the ego—thus the internal organ is threefold.
Of this object of knowledge, which consists of twenty-three divisions in the form of effects and instruments, the root cause is that single undivided principle called *pradhāna*. And so it is said:
The origin of the spear [Prakṛti] is unmodified; the seven, beginning with Mahat, are both modifications and origins;
the group of sixteen is modification only; and the Puruṣa is neither origin nor modification. (1)
And thus [it is said]: "From primordial nature (prakṛti) comes the Great One (mahat); from that, the I-maker (ahaṅkāra); from that, the group of sixteen;
and from five of that group of sixteen, the five gross elements," and so forth.
Thus, according to the Sāṃkhya school, the path of objects of knowledge is established through the distinction between the gross and the subtle. || 10 ||
If this is so, he asks: what is the cause, or what is the effect?
Oṃ! Now, there are thirteenfold external and internal faculties, and the group of effects is tenfold, distinguished by their gross and subtle natures. (11)
The five organs of cognition, the five organs of action,

and the triad consisting of mind, intellect, and ego— this is the series of thirteen internal and external instruments. It is established that the category of effects, however, consists of ten kinds on the other side.
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, desire, sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

Thus ends the first chapter, concerning the manifestation of the expansion of the venerable scriptures, in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī*, composed by the illustrious Utpaladeva, the best of the secret caves of the primordial [Lord], the venerable author of the *Pratyabhijñābhaṭṭāraka*.
This most auspicious work has been brought to completion by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka through the thorough investigation of reality.

Oṃ. We praise the Lord who has transcended all, who consists of the universe, who is both the object of knowledge and the knower, who is beyond what is known, who is both with form and without appearance, and who is perfect bliss. || 1 ||

Thus, that whose nature is the manifestation of the world up to the limit of Śiva’s vision, which consists of the means of knowledge, the knower, and the object of knowledge, and which has entered into the states of the perceiver, perception, and the perceived, as well as the nature of the knower,
the act of knowing, and the object known— wherein does it not reside within the "I"?

Through the contemplation of fullness, consciousness expands as the Full One; it is also the locus made triadic by being the site of "this-ness" (idantā) anywhere. In that regard, even within the fivefold group of qualified practitioners, there are those whose nature consists of the reflective awareness of "I-ness" (ahantā-vimarśa). Who [are they]?
In order to demonstrate that [the levels] consist of the reflective awareness of their respective limits, he now extends the introduction to the next chapter:
"The universe, from Śiva down to the earth, does not exist as a differentiated reality through its various respective functions."
It extends.

Oṃ. Therein, this [deity] Mātṛtā resides as the presiding deity (adhi-daivata) over the Mothers; when the expansion of objects of cognition is differentiated, Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established [therein]. || 1 ||

That very state, which is the locus of fullness— characterized by being the sustainer (*sahantṛ*), by the nature of all things as the full self-nature, by resting within one's own self, and by the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that "all this is indeed I"— is where Rudra is the presiding authority over this universe. For:

By abiding in introversion (*antarmukhatā*), one becomes one whose eye has transcended the outward proliferation; hence [the name] Caruka. [He] dissolves (*drāvayati*) the disease of *saṃsāra*. Because he is touched by way of introversion, he is Rudra. And so it is said: [The passage continues: "I go to Kaumārī," "I smell," and so forth, as is well known. He causes [the world] to melt away. Because he is touched through introversion, he is Rudra. And likewise:
When there is the state of being the presiding deity in that which is called the withdrawal (asaṃhāra),
it is by means of bringing about that [divine] power for his own circle of worshippers, by bestowing that power upon them,
and by bringing about the presence of one who has attained immersion in what is called that power, directed toward himself.
The venerable Lord Īśvara himself is Rudra, the Blessed One, who, in the state of Māyā,
is the light of the Middle Way— liberated from inhalation and exhalation, merit and demerit, sun and moon, day and night, and so forth.

This has indeed been stated by the former teachers in such passages as, "By touching the essential nature of the subject who perceives form, one becomes one whose third eye is opened," and so forth. Consequently, by means of the manifestation and the accomplishment of the expansion of distinct objects of knowledge, one partakes in the state of being the presiding deity.

Brahmā: Furthermore, when the object of cognition (*prameya*) has expanded and become differentiated, Viṣṇu is the presiding deity over its continuity, which is characterized by the process of flowing forth. For this very reason, one perceives those two as the expansion of the object of cognition, consisting of the nature of manifestation such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow."

Because there is an absence of immersion into the state of the Pradhāna (primordial matter) characterized primarily by the notion of "I," there is no opening of the third eye. This is the intended meaning: the nature of the third [eye] is divinity (*adhidaivata*), due to its essential character as the reflective awareness of "I."

Brahmā and Viṣṇu are established by their very nature as the objects of the reflective awareness "this"; and it is an established principle that not even a moment's blink occurs naturally for them. (1)
And for this very reason.
Oṃ! This cognizer is blinded by māyā, a transmigrating being bound by karma. And therefore:
One whose dense mass of consciousness possesses sovereignty manifested through knowledge and supernormal powers is called liberated. || 2 ||

Oṃ. In its own essential nature, the cognizer is called the Lord (pati) among all existing things; yet, due to Māyā, when [the objects] appear as distinct, he becomes the bound soul (paśu), defiled by afflictions, karma, and so forth. Blinded by this Māyā, this living being (jīva) wanders in saṃsāra, bound by karma through his actions. || 3 ||
He is called "bound. Sometimes he reflects, then acts, and pursues [his thoughts] therein; acting in this way and that, he is said to be a transmigrating being bound by the fetters of karma.
Thereafter, by means of the instruction given at the outset, he...
One who possesses the sovereignty manifested through knowledge and supernormal powers, and is a mass of consciousness, is for that reason called a "yogin" in this context.

For this very reason, the cognizer who contemplates "I am all this," having perceived his own essential nature within the entire aggregate of objective and subjective states such as the grasped and the grasper,
is called the "Lord of Cognizers" (pramātṛpati). Immediately thereafter, by virtue of being the locus of objectivity (*idantā*),...
It proceeds among those who have become distinct from illusion.
61b) In that regard, this state of being a bound soul (paśu) arises from the three impurities; thus, he clarifies that very point by stating, "corrupted by the three impurities."

Oṃ. The loss of sovereignty of consciousness, and likewise the lack of consciousness within sovereignty—this twofold impurity is the loss of one's own true nature. That which consists of the subject and the separate object of knowledge is called *māyā*; it bestows birth and experience. The impurity of action (*kārma-mala*) arises from the ignorance of the agent, through the power of *māyā* itself.
That [set] is threefold. || 5 ||

The loss of the consciousness of the conscious self, and the state of non-consciousness regarding that very consciousness— this twofold deprivation of one's own true nature is called the innate impurity (āṇavamala).

Regarding those entitled to the scriptures (*āgamādhikārin*): they say that the very manifestation of distinct objects of cognition is the impurity called *māyīya-mala*. And that alone bestows birth and experience; it is the cause of birth and experience. However, they say that the lack of awareness—namely, the thought "I am the agent"—is the *kārmika-mala*. But in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), [it is otherwise].
This entire triad, known as the impurities of *āṇava*, *māyīya*, and *kārmika*, has its root-pillar in the power of *māyā*;
those who propound the Āgamas call it the primary seed (*bīja*). || 5 ||
Now he defines the characteristics of the bound souls (paśus) who are fettered by the three impurities (malas).

Oṃ! Although they are of the nature of pure awakening, those who do not possess supreme agency are manifested by their own self as having an appearance distinct [from it], through which agency and so forth arise.

Even for those whose minds are detached from the mass of objects of knowledge (*vedyarāśi*), they are taught to be distinct from one's own Self because they lack the state of being the agent of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā-kartṛtva*). This is due to the futility of full subjectivity [in their case]. For this very reason, it is said that "because of the cessation of agency," and so forth. (7)
And for this very reason, it is exactly the same even in the case of one who has transcended [the world].

Oṃ. Although they are identical in their characteristic of having attained awakening and so forth, those who possess mutual differentiation therein due to the will of the Lord are the *vijñānakevalas*.

Although they are identical in their characteristic of being [aspects of] awakening and so forth, there is a mutual distinction among them; that is, their state of difference. Furthermore, even those known by the name *vijñānakevala* are indeed composed of duality and are merely external. [This is because] they are like the fall of the letter *ra* in the sacrifice of another’s wife (*paravadhvarephapāta*), which is just like [the case of] *tirmaṇāt*. They...
Those whose discernment is as if that of the Sāṅkhya puruṣa are called vijñānakalās. || 8 ||
62a) Now he states that very view.
Oṃ. Those who are of the nature of consciousness, beginning with the void, are the Pralayākalas as agents;
they possess the *kārmamala*, while their *māyīyamala* is conceptualized.

In the state where the intellect (*buddhi*) is empty, as if by a body imagined through appearance, there exists this agency (*kartṛtva*)—which is the union with the wonder of "I"—arising from the nature of both the insentient and the sentient. Its limit extends up to the *pralayākala* [state]. At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), there are the *akalas*; [the category] *kalā-tattva* [is excluded].

Those who are devoid of the causes characterized [by the impurities] are agents who do not understand the meaning [of reality]. And for them, there exists the *kārma-mala* (the impurity of action), but not the *māyīya* (the impurity of illusion); thus it is merely a conceptual construction. 9.
Now, in order to demonstrate that the impurity known as *māyā* is its object, he says:

Oṃ. Just as the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) possess the impurity of Māyā while experiencing distinct objects of knowledge, so too do those who possess the status of being agents even among the enlightened ones, when the impurity of Karma has been destroyed. || 3 ||

For those known as the Vidyēśvaras— who, by virtue of having transcended karma and by possessing distinct objects of cognition, still maintain the sense of "I" even with respect to agency— the impurity of *māyā* indeed continues to operate, because they serve as its locus. (3)
And yet:
Oṃ! Among all the impurities of the gods and others, there are three kinds; yet among those, the karmic alone is primary, as it is the cause of saṃsāra.
Of those who are destined to wander in cyclic existence.

The Vidyeśvaras, Vijñānākalas, and Kalās do not exist [in this state], because they have transcended the path ending with Māyā; likewise, the Pralayākalas are also [absent]. Furthermore, those such as the gods who reside within the interior of this [state] are separated by the principle of Māyā.

In the scriptures, all fourteen categories of beings, ending with the immobile (sthāvara), are enumerated as those who are destined for transmigratory existence (saṃsārin). Among them, it is established that there are only three who are free from impurity (nirmala). However, according to the tradition (sampradāya), the *kārmamala* alone is the primary cause of transmigratory existence. Thus:
And those with consciousness. The divine creation consists of eight varieties, and that of the animal kingdom is fivefold;
along with the human creation, the elemental creation is briefly of one kind—thus [it is said] in the verse beginning "The elemental creation... (SK 53).
62b) Now he states the twofold nature of the goddesses.
Oṃ! Within these [elements], consciousness (citattva) is bound to the dissolution of the body;
for that which is insentient in nature, such as the void and so forth, exists as a limited quality.

Oṃ. And therein: The preeminence, the agency, and the consciousness of the conscious Self (cidātman)—the knowledge of these qualities within the void and so forth is characterized by absorption (samāveśa) into that. 11.

The consciousness and agency of transmigrating beings such as gods, which belong to the aspect of pure awareness (saṃvid-bhāga), are submerged due to the predominance of impurity; thus, the true nature of the conscious essence— its sovereignty— is [obscured] by that which is called *kalā*.

Empowered by the power of the Supreme Lord (parameśvara-śakti), it is produced by impurity (mala) and exists as a subordinate quality belonging to the subject of Māyā (māyā-pramātṛ)— ranging from the void (śūnya) to the body— because it is limited (mita). This limitation consists of the "thisness" (idantā) of everything from the "I-notion" (man-man) and the body up to the void.

Because it is submerged within the objective aspect (*prameyabhāga*). And this very reality is that which is empowered by *kalā*, while the insentient forms such as the Void (*śūnya*) and so forth are subordinated and measured. For this very reason, it exists as both a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) and as the primary principle (*pradhāna*), because its true nature has been eclipsed by the veil of ignorance (*ajñānapūmapaṭala*). And this very [reality]...

The essential nature of that which is the subject of emptiness and so forth is the ego-subject (*ahaṃtṛ*), because [otherwise] there would be no subjectivity with respect to the body and other such things.
And in that context, [the ego] is secondary; for, by the grace of the Guru, agency is primary, while consciousness—the very nature of the conscious self—is primary because it is the ultimate reality.

The knowledge that arises from the void and so forth, due to their lack of primacy, is precisely what is characterized by immersion (*samāveśa*). This is the intended meaning of "the method of that immersion. Primordial agency (*kartṛtā*) is the state of being primary;
it consists of the nature of the "I" (*ahantā*), as in such expressions as "I am the void," "I am the body," or "I am the intellect."
And when it is not subordinate, this very consciousness is blissful Brahman for the knowers of Brahman, according to the Śruti:
"The knower of Brahman becomes Brahman itself. And they say that this very consciousness is characterized by absorption (*samāveśa*) into That; and that state is called *vyutthita* (the emerged).
I am [the agent], because of the predominance of agency. || 11 ||
Thus, it is established that this is the state of the Fourth (turyā) and the Beyond-the-Fourth (turyātītā) for one who has attained that condition. || 11 ||
63b) Now, he also states that these states which appear to the animal [the ordinary being] likewise have the nature of being empty of consciousness.

Oṃ. In the void, within the self of the intellect and other faculties, where there is the state of "I-ness" and agency, there is the emptiness of the knowable, consisting merely of the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of the form of non-existence. 12.

The internal function of the sense organs, which impels the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth, is called "life" (jīvana); alternatively, it is the state of the self characterized by the ego-sense (ahaṃtā) residing within the vital breaths. || 13 ||
When it remains in that state alone, it is said to be the state of deep sleep (sauṣupta), comparable to cosmic dissolution (pralaya);
it may be with object (savedya) or without object (apavedya), and may be joined with or free from the impurity of māyā.
When the intellect and the body are empty, there is the absence of "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) and agency (kartṛtva), and so forth.

Furthermore, when objects of knowledge (prameya) and the like are not perceived, there is the emptiness of the knowable; this is expressed by such statements as "I knew nothing at all. That very state is called deep sleep (suṣupta). That indeed...
The internal functioning of the senses is distinct from the functioning that involves the activity of the sense organs;

however, the meaning is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and the rest possess both the quality of being an impeller and the state of being active. That very [functioning] is called the "life-force" (*jīvana*) of the *prāṇa*, consisting of the eightfold group [of vital breaths], and it is designated as the "slayer" (*hantṛ*) because of its nature as a slayer (*hantṛtva*).
The "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭhaka*) consists of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell,
as well as mind, intellect, and ego. In that state, because of the predominance of form, these [faculties] constitute the nature of the knower within this eightfold city.

It is described as "perfectly tranquil" (*sauṣupta*) and resembling dissolution (*pralaya*), because everywhere the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth are rendered useless. That very state is "with cognition" (*savedya*) because something is seen; and it is "without cognition" (*apavedya*) because nothing is seen, as expressed by the thought, "I was not aware of anything."

And another [state] is characterized by being accompanied by the impurity of *māyā* when there is the state of being cognizable (*savedyatva*), and it is said to be free from the impurity of *māyā* when there is the state of being non-cognizable (*avedyatva*). The ancient knowers declare that this is merely the condition of the bound soul (*paśu*). (14)
Now, the excellent means of knowing that very nature of the bound soul (paśu) is being described.
Thus he says:

Oṃ. Because there is delusion regarding even that which consists of mind alone due to its being an object of the senses, and because of the absence of clear manifestation, the state of dream is considered to be a creation. 15.

Furthermore, when the internal organ (manas) is active, those appearances such as "this is a jar," "this is gross," "this is blue," or "this is yellow" which arise with a clear manifestation— though they appear as objects of the senses due to delusion— are that internal creation which is called *supramiti*.
Of the animal sacrifice. || 15 ||

In that regard, the creation which occurs during the waking state by means of all the organs of knowledge and action, as well as the mind and intellect—the locus of knowledge and the objects of knowledge—is clearly manifest through direct perception in the form of "this is this" and so forth; it is stable and possesses a clearly manifest nature. And yet...
Like a dream and so forth, it is of an indistinct nature due to its unreality; and that is called the "waking state" common to all subjects. (19)
And again:

Oṃ. Because of the predominance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, the quality of agency belongs to them; [the self] is devoid of that, due to its connection with pleasure, pain, and the like, which consist primarily of increase and decrease. || 19 ||
In this regard, since I am characterized by the quality of *ketmatā* (the state of being a knower), and since the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth are primary,

and since that aggregate of objects of cognition consists primarily of pleasure, pain, and the like— which are characterized by increase and decrease— and since agency belongs to the qualities such as *yoma* and the rest, for that reason, this triad is to be abandoned.
It is established that the states such as waking, dreaming, and deep sleep consist of the agitation of the mind.
Now, he manifests the fourth state (turya), and by means of the form of deep sleep, the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta).
Oṃ. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) consists of inhalation (*prāṇa*) and exhalation (*apāna*); it exists individually in both dream and waking states.
That which is called *samāna*, whose nature is the cutting off of those [breaths], exists in deep sleep as if pervading all three states. || 18 ||

Oṃ! He who moves ever upward, known as udāna, whose form is the fourth state (turya), consisting of the elements and the earth, the Lord of Mantras who is free from kalās and consciousness (vijñānākala), the pervasive one, the supreme soul of the universe. || 19 ||
64a) Here, "prāṇa" refers to the state of consciousness whose nature is living, characterized by the act of breathing;
it is a synonym for the individual self (jīvātman). And that [self], whether in the waking or dreaming state, consists of prāṇa and apāna;
it exists through the upward and downward movement of prāṇa, and that movement occurs both in the dream and the waking state.
If the self is praised as being identical with the *samāna* vital air, then its functions are those of cutting,
moving upward, and so forth; or else, its functions consist of the appearance of entering and exiting,
like water or clarified butter, and states such as "I knew nothing at all" during deep sleep and the like.

In that context, waking and dreaming occur through the activity of *prāṇa* and *apāna*, by virtue of the upward and downward movement of *prāṇa*; and deep sleep and so forth occur through the increase of the activity of *samāna*, as if due to the absence of movement in those two.

Then, by way of the upward path, there is the movement of those two; characterized by the offering [of the self] through the essence of non-duality within all duality, it begins from the *vijñānakalā* in the heart up to the end of Sadāśiva, and that state consists of the Fourth (*turyā*). In which:

The upward movement of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth [occurs]; and thereafter, when the differentiation of the entire world consisting of the moving and the non-moving has dissolved, there arises the state beyond the fourth (turyātīta), which is the nature of Paraśiva—the universal self—consisting of the functions of the vital breaths and so forth, yet transcending their specific forms. And wherein...

The subject (*pramātā*) is indeed *prāṇa*. It is in grammatical apposition [with the subject] as having the forms of *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *samāna*, *udāna*, and *vyāna*. And he is the *vijñānākala* and the *mandara*; and he is the *īśa*, who is that *udāna* consisting of the forms of *sadāśiva* and *īśvara*. He alone is [the subject].
The fire is the source of all oblations, for it is the cause of the combustion of everything; and that very fire is the supreme self of the universe. This is the intended meaning here.

64b) When these five, beginning with prāṇa, possess distinct natures and distinct forms, then, by abiding in their respective functions and being based merely on vibration, they constitute the fivefold states: waking (*jāgrat*), dreaming (*svapna*), deep sleep (*suṣupta*), the fourth (*turyā*), and that which transcends the fourth (*turyātītā*). And... [ya ca]... [text fragment].

When the reality of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as well as that of the *suṣumṇā*, has been realized within this entire world, the one, pure, and tranquil essential nature—the ultimate reality—arises everywhere. Even then, there is no desire for anything; thus, it transcends all.
By such statements as "one who touches the feet" and "whose intention is like the full moon," and so forth— thus,

when there is no further seeking [of a self] through the notions "this is mine" or "I am this"— there arises the stainless, pure, and absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) that is free from obstruction. And in that regard:

Because, upon the attainment of that knowledge, the causes for [the persistence of] the body and so forth no longer exist, the deceased body continues by the force of its residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), like a potter's wheel. And then, when the destruction of the body has been reached and its purpose has been fulfilled, [the body] ceases.

"By means of both the absolute and the final [cessations], one attains absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). This has been determined in great detail throughout the Sāṅkhya treatises. And likewise: "Beholding his own nature through the state of non-abiding in that [ignorance], he smiles..."
How could this crooked path belong to him, the son of the Immortal? || 1 ||
Then his uncreated nature, characterized by omniscience and omnipotence, arises;

for he knows and accomplishes everything that he desires. This alone is the emergence of that object of meditation within the mind of the meditator—that attainment of identity with it which occurs for the practitioner who so wills. (3)
Thus ends the Śrī Spanda [Kārikās].

And so it is said in the *Tantrāloka*: "In this way, the dissolution of the entire path of the universe occurs without effort within the Great Wheel of Bhairava, which is surrounded by pure consciousness.
Then, through the dissolution of that duality and the complete exhaustion of its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*),"

One should contemplate the wheel as being pacified; then it is tranquil, then it is stilled, and thereafter, through the complete exhaustion of even its formative impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is tranquil. Thus, at the very end, through the pacification of the wheel, it is indeed pure.
The meaning is that one should connect it with the "finder" (saṃvindātṛ). || 2 ||
By means of this yoga of meditation, the universe dissolves into the Wheel; then, from that proximity, consciousness shines forth as if its objects themselves had dissolved into it.
