In this way, one should dissolve the entire universe into the play of one's own self-awareness while circumambulating it; then, by emitting it once again, one should attain the state of Śambhu-Bhairava.
"The entire universe is his power, while the Great Lord is the possessor of that power"—thus was it stated by the venerable Śrīkaṇṭha in the *Māṅgalashāstra*. (5)
When one stands before the heart in the state of pure subjectivity within innate bliss,
and rests solely in emptiness, one should contemplate the "blissless" (nirānanda).
There, Ānanda is the object of cognition, surrounded by the emanation of Śapūraṇā; established in the state of Parānanda, he abides adorned by the moon of apāna. || 7 ||
Then, completely absorbed in the friction of the infinite, radiating objects of knowledge, having reached a state of equilibrium, one becomes composed of the bliss of Brahman. (8)

Even beyond that, one who is intent on the unreality of the conceptualization of the flood of means of knowledge and objects of knowledge should rest in the fire of *udāna* and contemplate the Great Bliss (*mahānanda*).
And here is the commentary.

Indeed, here [in this context], that which was previously non-existent is called "empty" (*śūnya*). It is said that one should meditate upon the empty; thus, non-existence (*abhāva*) is indicated where existence has come to an end. This is described as the single essence of consciousness (*saṃvid-ekātman*) within form.
65b) Relying on resting in mere emptiness alone,
within the heart— the abode where the arising of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth comes to rest—
there is bliss which is one's own nature because it is free from all adjuncts (*nirupādhi*); for such a subject, what [could there be] as an object of knowledge (*prameya*) and so forth?

Abiding in the state of identity with the subject by way of indifference toward the tranquil [state], and remaining established while directly realizing his own Self as absolute, he subsequently— according to the principle that "prior consciousness has transformed into the vital breath"—
[perceives] the vital breath, which is of the nature of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), from its origin up to its own final state.

During its arising through the process of exhalation (*recaka*), one should— due to some degree of outward orientation— contemplate, that is, perceive, a particular state that has emerged from one's own recognized bliss (*ānanda*) as "blissless" (*nirānanda*). Furthermore, it arises again within the object of knowledge (*prameya*) which consists of the downward breath (*apāna*).
One should contemplate the bliss produced by that supreme object of knowledge (prameya) from whatever source it may come; for at that stage of the emergence of the object of knowledge,
one should abide in the state of supreme bliss (parānanda), since [that bliss] is infinite in relation to the subject (pramātṛ) and other such factors.
The ancient *apāna* consists of the rays characterized as the objects of cognition;
through the grasping of various objects, it drinks the very state of being free from expectancy (*nairākāṅkṣya*).
By that drinking, there is cessation, because *apāna* alone, resting solely within its own self, acts as the moon through its nourishing nature, and is thus cool.

Adorned; by the sequence of the city, [the breath] reaches as far as the tenth stage, meaning up to the limit of the ten states. Even beyond that, one rests for a moment in the heart through the function of *kumbhaka* (retention); immediately following that—

This [cognition] is produced by that very conjunction, which consists of the mutual blending of infinite objects of cognition appearing as forms such as blue, yellow, and so forth; it is therefore absolutely and invariably established.
The meaning is that, having attained the ground of the essence of the self— which is immeasurable and identical to the Self through the realization of non-duality—
one should become composed of that bliss of Māyā which consists of the form of Brahman, because it has been expanded by the immeasurable [Self] made manifest as its own form. Immediately after that:

The "absorption" (grāsa) refers to that which is intent upon devouring those "calculations" (kalanā)— whose essential nature has been defined by such passages as "twenty-one thousand six hundred" and so forth— which constitute the flow or current of the means of knowledge and its objects, of the sun and moon, and of the prāṇa and apāna breaths.
Those two were intent upon that very occurrence.

66a) By means of the middle path, [the breath] moving upwards— having come to rest through the cessation of intermediate disturbances such as *prāṇa* and *apāna*— attains the Great [Bliss], which is superior to the [ordinary] measures (*pramāṇa*) and so forth,
and distinct from the [lower] states beginning with *nirānanda*, because it transcends the ten stages.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the bliss equal to the supreme emission (*pramabhrasa*) by means of reflecting upon it as having the nature of resting solely within one's own self. Now, one might ask: "What would happen to this [consciousness] through such a reflective awareness? To this, he says:
Oṃ! In that great light wherein all rests and everything is stilled.

The unconditioned Great Pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*), devoid of the limiting adjunct called "the pervasive" (*vyāna*), possesses no localized existence whatsoever here that is of an insentient nature. Therein, no exclusion whatsoever exists, for it vibrates everywhere as the universe; it is the unspoken consciousness, nourished by the supreme nectar, wherein [all] exists.

The connection of [the teachings on] meditation and so forth is not even primary; rather, that very [teaching] which is the bliss of the world and the essence of Śambhu was what Śambhunātha declared to us. The sense is that this was not merely stated by him as his own invention (*svopajñam*).

Thus, enough with excessive detail; the meaning is that even the words of instruction for the Great-Souled One need not be expanded upon, lest it lead to agitation in those very souls. In this way, the state of abiding in the stages beginning with waking, dreaming, and deep sleep, up to the Fourth (turya) and beyond the Fourth (turyātīta), has been clarified.
The ancient teachers have stated that there is no fault in this matter, as it has been explained through various contexts.
Thus ends the second chapter of the *Āgamādhikāra* in the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī*, composed by the illustrious supreme teacher, the venerable Utpaladeva, on the *Pratyabhijñābhaṭṭāraka*.

May there be auspiciousness for those men who are devotees of Śiva and who have realized the truth known through the Trika scriptures; may the glance of the true gurus arise for those Trikas who consist of Śiva, Śakti, and the individual soul, and who know the supreme reality.
Now, with strength.

Now, having contemplated the Supreme Lord as consisting of the dual powers of knowledge and action— He who is like a bird with two wings— by this much of the text, the intended meaning [is established]; and now,
for the purpose of manifesting the majesty of His essential nature, [it is stated] yet again and again.

For it has been stated [in scripture]: "The mind falls downward toward the feet; to whom does it not fall? and so forth. Furthermore, because its majesty cannot be fully grasped even when described again and again, its majesty—having reached its turn as that which remains to be described—is now described by means of sound (dhvanā).
Oṃ! One’s own self alone is the one Great Lord of all living beings; I am this universe, thus strengthened by uninterrupted awareness. || 1 ||
The Supreme Lord is the very Self of all this living world;

as has been established through such statements as "the Self alone is the root of the universe," Maheśvara is all-pervasive like the orb of the sun, appearing as the knower and the agent with the thought, "I am."
Consisting of the knower, the knowing, and the known, it transcends the ultimate nature (*paramārtha-svabhāva*). And thus:
even though there is a distinction between waking and the other states, it flows forth as non-different from that [ultimate nature]; it does not at all exist apart from its own [nature].

Because it is perceived through its own nature: "I am happy," "I am suffering," "I am attached," and so forth—such cognitions clearly occur as being permeated by the states of pleasure and the rest, yet they are distinct from them.

The Great Lord (Maheśvara), whose characteristics have been described by such passages as these, is one and the same everywhere, possessing the form of the universe, the witness of the universe, manifesting as "I," having the nature of direct perception, and is indeed directly perceived within the sphere of action and so forth. And thus:
Even the dull-witted know him; even those who merely fetch water recognize him. And for whomsoever there is no clear prostration, he is not the Lord of the Clan (Kulanātha). And so says the Veda:
"Whether he eats today, or whether he drinks water,

or whether he is seen by all beings— may he look upon us with favor," and so forth; "He who is in the elephant, in the leopard, who is in gold, in the cow-pen, in the horses, and in men," and so forth— it is he indeed.

And by this very statement, "I am," it is determined; thus everything has been explained. "I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings. I exist within all beings, pervading them from every side."

[He is] the mouth; for it is said: "You are the sacrifice, you are the *vaṣaṭ*-call, the waters, light, the syllable *oṃ*, and immortality," and so forth. Or rather, what is the use of much speaking? O Arjuna, when [true] knowledge has been attained, I stand supporting this entire world with a single fraction of Myself.

And likewise, the Self is consciousness. It does not produce an effect merely by its own nature, nor is it something that acts [without cause]. Because [the world] originates from Him through positive concomitance (*anvaya*), and because of such scriptural passages as "But because [Brahman] is seen [to be the cause]" and "On account of the word," and so forth, [He is the cause]; therefore, the Great Lord is indeed the Self.

The word "yam" refers to its own essential nature, which is established by itself; thus, enough of this. Now, he demonstrates that even the distinction between cause and effect exists therein for the sake of producing that [nature]: "And its status as the efficient cause."

Oṃ. Therein, within the portion of this [universe] created by itself, that which is led to the state of the reflective awareness of *ahaṅkāra* (the I-maker) by means of the self as the grasper of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, is [described] by this [verse]. 2.

By His own will, the Supreme Lord has created this entire universe in the form of objective existence; and within every effect, such as the intellect and so forth, He has established the state of the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃkāra-parāmarśa*) through the nature of the subject who grasps the state of being "I. Thus: "I am a human," "I..."

The meaning is that the locus of the reflective awareness of "I" (ahaṅkāra) has been established through such expressions as "I am an animal," "I am a dwarf," "I am dark," "I am stout," or "I am a dwarf. However, this occurs through identification with the limited "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) arising from contraction; it is not, however, the pure and perfect "I" (śuddhaparipūrṇāhaṃ).
In form, they would be like the Supreme Lord; such is the intended meaning. And for that very reason as well.
Oṃ. It is held that the individual soul (puruṣa) arises from the womb of non-recognition of its own true nature (*svasvarūpāparijñāna*). Within that [state], there is the activity of emanation;

therefore, the previously mentioned "perfect I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) exists by its very nature as the one Puruṣa, who—due to the non-recognition of his own true nature—is of an indeterminate essence and thus appears as many.

68a) It appears in the form of luminosity. And thus, due to the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments [of action], as well as from the distinctness of their activities, the plurality of Puruṣas is established, as is the non-contradiction of the three guṇas. || 1 ||

The Puruṣa exists because of the existence of the aggregate, the nature of being for another, the three qualities (guṇas), and so forth; because of their contrary nature; because of superintendence; because of being an enjoyer; because of the existence of the dispositions (bhāvas); and because of activity for the sake of liberation. || 3 ||
Just as the flow of milk occurs for the sake of the growth of the calf, so too does the Pradhāna proceed for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa. || 3 ||
"Therefore, the Puruṣa is manifold"—thus it is stated in the Sāṅkhya treatise. However, from the perspective of ultimate reality, it is certain that nothing whatsoever is manifold.

Because it is logically impossible for that which is of the nature of consciousness (citsvarūpa) to possess manifold perceptions; however, [it appears so] due to the assumption of limitation through the mental cultivation of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāvanā) produced by various bodies, vital breaths, the void (śūnya), intellect (buddhi), and so forth.

And because of its power, there is the arising of many; what is this? In the creation of that very [power], for the sake of enjoyment, there are action and bliss. The knower is the enjoyer; having both singular and manifold forms, action is the enjoyment.

[The form] consists of cooking and so forth. In that activity, there is a bliss (*ānanda*) due to its existence in a contracted form. "Aho! Aho!"—by this [exclamation], even that is indeed suffering (*duḥkha*) because of its grossness and because of the contemplation of non-self (*anahaṃ-bhāvanā*). Furthermore, these two—the activity and the bliss—are enjoyment (*bhoga*), yet they are ultimately suffering.

"Consisting of the mouth. Thus, even in the absence [of anything else], there is only suffering; for that reason, by His mere will—expressed in such passages as "May I become many"—He [created this]. That too is for the sake of that very [Self]. However, it is called "enjoyment" for the sake of the individual soul (jīva). || 3 ||

68b) Now, in order to demonstrate that for one whose consciousness is attached to the nature of the individual soul (paśu), objects are perceived through a contracted form as consisting of limited knowledge and action, he says:

Oṃ. For those whose consciousness and activity regarding the Lord are directed toward objects for their own sake, Māyā is the third; these very states constitute the *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* of the bound soul (*paśu*).

This pair of powers, knowledge and action, belonging to the glorious Lord Viśveśvara, consists of the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and is composed of the pure state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*).
That very same [pair], when its form is contracted, consists of ignorance (*avidyā*) and is synonymous with *māyā*.

The third [aspect] of the fettered soul (paśu) is Māyā; these three qualities (guṇas), consisting of the nature of sattva, rajas, and tamas, are thus described. Furthermore, sattva is light, illuminating, desirable, supportive, and mobile; rajas is passionate.

"In the Sāṅkhya system, it is said: 'The covering of the Guru is indeed darkness (tamas), while the function [of the intellect] is like a lamp in terms of its purpose,' and so forth. Therein, that which is called 'knowledge' is impure *sattva*, because it is light and illuminating. And that which consists of impure activity is intended as the supporting *rajas*, because it is mobile."

It is called *cara* by the name of *mala* (impurity), because it performs the act of veiling (*varaṇa*) through its power of knowledge (*vidyā*). It is designated as *tamas* (darkness) because it performs the act of veiling the Guru, and because it is a vast obscuration (*bṛhad-ācchādakatva*). These three are pure.
The will of the Lord consists of knowledge and action; that triad of deities consists of bliss (*ānanda*), *sattva*, and *rajas*. That same [triad], when impure, is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*);
for it is the threefold bond (*pāśatraya*) of the bound soul (*paśu*), namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Bound by these, one is called "bound. Because of this, [there is] manifestation...
Manifest and unmanifest: for the bound soul (paśu), these three consist of the nature of non-manifestation.

And that very [trio], consisting of light (prakāśa) and self-reflective awareness (vimarśa), consisting of supreme bliss, consists of the triad of powers (śakti)—namely will, knowledge, and action; such is the sense. And this...
He will establish this further on ahead. Existence, bliss, and activity belong to the Lord;

their absence belongs to the bound soul (paśu). That [absence] consists of both [bliss and activity], while its rectitude, suffering, and so forth consist of the qualities of rajas, tamas, and sattva respectively—and so on.
Now, demonstrating the mutual difference between the Lord and the individual soul (jīva), he says:

Oṃ. For that which possesses power, its state as power is not designated [as distinct] from its abiding in differentiation—namely, these qualities (guṇas) which undergo transformation through their status as instruments and effects. || 5 ||

This Puruṣa has as his essential nature only contracted light; for him, there is no innate path of objects of knowledge. Indeed, that sovereignty which belongs to her [Śakti] regarding creation, maintenance, and dissolution would not exist for him. Therefore, due to the absence of that [sovereignty], it is said that he possesses those qualities [of contraction].

Because of the distinction between attachment and non-attachment; therefore, since difference is established for that which possesses power, the possession of power is designated for objects of cognition and so forth.

It is due to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as between a quality and its possessor, and not due to inherence (*samavāya*). For it is certain that inherence does not exist [between them]; thus, there is only conjunction between the two, like that between two wrestlers.
And their conjunction and disjunction are such that they cannot be separated by the Lord (*prabhu*).
In that regard, its state of being both manifest and unmanifest is indeed certain, because that universe is composed of it;
and since the individual soul (jīva) and so forth are not composed of it, this is precisely what is expressed by conventional usage.

The meaning is "certainly. Therefore, those qualities of the *paśu* (the bound soul), by virtue of being both causes and effects that undergo transformation, are designated as its powers (*śakti*). That is to say: "These qualities are the powers of this *paśu*."
Rather, these are simply the powers (*śakti*) whose history is described [in the scriptures] as "May I become many," and so forth, produced by the Lord according to His own will.
For it is said: "Power and the possessor of power are declared to be two categories of reality;
the entire universe is His power, while the Great Lord is the possessor of power," and so on. This, therefore, is firmly established.
But from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), even those powers do not exist, because their mutual differentiation is untenable. And so it is said in the *Spanda*:
"Since the individual soul (*jīva*) consists of everything, because all things arise from everything, and because of the realization of identity through the nature of that consciousness. (1)

Therefore, the contemplation of the meaning of words, that very state of one's own nature, is Śiva; "the enjoyer alone exists everywhere at all times in the form of the enjoyed"—this realization of the Vāyavīya [Tantra] perceives the entire universe as play. Constantly seeing thus and ever-yoked [in yoga], he is liberated while living.

By the words "doubt" and so forth: through the logical necessity of differentiation, its nature as power has necessarily been accepted from the very beginning; however, [this is] because manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) consist of the essence of manifestation and reflective awareness.
Nor is there non-difference [between them], because they appear as distinct under the names of "knowledge" and "ignorance."

Through such reflections as "enveloped by the impurities of the *sajīva*," the Lord (*īśvara*) becomes omniscient once he has brought the reflection of *māyā* under his control. However, when subject to *avidyā*, he appears in many ways due to its manifold variety,
just as whirlpools in a river differ from one another.
Wandering from birth to birth, they never attain liberation.

And so it is said: "At the conclusion of the ripening of their virtuous deeds, those who have been uplifted by the Ocean of Compassion reach the shade of the tree of liberation and rest in bliss," and so forth.

70a) Therefore, because the distinction of the possessor of power (*śaktimat*) from power (*śakti*) is established, the state of being a possessor of power is not predicated [of power itself]. This refers to these qualities (*guṇas*), which are connected as being both causes and effects through their transformative nature (*pariṇāmin*). Thus, it is proven that there is indeed a mutual distinction between these two. And whoever...

Because everything vibrates [as] the individual soul (*jīva*), and so forth; and that [vibration occurs] upon the purification of impurity (*mala*), the cessation of ignorance (*avidyā*), the exhaustion of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*), the dissolution of the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) which is the cause of the gross body, and when the latent impressions (*vāsana*) have dissolved within the subtle body, as well as the causal body (*kāraṇa-śarīra*). [This pertains to] the knower (*vedaka*) and the knowing (*vedana*).
Upon the attainment of the unity of the object of knowledge, there arises the realization of non-difference through the purification of the mind; and thus:

"Just as the tuft of grass [is extracted] from the *uñja* stalk, so the Self is drawn forth by means of reasoning from the three bodies; for the wise, it becomes the Supreme Brahman itself. This is because such a state has been born.
It is thus established how the non-difference of these two is logically justified. Now, in order to analyze that very point, he says:
Oṃ. Existence, bliss, and activity belong to the Lord; their absence belongs to the bound soul (paśu).
That which consists of both is the state of passion (rajas) and suffering, composed of the qualities of purity (sattva) and darkness (tamas) in union.

For such is the ultimate, supreme, and free will (*paramāsvecchā*) of that Lord whose nature is sovereignty, which consists in the creation of the world: "I create all this," and "May I become many," and so forth; it is by this very [will] that his oneness arises.

The ultimate reality (*paramārthārtha*) is supreme existence (*parasattā*); this is what is called "being" (*sattva*). And thus, that radiance (*sphurattā*), which is great existence (*mahāsattā*) unconditioned by space and time, is described as "this very [reality] is proclaimed as the *āra* (the center) and the heart (*hṛdaya*) of the Supreme Lord," and so forth. In this way, the existence of the universe is established.
The nature of manifestation is the painless awareness (*vimarśa*). It has been stated that "the object of light, even if for the sake of another, is like an insentient crystal" and so forth;
because manifestation consists essentially of awareness, that which is its awareness brings about the world through the unification of all things into a single flavor. And that [unification]...

It is called "action" (kriyā). In that regard, the unfolding of the unity of light, reflective awareness, and the world, as well as the arising of supreme bliss within one's own self in the form of "I," is termed "bliss" (ānanda).

"I am the Great All, I am Brahman; I am Brahman, the bestower of the seed"—through such [utterances], the arising of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is described as supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). And this triad belongs to the Lord (*pati*), the self-effulgent Supreme Sovereign (*parameśvara*), who is joined on all sides by the multitude of his powers (*śakti*).

The knowers of the Āgamas say that the mobile [subject], his own self, his very nature, consists of this essential form which is composed of light (*prakāśa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and bliss (*ānanda*).

And that absence is distinct from this [existence]; it is the absence of such a reality. Furthermore, even that existence of the bound soul (paśu) is pervaded by darkness; indeed, the non-existence of the nature of the bound soul is also [pervaded by darkness].
Furthermore, because it is enveloped by *tamas*, this [state] is nothing but suffering, being born from its own nature; for there, *sattva* and *tamas* are joined, intermingled, and mutually blended.
"This is the very nature of the limited subject (paśu-pramātṛ)," so say the proponents of the Āgamas. || 6 ||
Now, having established the reality of the subject (*pramātṛ-tattva*), the reality of the object (*prameya-tattva*) is likewise demonstrated:
"Even those [objects] which arise from the Lord’s non-conventional awareness of 'this-ness' (*idantā-parāmarśa*), they too are distinct..."
And likewise, they appear as mixed and variegated. || 8 ||

Oṃ! These various distinct objects of illumination are to be conceptualized as belonging to the inner self (pratyagātman) through their respective diverse designations within the sphere of memory, inference, perception, and so forth.
Oṃ.
Her commonality consists in her being dependent on that which is created by the portion of creation; yet she exists as the very truth through the power of Īśa, whose nature is otherwise unknown. 9.

Oṃ! By means of the activity of conceptualization—which is of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), which is unswerving because it obstructs one's own rest, and which is variegated by the diversity of various phonemes—[the universe is manifested]. 10.

By its non-temporal nature, it dispels the state of being limited by time; the sense is that these [objects] are always manifest as direct perception. "The grounds of reflective awareness" (parāmarśabhuvaḥ) means the locations or supports of reflective awareness. And those [objects], such as blue and so forth, are distinct due to their vividness.

And because those who possess discernment realize that there is no difference between knowledge and the object of knowledge; likewise, they appear as variegated due to their clarity. Furthermore, those very objects which appear as distinct natures are, in reality, the natures of the inner self (*pratyagātman*).
For the sake of the soul that is like a pillar or a beast, the unimposed reality is the state of being established as an immovable pillar (*kūṭastha*).

Through various distinct designations such as "pot," "cloth," "blue," or "red," with respect to objects that fall within the range of memory, direct experience, and imagination, the creation of that bound soul (paśu) depends upon the creation of the Lord; for it exists through the state of the thought "I am not" regarding the Lord as the cause.

It appears as variegated because it is an object of knowledge (*jñeya*). However, when that [variegation] is not attained, there are specific manifestations of consciousness (*cit*) and its particularities (*viśeṣa*).
Its manifestation is well-known through the conventional usage of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and so forth;
and that [manifestation] exists as a reality precisely when it is unknown through the realization of unity by the power of the Lord (*īśa-śakti*).
Because this world is pervaded by the play of illusion, it consists of the means of knowledge, the objects of knowledge, and qualities such as blue and so forth.

Likewise, it is mobile because it obstructs repose in itself; likewise, it is of the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa). For the purpose of obstructing the sovereignty characterized by repose in one's own nature, it is mobile. Because it is always bent away from its own true nature within that which is called Māyā, it is immobile in that very same [state].

[The subject] has been attained by you through the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and again through the activity of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the variety of various colors. [This refers to] that unique creation consisting of the variegation of various colors such as blue, yellow, and so forth, belonging specifically to the bound soul (*paśu*) who is not to be destroyed; such is the connection [of the words].
Therefore, since it subsists upon those very appearances created by the Lord, it is said that the entire emission belonging to the bound soul (paśu) subsists upon the emission of the Lord. || 10 ||
And thus, as well as otherwise.
Oṃ. This creation is both common and otherwise, because it appears as if touched [by the mind].
Through the abandonment of conceptual construction and one-pointedness, the state of lordship is attained through a gradual process. (11)
This creation of the Lord is common everywhere, due to its similarity and commonality in the well-known perception of blue, yellow, and so forth;
such is its commonality. And there is also its uncommonality, as in the case of a double moon and the like, which occurs nowhere else.

Because that is observed; for instance, it is seen in such passages as "the sky was seen by Anūramalla as having a hundred moons," and so forth. Likewise, there is a creation otherwise, as in "like a city of Gandharvas" or "as water and wind are gross," and so on, because of their clear manifestation.
In this regard, by abandoning conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) through one-pointedness (*ekāgryatva*),

all this universe is realized as consisting of nectar, as one, as having many rays for its object, as firmly established, and as tranquil; it is the very nature of consciousness and its true essence— this being so, because of the attainment of one-pointedness through the abandonment of conceptual construction.
From the state of being a *prāhu* (one who has attained), there is, in due order, the attainment of the station of Īśvara, the conferral of lordship (*īśvaratva*),
and the increase of the perfection of Māheśvara.

72a) And upon their increase, the attainment of lordship is established. In this regard, the very elimination of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is the cause for obtaining the perfection of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*). For that perfection is the cause for the destruction of obstacles; because when obstacles arise, there is a loss of the perfection of the Lord.
The attainment of excellence is [the result], while in its absence, the manifestation of one's own lack of excellence is declared. And it has been said:

When the island of the body's perception has perished at birth, having reached the state of being alone upon the ocean of consciousness with the neck [of the throat] unobstructed, you shine eternally as the one Self of the universe, without ever withdrawing the collection of senses within.
In this context, by the phrase "in sequence," it is meant that through the abandonment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one-pointedness (*ekāgrya*) is attained;

through its attainment, the attainment of sequence occurs. When the sequence has been transcended and [the state of] completeness is achieved, the supreme state of lordship (*īśvaratva*) is attained. And so says the Sāṅkhya: "When the dissolution of the body has occurred, because the purpose has been fulfilled..."
Upon the cessation of Pradhāna, one attains both the absolute and the ultimate isolation (kaivalya);
and likewise, upon the attainment of supreme lordship, all those prosperities that flow from it as its natural outflow spread forth.
May there be auspiciousness for those who worship the lotus feet of Śambhunātha, whose minds have become absorbed in Him— just as the attainment of the Rohaṇa mountain results in a wealth of jewels—
and for whom the supreme state is the unification of all things belonging to the past, present, and future.
For those whose hearts are firmly rooted [in this realization]—
whose hearts have been purified by the contemplation of the identity between their own self and the universe abiding within it,
and whose lotus-hearts are fully blossomed by the rays of light from the venerable Śambhunātha— enough of further elaboration! (11)

Thus, when conceptual construction has ceased everywhere, and when there is equality in the vision of the distinction between self and other, one attains liberation and identity with Maheśvara; having directly realized this, one is indeed Maheśvara himself. Thus it is proclaimed.

For one who thoroughly understands that "Oṃ, all this is indeed the manifestation of the Self," there is the state of the Great Lord even amidst the proliferation of conceptual constructions regarding the Universal Self. 12.

For there is no such self, nor even any living being bound like an animal; rather, he remains as if smiling, from whose [perspective] this "crooked path" arises— this very one named Maheśvara, who, by the reasoning already established, stands within all while supporting this entire universe.
Thus, it is established that Maheśvara is one who, being pervaded [by all], has the nature of concealing his own self. And so it is said:
"Because the individual soul (jīva) consists of everything due to the arising of all states of being, and because of the realization of identity through the form of their cognition. (1)
"Therefore, Śiva, who is beyond the contemplation of words and meanings and is unborn, exists always and everywhere as the enjoyer himself in the form of the object of enjoyment. Thus,
for one whose consciousness perceives the entire universe as the play of Vāma, he is joined with the state of realization.
He is undoubtedly liberated while living. || 3 ||
And so it is:

The outflows resulting from the vibration of the qualities (guṇas) and so forth, having found their footing through reliance on the common vibration, would constantly become obstacles for the knower. || 4 ||
These [views] of those whose intellects are unawakened— whose nature is the concealment of the established state— cause them to fall onto the difficult-to-cross path of saṃsāra.
Therefore, one who is diligently engaged in discerning the true nature of vibration (spanda-tattva) attains, before long, the state of being awake even while in the midst of worldly existence.

By this path, knowing "all this is indeed my own power," even while moving amidst conceptual constructions, what [obstacle] can exist? Because of the absence of [dualistic] being, there is the state of the Great Lord (Maheśatā).
Due to identity with Maheśvara, his activity proceeds as "I am Maheśvara. This is because he abides in the state that transcends all things.
For it is stated in scripture: "All this is his manifestation. Therefore, it has also been said:
These would be the enemies of the path of the wise man.

Therefore, because there is no state of non-existence for this [Self], there is nothing else whatsoever that exists or does not exist; it has not come into being, nor will it ever come into being, since it is the manifestation of the essential nature of all this. There is no other path leading there than this: he who shines as heat for the gods, he who was the first-born among the gods.
By such passages as, "He who was born before the gods," and by such passages as, "In the beginning Hiraṇyagarbha arose; once born, he was the sole lord of all that exists."

"I alone existed in the beginning; there was nothing else, whether manifest or unmanifest, nor anything beyond. Afterwards, I am that which remains here and that which is yet to be. And I am seated in the heart of all;
from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. And by the Vedas..."
"By all [beings] I alone am to be known; I am the author of the Vedānta and the knower of the Vedas," and so forth.

I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, dwelling in the heart of all beings; I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings. There is no one else here besides Me, nor is there any object of meditation to be found here. [The mind] is dissolved in the state of bliss, having attained the state of being of a single flavor with the essence of all things.

He who has all-seeing eyes, whose face is on every side, whose hands are on every side, and whose arms are on every side— he, the one God, supporting the earth and heaven with his arms, alone generated them for the sake of sacrifice.
By such statements as these, all this [universe] is his own body; it both shines forth and is luminous—this is the meaning.
(73b) In this manner, in this way, even this is exactly so. Thus he says.

Oṃ. This object of knowledge is common [to all], yet the liberated one perceives it as non-different from his own self, just like Maheśvara; the bound one, however, perceives it as possessing absolute difference. (13)
And this is the point here: that which is this common object of knowledge (*meyam*), extending from Sadāśiva and Īśvara down to the earth (*kṣiti*), all of that is his own self;
yet he conceives it as being most intensely differentiated. This entire mass of entities is his very own manifestation.
Because it has been stated thus: "The universe has emerged from me and dissolves back into me alone," and so forth.

"I alone am the imperishable Time; I am the Giver, facing in all directions; I am Death, the destroyer of all, and I am the Source of those yet to be. By such statements, he considers this entire universe as non-different from his own Self, just as he considers himself to be Maheśvara. Therefore...

Thus, the universe that had emerged from that [source] dissolves back into it alone. Now, by the reversal of this state, one who remains bound through the condition of non-awakening (aprabuddhatā) again becomes as if possessed of absolute difference.
The connection is as follows: like a bound animal (paśu), he proceeds in the world characterized by absolute difference, remaining unstable. Like seeds in a river...

"Moving from one whirlpool to another whirlpool, they go from birth to birth and never attain liberation"— according to this and other such passages, they are said to be "bound. At the end [of the verse], they are "bound" because they are brought under control by the noose of Māyā and by the fetters such as the vital breath (prāṇa).

74a) For this very reason, although [the world] consists of absolute difference— such that blue is only blue, yellow is only yellow, a jar is only a jar, a cloth is only a cloth, and even a horse is only a horse—
it possesses absolute difference through such various occurrences. Indeed, all this [world] does not occur apart from that [consciousness].
The entire mass of existents is said to be clearly manifest as non-different from me.

Now, through the power of your grace, this entire universe appears to me as being composed of you alone; and you, O Great Lord, are forever my very self—making everything consist of your own self through the realization of "mine-ness" [as yours]. || 1 ||
Since You, the Lord, are present within one's own self as the all-pervading, there is no talk of fear regarding the cycle of existence.
By such statements as these, [the author] asks: "In what manner (*sakatham*) and by what mode (*kena prakāreṇa*) does the Person (*puruṣa*) shine forth? To this, he says: || 13 ||
Oṃ! Śiva is filled with the infinite flood of principles merged within his very essence in every way;
he is a mass of consciousness and bliss, whose form is the supreme syllable.

He is directly Śiva. As the "I," manifesting as his own essential nature, he is absorbed within himself while the universe remains latent; yet, being identical with that universe, his body is filled to overflowing with the universal self, like the fluid within a peacock's egg.

He who has assumed a body, who is all-pervading, whose form is that of the pervasive instruments [of action], and who is a mass of consciousness consisting of eternally manifesting light, bliss, and so forth, is called Śiva himself; he is by his own nature the supreme syllable "I" (Aham).
For even there, the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, starting from the vowels (*mātrā*),
are the pervasive nature because they encompass their own internal pervasion.

74b) This is the partless body (*niṣkala-vapuḥ*). From that [body], there arise the infinite forms: a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ; ka kha ga gha ṅa ca cha ja jha ña; ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa; ta tha da dha na; pa pha ba bha ma; ya ra la va; śa ṣa sa ha; laṃ kṣa.

Thus, through various diversities and as the sovereign (*virāṭ*), that which has shone, is shining, and will shine is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*); and from that, those various *vidyās* [arise]. Just as [the universe] shines, shining, and manifests as the ornamentation extending from Śiva down to the earth, so too does the Power (*śakti*) emitted by Him manifest.

Sadāśiva, Īśvara; Śuddhavidyā, Māyā; [the principles of] Vidyā, Śiva, Kāla, Kalā, Rāga, Niyati, Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Manas, Buddhi, Ahaṅkāra, and the qualities of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, along with the sense organs of hearing, skin, eye, tongue, and nose.
Speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals; ether, air, fire, water, and earth—from these [elements] arises the world, consisting of Brahmā down to an ant, both moving and stationary; such is the sense.
Thus, the manifestation of duality is established as having the form of the supreme imperishable (paramākṣara). And yet—

The body (vigraha) is characterized by the supreme, most excellent, imperishable nature of the syllable (akṣara-rūpa), [and performs] the fivefold activity consisting of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth. || 14 ||

Thus, when the nature of sound has been established by means of such arguments as recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like, the Teacher now restricts this entire meaning of the treatise for the awakened disciple according to the method of a *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context).
When one point has been established, other points that follow as its necessary consequence are also established;
this is known as the *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (the established conclusion based on the context), and so forth.
Oṃ. Thus, by means of this right knowledge and action, one perceives the Self; then one knows and accomplishes all desired objects. || 15 ||

75a) By the word "thus" (evam), Maheśvara is designated as Śiva, who consists of the fivefold activity (pañcakṛtyamaya) by way of his nature as creation, maintenance, withdrawal, concealment, and grace— just as he knows through the power of knowledge (jñāna) and acts through the power of action (kriyā). [This is] the sixty-fourth [verse].

Just as in the *Tantravārttika* and other extensive treatises, this [system] is also established (*siddha*) in its ultimate form; and since that is established, all effects such as knowledge and action, as well as all causes, are likewise established—this is the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). For the Lord (*īśvara*)...
And it blinks and opens its eyes externally; likewise [it performs] creation and so forth according to its desire.

By means of the two forms of knowledge and action, it moves like a swan; it sits down and it goes everywhere, at all times, and in every way. For one who has attained the state beyond dispute, the manifestation of the nature of the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is indisputable, overflowing with the mass of infinity.
She is completely filled with consciousness and bliss;

her nature is that of the great void; she is the light of consciousness, utterly free from darkness; her single body is replete with the sixty principles; she is of the nature of luminosity; she is the ultimate reality of both the conscious and the unconscious; she is eternal.

In the eternal abode of one's own nature, there exists she who has eyes of the measured moon, sun, and fire; she is the presiding authority over all eyes, the inner essence of all dharmas, ignited by the *ci* [syllable], and her form is the supreme syllable—this path of instruction, which is the domain of the heart, is beyond dispute. (15)

Thus, this meaning of the treatise, which is a compendium of the essence of the ultimate truth, has not been composed by me through my own intellectual fabrication. Rather, having reflected with my own intellect upon those various meanings, I have established the ultimate truth as conceived by the masters; this is for the sake of benefiting others.

It has been made manifest; moreover, it has been established as precisely regulated in accordance with the essence as it was propounded by former teachers. Thus he says to the opponent by way of summarizing the purport of the subsequent verse.

Oṃ! This path of the *Mugdhabodha* has been revealed by me, just as it was taught by the great new gurus in the treatise *Śivadṛṣṭi*. Therefore, one who places their foot here, having contemplated the state of being Śiva, shall enter incessantly and, becoming the agent of the universe, will drench [all things] with the nature of Śiva.
Thus by me, named Utpaladeva,
whose pair of lotus-feet are worshipped by the most excellent supreme teachers— this Śaiva path called Trika, which follows the ultimate reality of the unsurpassed path, is ever-new.

From moment to moment, it is indeed easily accomplished because, through the compendium of the science of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), once the supreme reality has been received from the mouth of the Guru, the attainment of the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) is certain to occur;
thus, it is indeed easily accomplished. [This applies even to] fasting, ascetic hardships, heat-penances, and so forth.

Because the practice of the five fires (*pañcāgni*), the *āntrāyaṇa* sacrifice, and so forth, serve as causes for the cultivation of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) through the application of reasoning and reflection; for this very reason, it is easily accomplished (*sughaṭa*).

Because the mastery of reciting the scriptures is already established; for this has not been taught by me even to my own son, since the mastery of reciting the scriptures occurs without the skill of meditation and so forth. Thus, this path of instruction is established. Moreover, just as it was by the great gurus...

[By the venerable Śrī Somānanda] it was previously stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* and other scriptures that there is no loss or affliction for Utpaladeva regarding knowledge and the rest; therefore, whatever was previously taught by the predecessors as being established is authoritative—this very point [is as follows]: just as he himself...
The Blessed One has validated the *Jñānakāṇḍa* and other portions of the *Śrī Bhagavadgītā* as authoritative;

they say that this very portion is the most authoritative in all respects. For it is said: "Whatever a superior person practices, that very thing other people also do; whatever standard he sets, the world follows."

Thus, that which was previously established by the predecessors through the aforementioned reasoning is indeed the authoritative proof (*pramāṇa*). For this very reason, it is rightly stated by the Great Teachers in the *Śivadṛṣṭi* Śāstra: "Just as... Therefore, for this reason, one should place one's foot here; right here.
If it were to have a creator, it would be like Maheśvara, as if entering into the state of being the creator of the world.
He alone creates; he alone destroys.
From that very [state], having contemplated the state of being the creator of the worlds as consisting of the nature of Śiva;

Having meditated upon and ascertained her to be of the very nature and essence of Śiva, one enters into that state immediately at that very moment; having meditated upon the state of being identical with Śiva, one becomes perfected (*siddhyati*). The meaning is that one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtya*); this alone is the intended sense of the connection.
And so it is stated in the Tantrāloka:
He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru. There is no difference between these two—the Guru and Śiva.
These three powers, beginning with Parā, manifest as His very own;
because they appear in the states of emission, maintenance, withdrawal, and the fourth (turya), they are thus declared to be twelve.
This supreme Śiva is said to be of such a nature that he is never incomplete.
Therefore, the lay practitioners (upāsakas) are established right here, directly in that very place. || 3 ||
And for those [energies] as well, there is the application of their divisions, such as deficiency, excess, and so forth.
It is precisely by the power of its own autonomy that it is defined as such in the technical treatises.
He is the solitary hero (Ekavīra), then the twin (Yāmala), the triple power (Triśakti), and the fourfold self (Caturātmaka);
he is the fivefold liberation (Pañcamukti), the sixfold tradition (Ṣaḍāmnāya), and adorned with the seven chambers (Saptakoṣṭha). || 5 ||
"Bhairava is you—the lord of the great twelve-spoked wheel, whose nature consists of the ninefold self, the powers of the ten directions, and the eleven kalās. (6)
In this way, up to the thousand-spoked wheel or even the innumerable ones,
the Great Lord, the power of the universe, manifests within the universal wheel.
Power and the possessor of power are said to be the two categories of reality;
the entire universe is his power, while the Great Lord (Maheśvara) is the possessor of power.

And for those very scriptures as well, a distinction has been described in various places according to their respective groups, through their conformity to their own class and through their unity within that cycle.
Indeed, for this Lord of Consciousness (*saṃvinnātha*), no other [entity] appears as a support;
he abandons the gentle or otherwise limited wheel of the waves of consciousness.

"From this [consciousness] proceeds emission"—thus it has been stated; for the Goddess is so described because she is the source of the internal discourse that mingles with the external activities of the senses. (11)
Therefore, Viśveśvara, the Bhairava of awakening,
is worshipped by people seeking worldly enjoyment and liberation, so that they may be freed from the limitations of their own fragmentation.
Therefore, the uninterrupted state of the self, which consists of the manifestation of "I am all forms," is itself the primordial rule of creation. || 13 ||
"Pūrvaśas" means occurring previously. || 13 ||
This very [Self], having been enveloped by the supreme [ignorance], is considered to be in a state of insentience;
yet the Self, whether enveloped or unenveloped, exists as everything from the gods down to the lowest beings. (15)
For whatever he might contemplate, his state is indeed independent;
thus it is said in the *Triśaraḥ-śāstra*: "He who knows [this] is a Buddha. (15)
In that regard, whatever manifests clearly and directly within the first [state], the abode of non-conceptual self-awareness, is proclaimed as that which is called Will (icchā). || 16 ||
Just as for those with wide-open eyes, the manifestation of objects becomes clearly evident even without mental synthesis, so too it is for some through the nature of Śiva.

Know that the means of knowledge (*jñānopāya*) is that reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) which one attains by repeatedly chewing upon conceptual construction through the process of firm determination. 18.
That which establishes external objects constructed by conceptualization is traditionally taught as the means of action (kriyopāya); herein, there is no difference regarding liberation. || 19 ||

Thus, this which was previously explained by the Great Teachers extensively or concisely in the *Tantrāloka* or elsewhere, has been set forth here as well; having established its foundation in this [work], one enters into the state of being the creator of the worlds. And therefore—

Having meditated upon the meaning of Śiva, one then enters incessantly; and from that, one attains perfection. The meaning is that one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. || 19 ||

Now, an objection: "Was this not already established at the very beginning of the treatise? [In the verse: 'Who could effect a negation or an affirmation regarding the non-inert Self—the Great Lord who is established from the outset as the agent, the knower, and one's own self'? (1)

However, due to delusion (*moha*), even when this [object] is seen, it is not perceived; and since it is possible for it to be manifested, this [recognition] does not rest upon the object. By this, one perceives exactly this: who is able to effect either a negation or a non-establishment [of the object]? Therefore, even though this has been created, it remains unperceived.

Therefore, the connection is as follows: by manifesting his two powers of knowledge and action, his mastery over the supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) and the creative emanations (*visarga*) is brought forth. What has been said here? It is this:
having established its station, it enters into the state of being the creator of the worlds, while manifesting the nature of Śiva-ness.

"Entering into the Manīśa, one succeeds. What is established here? If you say it is the pair of powers consisting of knowledge and action, then what follows from this? It has been stated that the proof of the Supreme Lord occurs through experience—such as the recitation of the *Pratyabhijñā*—and not merely through deception.
Regarding this, the Teacher says: Here others maintain the following position:

"Oṃ! Even though he has arrived through various prayers and is present before us, he remains as one who is fully known by the world, just like any other person in the world. This is his nature for the world.

Likewise, even though the Lord of the Universe has perceived His own nature as consisting of the qualities and the essence, He is not yet fully satisfied; therefore, this "Recognition" (Pratyabhijñā) has been proclaimed. 20.
Just as a certain amorous woman, though her own activities have ceased, remains intent on meditating upon her lover, thinking, "How shall I embrace him?
How shall I converse with him? or "How indeed shall I..."
Thinking, "I shall sit down," she, distressed by the impending destruction of her activity, remembered this very thing.

Immediately thereafter, by means of activities such as sending a female messenger (*dūtī*), or through the composition of love letters, [she learns] that "your creeper-like body remains emaciated by separation.
Then, accordingly, when the beloved has arrived nearby in her presence...

Commonality with others is a source of evil; because of this commonality with father, mother, brother, son, and so forth, when one dwells near them, the heart does not attain fullness through gazing upon them or similar acts.
Even there, because of the absence of seclusion and immersion, whenever by chance a secret union occurs,

through such acts as embracing and kissing, once the attainment of the "mother" and so forth has arisen and the bliss of the heart is produced, the emergence of supreme bliss is called the bliss of Brahman (*brahmānanda*).

And so it is said: "Whether one is extremely angry, or intensely excited, or singing 'kiṃkalī', or running—wherever the foot goes, there vibration (spanda) is established. Here, the state of being "intensely excited" (atiprakṛṣṭhatva) is indicated by the nature of great bliss (mahadānanda). Thus, when the removal of delusion (moha) is accomplished:

Just as there is the arising of supreme bliss (*paramānanda*), so too, when the body and the sense of "I" have perished, the state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvaratā*) is attained. And likewise: "Just as the *iṣīkā* reed is extracted from the *muñja* grass by means of skillful technique, so the wise extract the Supreme Brahman itself from the three bodies. (78b)
Regarding the statement "it is born": Furthermore— when the island of the body's perception has been shattered at birth,
and the realization of the singular Brahman has been attained through awakening,
you shine as the one, eternal Self of the universe within, like the sun, with your sensory grasp unshakable.

By this [it is meant]: as long as there is delusion (*moha*), so long does the notion of ignorance persist; once delusion has been removed, everything indeed becomes manifest at all times and in all places, just as [the true nature of] the heroine and hero [is revealed]. Thus, from the words of the Guru, the triad of powers consisting of knowledge and action [is realized].

Immediately upon that investigation, through that very means, the state of the Supreme Lord’s excellence becoming internalized within the heart arises; at that very moment, there is liberation while living (jīvanmukti), whose essential nature is perfect bliss.

Thus it is established that, through the delight in the practice of *samāveśa*, upon the attainment of the sovereign power of supreme majesty, it is *pratyabhijñā* alone that is considered the bestower of the highest accomplishment (*siddhi*). And so it is stated in the *Tantrāloka*:

In that regard, when there is no mental reflection upon objects within the singular abode of the non-conceptual, that which flashes forth manifest and directly is proclaimed as the power called Will (*icchā*). Just as an object appears clearly and vividly even without any subsequent synthesis when the eyes are wide open.
Therefore, even for those who are devoid [of knowledge], there is the nature of Śiva.
That reflective awareness which one attains through the repeated contemplation of conceptual thought and its various modes is known by the wise as the means of knowledge (jñānopāya).
That which is established as external through the cessation of conceptual construction is taught as the means consisting of action; herein, there is no difference regarding liberation.

Since there is no action other than knowledge, and this [knowledge] is likewise established as such, it attains the state of being the ultimate goal; thus it is said in the Śrīgamasaśāsana: "There is no yoga other than this, nor any action other than this, for that which is called 'intellect' (mati) is indeed ascended to reality."
The cessation of the habitual tendencies of one's own mind is designated as "non-action."

The activities of latent impressions and the impurities born from them reside within one's own mind; that consciousness which is of the nature of self-awareness exists for the purpose of pacifying them.
Yoga is indeed that very action which, having dissolved the multitude of external principles that initiate embodied existence, causes the mind to rest within those very principles.
Even in the world, that which is known as "I go," which is merely a vibration of thought,
is the activity of motion that enters into the body, the location, and the senses.
Therefore, even ritual action is indeed nothing but ignorance from the perspective of valid cognition;
for it has been declared that only knowledge leads to liberation, and this is logically consistent.
For liberation is not something other than the self; it is indeed the manifestation of one's own true nature.
And the true nature of the self is consciousness, nothing else; that which is beyond this is [liberation]. || 11 ||
Therefore, that very sovereignty which is [the source] is indeed nothing other than consciousness itself; and that is sufficient.
Entering into the sacrificial fires, it comes to rest within the powers.

Therefore, knowledge and action lead to liberation; this is the innate truth. Immediately thereafter, the attainment of immersion (*samāveśa*) occurs through this gateway consisting of knowledge and action.
May there be auspiciousness for those whose hearts are purified by the nectar flowing from the pair of lotus-feet of Śambhunātha.
"Of those spoken by the Supreme Lord"—thus it is auspicious; enough with excessive prolixity.

79b) Now, having tasted the sweetness of this treatise, people should also hear of its excellence: that such an intellect as this, engaged in the composition of this scripture, is proven to be the very incarnation of the Great Lord Maheśvara; may he be victorious!
"He is devoted to helping others"—and as to who that is, he says:
Oṃ! For the sake of the spiritual perfection of people, the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* has been established by Utpala, the son of Udayākara. (20)
From the beginning. || 193 ||
There was a certain person named Udayākara, whose heart was purified by the lotus-feet of Śambhunātha, who had attained the supreme reality through the state of *ghūrṇa*,
and who was a jewel among the sons of Utpaladeva, having received grace merely through [his teacher’s] favor.

And this *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* (Recognition of the Lord) has been set forth for the sake of the accomplishment of the aims of people; so that, by its very accessibility, the recognition of Him may arise effortlessly for those who are weary of exertion, as if they were sitting right beside their own Mother, rather than through laborious effort.

Is it not fear that existence itself arises for that very purpose? Indeed, it is from this very source that the supreme attainment known as liberation has emerged; for through the treatise *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*, which has arisen therefrom, one is endowed with the desired perfection consisting in the attainment of the supreme nectar.

The attainment of the status of a Great Maheshvara is thus accomplished; this complete path of the compendium of scriptures is [attained] solely through the grace of the Guru. May there be auspiciousness!
From the beginning. || 193 ||
This *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* is completed.

Oṃ! In the year [of] Veda (4), on the seventh lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Pauṣa, when the sun was in conjunction with the constellation Puṣya, and at a fixed (sthira) lagna endowed with auspiciousness,
[I have composed this] with an intellect exceedingly sharp-pointed and devoted to the lotus feet of Śrīvidyā.
The *Kaumudī* has been composed and perfected by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka himself. || 1 ||
In this matter, others may either censure you or praise you in every way; they will strike one another and hurl insults at each other.
Or even if, through delusion of mind, [one acts] out of wonder and so forth arising from the primordial source;
nevertheless, there is neither delusion nor the intoxication of thought.
Having observed the arrangement of categories previously expounded by the ancient teachers,
people whose intellects are like that of children are struck with fear regarding the Pratyabhijñā.

Therefore, this [work], which is worthy of study and captivating to the mind, is free from the need for further deliberation; it has been composed after thoroughly investigating the scriptures according to the capacity of one's own intellect. (5)
This beautiful *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* has been composed for the benefit of oneself and, incidentally, for the sake of others as well. (6)
One should recite it for the sake of pacifying the flood of obstacles, through the grace of Śambhunātha.
By his grace, may there be absorption into him for those whose minds have been fashioned [by him].
May there be auspiciousness for those who recite the Pratyabhijñā.

Thus concludes the *Sūtravimarśinī*, a commentary on the *Sūtrāvalī* of the venerable Utpaladeva, composed by the illustrious Rāmakaṇṭha; [and] the *Śrīvidyāpārijāta*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭārakasundarīdāsa,
who was born of a noble lineage and was the direct incarnation of Śaṅkara.

The *Kaumudī* commentary on the *Pratyabhijñā*, titled *Pratyabhijñākaumudī*, composed by the eminent Śrī Śrī Śaṅkarācārya upon the jewel-like son [of his], has been completed for the hundred-verse collection.

May there be auspiciousness for Śiva, Sambhu, Sambhunātha, and the practitioners (sādhakas), who possess the supreme authority of the mantra, in whom all the principles of the ultimate reality arise, and who are knowers of the absolute truth.
The *Pratyabhijñākaumudī*, composed by the venerable Bhaṭṭāraka, is completed.
In the year 74, on the seventh day of the dark fortnight of Śrāvaṇa, under the asterism Revatī,
the yoga Saubhāgya, the karaṇa Viṣkambha, and the conjunction Phaṭtra (?), and at the Āccika lagna, the *Pratyabhijñākaumudī* reached its completion.
[This is] the [result] of the falling of the glance of the illustrious, most illustrious Guru.
Auspicious! Auspicious! Auspicious!
Oṃ! Those goddesses who are most excellent, whose sharp intellects shine with right vision—those great-souled ones, radiant with all powers, may they be victorious! (1)
May there be auspiciousness everywhere; may there be the state of equilibrium between Śiva and Śakti.
